Understood: you want to know how the NetBird "agent-network" feature (docs.netbird.io/agent-network) integrates with the LiteLLM AI gateway. Specifically: does NetBird create groups in LiteLLM, how are budgets handled per team, and are you limited to the teams defined in the identity provider?**Short answer:** NetBird does not create groups, teams or budgets in LiteLLM. It forwards the caller's groups as request tags, and you define any LiteLLM budgets yourself. NetBird also enforces its own budgets before the request reaches LiteLLM. The sources don't map groups to LiteLLM teams.

## 1. How the integration works

- **Setup.** You add "LiteLLM Proxy" under Agent Network → Providers. You set the upstream URL of your self-hosted instance and paste a LiteLLM virtual key. NetBird stores the key server-side, so agents never hold it. A policy must then connect a source group to that provider, because nothing is allowed by default ([LiteLLM integration](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/integrations/litellm)).
- **Identity forwarded on each request.**
  - Groups are written into `metadata.tags` in the JSON body.
  - The user identity goes in the `x-litellm-end-user-id` header.
  - The proxy strips any client-supplied values first, so an app can't spoof them.
  - You can turn this off per provider with "Forward identity metadata", which is on by default ([Providers](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/providers#identity-metadata)).
- **Prerequisite.** The configured key must be a LiteLLM virtual key with `metadata.allow_client_tags: true`. Otherwise "LiteLLM silently drops the forwarded tags."

## 2. Are groups "created" in LiteLLM?

Not as groups or teams. They show up as **tags**. The NetBird docs say each NetBird IdP group is "listed as a tag passed dynamically in the request" under Experimental → Tag Management. You can see per-group spend in Usage → Tag Usage.

## 3. How budgets are handled

There are two independent layers, and both apply.

**Layer 1: NetBird (enforced first)**
- Policies can carry token and USD caps per user and/or per group over a fixed window. Windows are epoch-aligned, not sliding ([limits](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/policies/limits)).
- Global limits are account-wide ceilings that can target groups, users, or everyone ([global limits](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/global-limits)). They can only tighten what a policy allows.
- The check is `used >= cap` before the request runs. One request can therefore overshoot the cap, and the next one is blocked.

**Layer 2: LiteLLM (applied afterwards)**
- NetBird says LiteLLM "applies its own tag and end-user budgets on top."
- You create the tags in LiteLLM yourself. The `/tag/new` call takes `max_budget`, `budget_duration`, `rpm_limit` and `tpm_limit`. A request carrying any tag over its budget is rejected with HTTP 422 ([LiteLLM tag budgets](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/tag_budgets)).
- The tag name must match the NetBird group name exactly. NetBird does not push budgets into LiteLLM.
- LiteLLM counts spend for a tag from its first request, even before the tag exists. Creating the tag later with `/tag/new` resets its spend counter. Create budgeted tags before rolling out.

## 4. Are you limited to the teams in your identity provider?

Not entirely, but the sources only partly answer this.

- **Groups are the unit, not LiteLLM Teams.** Policies and limits are written against NetBird groups. For humans, those groups come from your IdP. NetBird can sync them through SCIM or the Entra, Okta, Google Workspace, JumpCloud and Keycloak connectors, or through JWT group claims.
- **IdP sync has a licensing condition.** It is in NetBird Cloud on the Team plan and above. Self-hosted needs an Enterprise Commercial License, and "the open source Community Edition does not include it" ([IdP sync](https://docs.netbird.io/manage/team/idp-sync)). The JWT-claim route is documented for self-hosted ([IdP docs](https://docs.netbird.io/selfhosted/identity-providers)), but I did not fetch that page, so I haven't confirmed its limits.
- **Autonomous agents don't need an IdP group.** Their identity is "the agent's own NetBird peer identity and the groups assigned to that peer" ([How it works](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/how-it-works#identity-and-authentication)). My inference is that you can create custom groups in NetBird for agents or cost centres that don't exist in the IdP. I did not find a page that states this explicitly for Agent Network.
- **Per-user budgets** don't need teams. They go through `x-litellm-end-user-id`, which carries the user's email, and LiteLLM end-user budgets.

## Points to check before you design around this

- **Which groups are sent.** The LiteLLM page says "Groups" are written to `metadata.tags`. The Providers page says NetBird stamps "the group that authorized the request." I could not tell whether you get all of the caller's groups or only the matching policy's group. This matters when a user is in several groups. Test it with a request and look in Tag Management.
- **Multiple tags.** LiteLLM rejects the request if any tag is over budget. A user in many groups can therefore be blocked by the tightest one.
- **Beta status.** Agent Network is in Beta, so behaviour may change.
- **Not verified.** I did not confirm whether LiteLLM tag budgets need an enterprise licence, and I found no documented mapping to LiteLLM Teams or `team_id`. If you need LiteLLM Teams, you would have to attach the team to the virtual key yourself, which gives one team per key rather than per caller.

Confidence: high on the mechanism, which comes from first-party docs for both products. Medium on the custom-group and multi-group behaviour, which are inferences.

Understood: you want to know how KServe serves models with vLLM. That covers how multiple GPUs are handled, which parallelism modes apply (tensor, data, pipeline), and how vLLM options are passed through KServe.## KServe + vLLM: GPU handling, parallelism and options

Sources are the KServe v0.20 docs, the v0.18 release blog and the runtime YAML on GitHub master. I could not fetch the vLLM parallelism pages (HTTP 429). The vLLM statements below rest on search snippets and on what the KServe docs quote from vLLM.

### 1. How KServe and vLLM fit together

KServe has two ways to serve an LLM, and they handle GPUs differently.

**InferenceService with the Hugging Face runtime** (`kserve-huggingfaceserver`)
- KServe runs a Python model server (`python -m huggingfaceserver`) with vLLM as the backend engine.
- The server exposes OpenAI-compatible routes under `openai/v1/completions`, `chat/completions`, `embeddings` and `rerank`.
- If vLLM does not support the model, KServe falls back to the plain Hugging Face backend. You can force a backend with `--backend huggingface|vllm|auto`.
- KServe picks the CUDA image if the pod requests `nvidia.com/gpu`, and the CPU image otherwise.
- Source: [Runtime Overview](https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/overview).

**LLMInferenceService** (the newer, GenAI-specific CRD, built on llm-d)
- You write the vLLM container (`vllm/vllm-openai`) and its args yourself.
- KServe adds the following around it:
  - A Gateway API route.
  - An inference scheduler that routes on KV-cache awareness and load.
  - Prefill/decode separation.
  - LeaderWorkerSet (LWS) for multi-node workloads.
- Source: [LLMInferenceService overview](https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/llmisvc/llmisvc-overview).
- The same page says an InferenceService can serve LLMs, but only for basic single-node deployments.

### 2. How multiple GPUs are handled

KServe does not parallelise anything itself. It does three things:
- It requests GPUs through Kubernetes resource limits.
- It starts the right number of pods.
- It passes the parallelism settings to vLLM, which does the actual sharding.

**Single node, several GPUs**
- Request N GPUs on one pod and set vLLM's tensor parallel size to N.
- The overview page lists `--tensor_parallel_size` among the vLLM options you can pass.
- The vLLM docs snippet says tensor parallelism is for "a model too large for a single GPU but fits on a single node with multiple GPUs".

**Multi-node with InferenceService** (`workerSpec`, `kserve-huggingfaceserver-multinode` runtime)
- KServe starts one head pod and N worker pods.
- Ray connects the pods in the YAML I fetched. The head runs `ray start --head` and workers join with `ray start --address`.
- The head then launches `python -m huggingfaceserver --tensor-parallel-size=${TENSOR_PARALLEL_SIZE} --pipeline-parallel-size=${PIPELINE_PARALLEL_SIZE}`.
- GPU arithmetic from the [multi-node guide](https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/multi-node):
  - Total GPUs = tensorParallelSize × pipelineParallelSize.
  - Ray node count = ceil(Total GPUs / `workerSpec.resources.requests.gpu`).
- Example: with TP=16, PP unset and 8 GPUs per pod, KServe internally sets PP=2 and TP=8.
- Since v0.18 you can avoid Ray. The `multinode/executor-backend` annotation on the ServingRuntime switches between `ray` (default) and `mp` (vLLM multiprocessing). In `mp` mode, the number of nodes comes from PP and GPUs per node from TP ([release blog](https://kserve.github.io/website/blog/kserve-0.18-release)).

**Restrictions on the InferenceService multi-node path**
- Standard deployment mode only.
- Autoscaling is not available (`autoscalerClass: none`).
- It needs a PVC with ReadWriteMany access, and `pvc://` is the only supported storage URI.
- There must be exactly one head pod.
- Do not mix GPU types.
- NCCL is the only supported communication backend.
- Changing the pipeline parallel size on a running service disrupts it. The docs say it "is not an autoscaling concept".

**Multi-node with LLMInferenceService**
- Setting `spec.worker` creates a LeaderWorkerSet.
- The LWS size is `data / dataLocal`.
- Autoscaling of multi-node LWS workloads is supported since v0.18, through the Workload Variant Autoscaler (WVA).

### 3. Which parallelism is used

| Type | InferenceService (HF runtime) | LLMInferenceService |
|---|---|---|
| Tensor (TP) | `workerSpec.tensorParallelSize`, or `--tensor-parallel-size` on a single node | `spec.parallelism.tensor` |
| Pipeline (PP) | `workerSpec.pipelineParallelSize` | No dedicated field in the docs I read |
| Data (DP) | Not built in. Scale by running more replicas, but multi-node services cannot autoscale. | `spec.parallelism.data` and `dataLocal` |
| Expert (EP, for MoE models) | Not documented | `spec.parallelism.expert: true` |

- **Tensor parallelism** shards each layer's weights across GPUs. It is best inside one node.
- **Pipeline parallelism** splits the model by layers across nodes.
- **Data parallelism** replicates the model to raise throughput. In LLMInferenceService it is combined with expert parallelism for MoE models such as DeepSeek-R1. In plain InferenceService it is just more replicas.
- The KServe docs state that `tensorParallelSize` and `pipelineParallelSize` do not map 1:1 to GPUs and nodes. They only control how weights and layers are split.
- Be careful with the LLMInferenceService example "data: 8, dataLocal: 4, tensor: 4". The docs describe `data` as the "total data parallel instances" and `dataLocal` as "GPUs per node", which is loosely worded. GitHub issue [#4946](https://github.com/kserve/kserve/issues/4946) reports wrong pod counts when `tensor > dataLocal`. I only saw its title in a search snippet, so I did not verify the details.

### 4. How vLLM options are handled

**InferenceService with the Hugging Face runtime**
- The runtime "supports all vLLM engine arguments". You pass them as container `args` on the model spec.
- The same parser also accepts KServe's own flags: `--model_name`, `--model_dir`, `--model_id`, `--dtype`, `--task`, `--backend`, `--max_model_len` and others.
- Common vLLM options named in the docs:
  - `--quantization`
  - `--gpu_memory_utilization`
  - `--max_model_len`
  - `--enforce_eager`
  - `--tensor_parallel_size`
- Environment variables also work. For example, CPU deployments use `VLLM_CPU_KVCACHE_SPACE` and `VLLM_CPU_OMP_THREADS_BIND`.

**Multi-node exception**
- `TENSOR_PARALLEL_SIZE` and `PIPELINE_PARALLEL_SIZE` cannot be set through environment variables. Use the `workerSpec` fields.
- The runtime script injects them as `--tensor-parallel-size` and `--pipeline-parallel-size`, and appends your own args after them (`$0 $@`).
- If you also pass your own `--tensor-parallel-size`, it conflicts with the injected one. That is my inference from the script, not something I tested.

**LLMInferenceService**
- Options go in the vLLM container's `args`, as in the docs example (`--model /mnt/models --tensor-parallel-size 4`).
- The docs example sets `--tensor-parallel-size` twice: once in `spec.parallelism.tensor` and once in the container args. I could not confirm from the docs whether the controller injects it automatically, so keep the two consistent.
- Config composition lets you share base settings. `LLMInferenceServiceConfig` objects are merged through `baseRefs`, and any field can be overridden in the service.

### 5. Practical notes
- KServe 0.18 ships vLLM v0.19.0. The docs list v0.21 as the newest release, so check which vLLM version your KServe install bundles.
- Choosing a layout:
  - Use TP only if the model fits in one node.
  - Use PP across nodes only if it does not.
  - Use replicas, or DP in LLMInferenceService, for throughput.
- Some details need checking against the vLLM docs and GitHub issues: the exact merge behaviour between `spec.parallelism` and container args, and the issue #4946 behaviour.

**Confidence:** high on the InferenceService runtime, `workerSpec` and the GPU formula (taken from the fetched YAML and docs). Medium on LLMInferenceService internals, which are an alpha-stage API and described only at a high level in the docs.

Compris : vous voulez savoir comment le routage des experts (MoE, Mixture of Experts) fonctionne lorsque le modèle est réparti sur plusieurs GPU. Cela couvre le gating, l'expert parallelism, les communications all-to-all et l'équilibrage de charge. Je fais une recherche de niveau standard avec des sources citées.Le routage lui-même ne change pas avec plusieurs GPU. Chaque token est toujours noté par le routeur, qui garde les top-k experts. Ce qui change, c'est que ces experts peuvent se trouver sur d'autres GPU, donc les activations doivent circuler entre GPU.

## 1. Routage sur un seul GPU
- Le routeur donne un score à chaque expert pour chaque token et garde les top-k. Qwen3-30B-A3B, par exemple, retient 8 experts parmi 128 (source : Daily Dose of DS).
- Le runtime groupe ensuite les assignations (token, expert, poids) par expert. C'est le *dispatch*.
- Chaque expert calcule sa matrice, souvent via un grouped GEMM.
- Le *combine* applique les poids de routage et additionne les contributions de chaque token.

## 2. Avec plusieurs GPU : l'expert parallelism (EP)
- **Répartition** : les experts sont répartis entre GPU. Dans l'exemple de la source, le GPU A porte E1 et E2, et le GPU B porte E3 et E4. Les poids des experts restent en place. Ce sont les activations des tokens et leurs métadonnées (identifiant du token, expert cible, GPU source, poids) qui voyagent.
- **Dispatch** : un token qui choisit E1 et E3 depuis le GPU A garde son assignation E1 en local. Son assignation E3 part vers le GPU B.
- **Calcul** : chaque GPU regroupe les assignations locales et reçues par expert, puis exécute ses experts.
- **Combine** : les résultats distants repartent vers le GPU source. Celui-ci rétablit l'ordre des tokens, applique les poids et additionne.
- **All-to-all** : avec beaucoup de GPU, chacun envoie à plusieurs pairs, ce qui donne un schéma all-to-all, une fois pour le dispatch et une fois pour le combine. Ce cycle se répète à chaque couche MoE.
- **Volume transféré** : au plus T × K × H × b octets pour le dispatch (T tokens, K experts par token, H dimension cachée, b octets par valeur). Les assignations restées en local ne coûtent aucune bande passade réseau.

Source pour ces points : https://blog.dailydoseofds.com/p/moe-inference-engineering-clearly

## 3. Limiter le coût de communication
- **Routage limité par nœud** : DeepSeek-V3 impose que chaque token soit envoyé à au plus M nœuds, choisis selon les meilleurs scores d'affinité. DeepSeek-V2 faisait de même avec 3 appareils au maximum. Cela évite de saturer les liens inter-nœuds (InfiniBand), plus lents que NVLink. Source : https://arxiv.org/html/2412.19437v1 et https://arxiv.org/html/2405.04434v5. Le snippet d'un site tiers indique « at most 4 nodes » pour V3, ce que je n'ai pas vérifié dans le papier.
- **Noyaux de communication spécialisés** : DeepEP propose un chemin « haut débit » pour le prefill et un chemin « faible latence » pour le decode.
- **Chevauchement** : le chevauchement calcul/communication (Dual Batch Overlap dans vLLM) masque une partie de la latence.

## 4. Équilibrage de charge
La distribution des tokens entre experts est souvent très inégale, et le GPU le plus chargé ralentit toute la couche. Il existe deux approches :
- **À l'entraînement** : DeepSeek-V3 ajoute un biais par expert à la sélection top-k, sans perte auxiliaire (« auxiliary-loss-free »). Source : https://arxiv.org/html/2412.19437v2
- **À l'inférence** : vLLM propose l'EPLB (`--enable-eplb`). Il collecte les statistiques de charge sur une fenêtre de pas (1000 par défaut) et redistribue périodiquement les experts (tous les 3000 pas par défaut). Il peut aussi répliquer des experts populaires avec `num_redundant_experts`. Le surcoût mémoire est d'environ 2,4 Go par expert redondant et par rang pour DeepSeek-V3. Source : https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/EasySteer-vllm-v1/blob/main/docs/serving/expert_parallel_deployment.md (miroir de la doc vLLM, car le site officiel a renvoyé une erreur 429).

## 5. Mise en pratique dans vLLM
- **Taille de l'EP** : `--enable-expert-parallel` donne `EP_SIZE = TP_SIZE × DP_SIZE`. Les couches d'experts sont réparties sur tous ces rangs. Pour l'attention, les poids sont répliqués si TP=1, ou shardés en TP sinon.
- **Sans ce flag**, les couches MoE sont en tensor parallelism, comme un modèle dense. Ce n'est pas de l'expert parallelism.
- **Backends all-to-all** : `--all2all-backend` accepte `allgather_reducescatter` (défaut), `deepep_high_throughput`, `deepep_low_latency` et des variantes FlashInfer pour NVLink multi-nœud.
- **Exemple de la doc** : DeepSeek-V3 sur 8 GPU avec `--data-parallel-size 8 --enable-expert-parallel`.

## Points à vérifier selon votre cas
- **Mémoire** : le EP répartit la capacité mémoire des poids, mais tous les experts doivent rester résidents. Les paramètres actifs (3,3 Md pour Qwen3-30B) ne réduisent pas la mémoire nécessaire (30,5 Md).
- **Interconnexion** : sans NVLink, l'all-to-all peut devenir le goulot d'étranglement. Si vous avez 2 GPU sur PCIe, comparez EP et TP sur votre propre trace de requêtes avant de choisir.
- **Limites de mes sources** : la page Daily Dose a été tronquée au milieu (section topologie et placement). Les performances réelles dépendent du modèle, du backend et du matériel, et je n'ai pas de benchmark vérifié.

Si vous me dites quel modèle, combien de GPU et quelle interconnexion vous utilisez, je peux préciser la configuration (EP ou TP, backend, EPLB).

Compris : you want to know how the NetBird "agent network" feature (docs.netbird.io/agent-network) integrates with the LiteLLM AI gateway. Specifically: whether NetBird creates groups in LiteLLM, how budgets are handled per team, and whether you are limited to the teams that exist in your identity provider. I'll start by reading the page.Next I'll check the policy and limits pages, plus how groups are sourced, since your IdP question depends on that.The remaining gaps are how NetBird groups are built (IdP sync versus manual) and what LiteLLM tag budgets need on its side.## Summary

NetBird does not create groups, teams or budgets in LiteLLM. It forwards the caller's identity on each request, and LiteLLM then treats that identity as tags and an end-user ID. All the budget logic stays in two separate places: NetBird policies and LiteLLM tag budgets. Groups are not limited to those from your IdP.

## How the integration works

Source: [NetBird LiteLLM integration](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/integrations/litellm) and [How It Works](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/how-it-works).

- **Setup:** you connect LiteLLM as a provider ("LiteLLM Proxy") and paste a LiteLLM virtual key. NetBird stores the key server-side. Clients call the NetBird endpoint over the tunnel and send no key.
- **Identity forwarding:** the proxy adds the caller's identity to each request. It does this by default and you can turn it off per provider ("Forward identity metadata").
  - "**Groups** are written into `metadata.tags` in the JSON body, so LiteLLM can apply tag budgets and rate limits."
  - "The **user identity** is sent in the `x-litellm-end-user-id` header."
  - The proxy strips any client-supplied value first, so callers can't spoof their identity.
- **LiteLLM key requirement:** the virtual key must have `metadata.allow_client_tags: true`. Otherwise "LiteLLM silently drops the forwarded tags."
- **Groups in LiteLLM:** they show up as tags. You can see them under Usage → Tag Usage and under Experimental → Tag Management, "where each NetBird IdP group is listed as a tag passed dynamically in the request."

## Are groups "created" in LiteLLM?

Only in the sense that tags appear dynamically from request traffic. NetBird does not call LiteLLM's `/tag/new`, and nothing in the docs says it sets budgets on those tags. LiteLLM's own docs say that to enforce a budget you create the tag with `max_budget` and `budget_duration`. Its docs also say the proxy counts spend for a tag from the first request that carries it, even before the tag exists. Creating the tag later resets that tag's spend counter. See [LiteLLM tag budgets](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/tag_budgets).

In practice you have to create a LiteLLM tag with the same name as each NetBird group, for example `Engineering`, and give it a budget. The name must match exactly, so check case.

## How budgets per team are handled

There are two independent layers, and a request must pass both.

1. **NetBird layer** ([Limits](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/policies/limits), [Global Limits](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/global-limits)):
   - A policy links source groups to providers. It can set token or USD caps per user and per group over a fixed window aligned to the Unix epoch.
   - Account-wide global limits can target groups, users, or everyone.
   - Enforcement is `used >= cap`, checked before the request. The request that crosses the cap still completes, and the next one is blocked.
   - NetBird denies with a 403.
2. **LiteLLM layer:**
   - Tag budgets (`max_budget`, `budget_duration`, rpm/tpm limits) are enforced on the forwarded tags. LiteLLM rejects with a 422 if any tag is over budget.
   - The end-user ID from `x-litellm-end-user-id` is used for per-user attribution. NetBird's docs say LiteLLM applies "tag and end-user budgets", but they don't describe how to configure end-user budgets. I didn't verify that on the LiteLLM side.

NetBird does not map groups to LiteLLM Teams, which are a separate LiteLLM concept. Team-style budgets are done through tags, so a LiteLLM "team" budget would not apply unless the virtual key itself belongs to a LiteLLM team. All requests through NetBird use the same virtual key.

## Are you limited to teams in the identity provider?

No, but IdP groups are the main source. The docs describe three sources:

- **IdP groups:**
  - They come in through [IdP sync](https://docs.netbird.io/manage/team/idp-sync) (Entra, Okta, Google Workspace, JumpCloud, Keycloak, generic SCIM) or through [JWT group sync](https://docs.netbird.io/selfhosted/identity-providers) from a claim.
  - IdP sync is not in the open-source Community Edition. It needs the Cloud Team plan or higher, or an Enterprise license for self-hosted. JWT group sync is documented as optional and I saw no edition restriction on it.
  - A group with the same name in NetBird and the IdP will not sync. You have to delete the NetBird one first.
- **Groups made in NetBird:** NetBird groups are used throughout the product, and policy source groups are NetBird groups.
- **Autonomous agents:** their identity is "the agent's own NetBird peer identity and the groups assigned to that peer." Such agents have no IdP user, so you can budget them by NetBird-only groups such as `ci-agents`.

## Open points (not confirmed in the docs)

- **Which groups get forwarded:** the LiteLLM page says the caller's groups go into `metadata.tags`. The [Providers page](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/providers#identity-metadata) says NetBird stamps "the group that authorized the request", which could be just one group, the one matching the policy. If a user is in several groups, LiteLLM may therefore see only one tag. Test with a user in two groups and check LiteLLM's Tag Usage.
- **Manual NetBird groups as tags:** I found no explicit statement that groups not from the IdP are forwarded as tags in the same way. This is probably the case for autonomous agents, but I didn't confirm it.
- **LiteLLM licensing:** I did not confirm whether tag budgets need a LiteLLM Enterprise license. A search snippet on LiteLLM's budget-routing page suggested that some tag-budget features do. Check this on your LiteLLM version.
- **Page dates:** both NetBird pages are marked Beta and carry dates in 2026, so details may change.

Confidence: high on the forwarding mechanism and the two budget layers, which come straight from the docs. Medium on multi-group and non-IdP group forwarding, and on LiteLLM licensing.

Understood: you want an explanation of how KServe serves models with vLLM. That covers how multiple GPUs are handled, which parallelism modes apply (tensor, data, pipeline), and how vLLM options are passed and handled. I'll check the current KServe and vLLM docs.Next I'll read the LLMInferenceService configuration guide and retry the vLLM parallelism page.I still need to confirm how options are passed (`args`, `VLLM_ADDITIONAL_ARGS`) and what the standalone vLLM runtime in 0.20 does.Understood: you asked how KServe and vLLM fit together, how multiple GPUs are handled, which parallelism modes are used, and how vLLM options are passed. I answered from the KServe 0.20 docs, the KServe `master` templates and the vLLM docs. This is a Standard-tier answer.

## 1. How KServe and vLLM fit together

KServe is the Kubernetes control plane. vLLM is the engine that runs inside the pod. There are three ways to use them together:

| Path | What it is | vLLM's role |
|---|---|---|
| `InferenceService` with the Hugging Face runtime (`modelFormat: huggingface`) | The KServe Python server wraps vLLM. | It is the default backend. KServe falls back to the Hugging Face backend if vLLM doesn't support the model. You can force a backend with `--backend=huggingface` or `--backend=vllm`. It exposes OpenAI-style routes under an `openai/` prefix, such as `openai/v1/chat/completions`. |
| `InferenceService` with standalone vLLM (`modelFormat: vllm`) | A dedicated runtime added in v0.20. | It is a separate runtime from the Hugging Face one. The only source I found is a docs issue (kserve/website#735), and that page is not yet written, so check the PR (kserve#4769) before relying on it. |
| `LLMInferenceService` (LLMISVC) | The newer generative-AI CRD. | The controller renders a `vllm serve ...` command from preset `LLMInferenceServiceConfig` templates. |

For LLMISVC, the workload type depends on which fields you set:
- `spec.worker` present: multi-node, run as a LeaderWorkerSet.
- `spec.prefill` present: disaggregated prefill and decode.
- Neither: a plain Deployment.

The router layer adds a Gateway, an HTTPRoute, and an InferencePool with a scheduler (EPP). The scheduler routes between replicas.

Sources:
- https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/overview
- https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/llmisvc/llmisvc-configuration

## 2. How multiple GPUs and parallelism are handled

KServe does not implement parallelism itself. It requests GPUs from Kubernetes, then passes vLLM the flags that make it shard the model.

**Tensor parallelism (TP)** splits each layer's weights across GPUs.
- vLLM recommends it when the model doesn't fit on one GPU but fits on one node. Its implementation follows Megatron-LM.
- Legacy path: set `workerSpec.tensorParallelSize`, or pass `--tensor_parallel_size`. The overview doc lists the latter as a common vLLM argument.
- LLMISVC path: `spec.parallelism.tensor`, or `--tensor-parallel-size` in args.

**Pipeline parallelism (PP)** splits the model by layers across nodes.

Compris : vous voulez savoir comment le routage des experts (MoE, Mixture of Experts) fonctionne lorsque le modèle est réparti sur plusieurs GPU, c'est-à-dire le mécanisme de gating et la façon dont les tokens sont envoyés aux experts situés sur différents GPU. Je fais une recherche de niveau standard et je livre une réponse sourcée.## Comment fonctionne le routage MoE sur plusieurs GPU

### 1. Le principe : un routeur local, des experts répartis

Dans une couche MoE, un petit réseau de routage (*gating*) calcule pour chaque token un score par expert. Il retient les top-k experts. Exemple cité par AMD : DeepSeek-R1 a 256 experts routés, dont 8 sont activés par token, plus 1 expert partagé toujours actif.

Le routage lui-même est peu coûteux et s'exécute sur le GPU qui détient le token. La difficulté vient du fait que les experts choisis peuvent se trouver sur d'autres GPU.

### 2. Expert Parallelism (EP) : répartir les experts

Avec l'EP, chaque GPU héberge un sous-ensemble d'experts complets. Pour les experts routés, le guide AMD/vLLM donne :

- `EP_SIZE = TP_SIZE × DP_SIZE`
- Experts routés par GPU = nombre total d'experts routés / `EP_SIZE`.

Exemple : 256 experts sur 8 GPU donnent 32 experts par GPU (GPU 0 : experts 0-31, GPU 1 : 32-63, etc.).

Sans EP, tous les experts sont présents sur chaque GPU, mais leurs matrices de poids sont découpées en tranches (*sharded*, façon tensor parallelism). Cela nécessite un AllReduce.

### 3. Le trajet d'un token : dispatch, calcul, combine

Avec l'EP, chaque couche MoE suit ces étapes :

1. Chaque GPU exécute le gating sur ses propres tokens et obtient les top-k experts.
2. **Dispatch** : un échange all-to-all envoie chaque token vers les GPU qui hébergent ses experts.
3. Chaque GPU calcule ses experts sur les tokens reçus.
4. **Combine** : un second all-to-all renvoie les sorties vers le GPU d'origine. Elles y sont pondérées par les scores du routeur et sommées.

Des bibliothèques dédiées implémentent ces deux étapes. DeepEP (DeepSeek) la décrit ainsi : « high-throughput and low-latency expert-parallel (EP) all-to-all GPU kernels for MoE dispatch and combine, including FP8 dispatch ». Sources : https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepEP et https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/optimizing-communication-for-mixture-of-experts-training-with-hybrid-expert-parallel/

### 4. Combinaison avec les autres parallélismes (exemple vLLM)

L'EP n'est pas une stratégie autonome. D'après le guide AMD sur vLLM (https://rocm.blogs.amd.com/software-tools-optimization/vllm-moe-guide/README.html), c'est un modificateur (`--enable-expert-parallel`) qui se combine avec TP ou DP. Il n'a d'effet que si `TP_SIZE × DP_SIZE > 1`.

- **DP + EP** (« DP attention ») : l'attention est répliquée, avec un KV cache partitionné par requête. Les experts sont répartis et la communication passe par un all-to-all (ou un gather/slice autour de la couche MoE). Le guide cite la condition du code, `use_all2all_kernels = dp_size > 1 and use_ep`.
- **TP + EP** : les experts sont répartis, mais la communication reste un AllReduce, sans all-to-all. Pour les modèles MLA (DeepSeek), le KV cache est dupliqué entièrement sur chaque GPU.
- **Sans EP** : tous les experts sont présents sur chaque GPU, avec des poids découpés en tranches et un AllReduce.

Pourquoi l'EP aide : selon le même guide, le goulot d'étranglement d'un MoE est la bande passante mémoire (chargement des poids d'experts), pas le calcul. L'EP agrège la bande passante de tous les GPU. Le coût du all-to-all est « much smaller » que ce gain, sauf pour les modèles très creux (moins de 1 % d'activation).

### 5. Contraintes de routage liées au multi-GPU

- **Coût de communication** : le all-to-all est coûteux, surtout entre nœuds. DeepSeek-V3 limite donc le nombre de GPU/nœuds que peut viser un token (*device-limited routing*). Les diapositives de présentation du rapport disent : « Individual experts are often loaded on different GPUs (expert parallelism). Communication between the GPUs is costly. » Je n'ai pas relu le rapport technique original (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.19437), seulement ce résumé.
- **Équilibrage de charge** : si trop de tokens vont vers les mêmes experts, certains GPU deviennent des points chauds et tout le groupe attend le plus lent. C'est pourquoi les modèles utilisent des mécanismes d'équilibrage. Je n'ai pas vérifié ici les détails de celui de DeepSeek-V3.
- **Experts partagés** : toujours actifs, ils sont traités comme un MLP dense. Ils sont découpés en tranches ou répliqués selon la configuration.

### 6. Choisir entre TP+EP et DP+EP

Le guide AMD mesure sur MI300X (DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-235B, Llama-4-Maverick) :

- TP+EP donne la meilleure latence à faible concurrence.
- DP+EP passe mieux à l'échelle pour le débit à forte concurrence.
- Aucune configuration n'est optimale partout. Il faut mesurer sur votre charge de travail.

### Limites

- La page de documentation vLLM officielle (`docs.vllm.ai/.../expert_parallel_deployment/`) a renvoyé une erreur HTTP 429. Je n'ai donc pas pu la lire, et les détails vLLM viennent du guide AMD.
- Les résultats de benchmark d'AMD valent pour du matériel AMD, pas forcément pour d'autres GPU.
- Je n'ai pas détaillé les fonctions de perte d'équilibrage.

Si vous voulez, je peux approfondir un point : l'équilibrage de charge, DeepEP, ou une configuration vLLM/SGLang précise pour votre nombre de GPU.

Understood: you want to know how the NetBird "agent-network" feature (docs.netbird.io/agent-network) integrates with the LiteLLM AI gateway. Specifically: whether NetBird creates groups in LiteLLM, how budgets are handled per team, and whether you are limited to the teams defined in your identity provider.**Short answer:** NetBird does not create groups, teams or budgets in LiteLLM. On every request it sends the caller's NetBird groups to LiteLLM as tags and the user's identity as the end-user ID. LiteLLM then applies whatever tag and end-user budgets you have defined there. NetBird also enforces its own per-user and per-group limits before the request reaches LiteLLM.

## 1. How the integration works

- **Setup.** You add "LiteLLM Proxy" as a provider in NetBird. The upstream URL is your self-hosted LiteLLM, and the API key is a LiteLLM virtual key that NetBird stores server-side. Not as groups or teams. They show up as tags, and only dynamically:

- They appear in LiteLLM under Usage → Tag Usage, and in Experimental → Tag Management, "where each NetBird IdP group is listed as a tag passed dynamically in the request."

Budgets are enforced in two independent layers, and a request must pass both.

**Layer 1: NetBird, before the request is forwarded.**
- Policy limits cap tokens or USD per user and per group over a fixed window. The window is epoch-aligned, not sliding. ([Limits](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/policies/limits))
- Global limits are account-wide ceilings. They can target groups, users, or everyone, and they can only tighten what a policy allows. ([Global limits](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/global-limits))
- The check is `used >= cap`, made before the request runs. One request can therefore overshoot the cap, and the next one is blocked.

- They say the groups are written into the tags. The Providers page says NetBird stamps "the group that authorized the request." - **Budget granularity.** A budget is only as fine as the NetBird groups or LiteLLM tags you define. You can create cross-cutting groups such as "project-x" or "contractors" and budget them separately.

Test it on your LiteLLM version.
- **No automatic sync.** Because NetBird doesn't create tags or budgets in LiteLLM, you have to create and maintain each tag budget in LiteLLM yourself.
- **Beta.** Agent Network is labelled Beta, so behaviour may change.

Understood: you want to know how KServe serves models with vLLM, how multiple GPUs are handled (tensor, data or pipeline parallelism), and how vLLM options are passed through KServe. I'll check the current official docs.# KServe with vLLM: architecture, multi-GPU parallelism and option handling

I checked this against the KServe 0.20 docs, the 0.18 release blog and one GitHub issue. KServe has two serving paths for vLLM, and they handle GPUs and options differently.

## 1. How KServe and vLLM fit together

KServe is the Kubernetes control plane: it creates the pods, routing, autoscaling and model download. vLLM is the inference engine inside the pod. KServe does not run any model code itself.

**Path A: `InferenceService` with the Hugging Face runtime.**
- The runtime is a Python model server with two backends, vLLM and plain Hugging Face. It falls back to Hugging Face if vLLM does not support the model.
- It exposes OpenAI-compatible endpoints under an `openai/` prefix: `openai/v1/completions`, `openai/v1/chat/completions`, `openai/v1/embeddings` and `openai/v1/rerank`.
- The image is chosen from your resource requests: a CUDA image if `nvidia.com/gpu` is requested, a CPU image otherwise.
- Source: [Runtime Overview](https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/overview).

**Path B: `LLMInferenceService` (LLMISVC), the GenAI-first CRD built on llm-d.**
- Your container runs `vllm serve` directly.
- KServe adds a Gateway API route and an inference-aware scheduler (KV-cache-aware routing).
- It supports prefill/decode separation, LoRA adapters and WVA autoscaling.
- The docs say `InferenceService` can still serve LLMs, "but only for basic single-node deployments".
- Source: [LLMInferenceService overview](https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/llmisvc/llmisvc-overview).

## 2. Multiple GPUs: which parallelism is used

All four kinds appear, depending on the path. The vLLM engine does the actual sharding. KServe only decides how many pods and GPUs exist and passes the sizes to vLLM.

**Single node, several GPUs (both paths): tensor parallelism.**
- You set vLLM's `--tensor_parallel_size`, which the docs list as "Number of GPUs to use for tensor parallelism".
- The request is `nvidia.com/gpu: N` in the resources, plus the flag.

**`InferenceService` multi-node (`workerSpec`): tensor and pipeline parallelism.**
- Source: [Multi-node/Multi-GPU Inference](https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/multi-node).
- You use the `kserve-huggingfaceserver-multinode` runtime and add `workerSpec.tensorParallelSize` and `workerSpec.pipelineParallelSize`.
- Without `workerSpec` on the InferenceService, multi-node is not enabled, even if the runtime defines it.
- The docs state the GPU arithmetic as `Total GPUs = tensorParallelSize × pipelineParallelSize`.
- Example from the docs:
  - `pipelineParallelSize: 2` with `tensorParallelSize: 8` and 8 GPUs per pod gives 2 pods and 16 GPUs.
  - This is equivalent to `vllm serve --tensor-parallel-size 8 --pipeline-parallel-size 2`.
- If you ask for TP=16 with 8 GPUs per pod, KServe rewrites it internally to PP=2 and TP=8.
- By default a Ray head pod and worker pods coordinate the nodes.
- Since v0.18, a `multinode/executor-backend` annotation on the ServingRuntime can switch from `ray` to vLLM's `mp` backend, which needs no Ray head ([0.18 release blog](https://kserve.github.io/website/blog/kserve-0.18-release)). In `mp` mode, nodes come from PP and GPUs per node from TP.
- Restrictions:
  - Standard (raw deployment) mode only.
  - A ReadWriteMany PVC is required (`pvc://` is the only storage URI).
  - Autoscaling is not available.
  - Exactly one head pod.
  - Pipeline size is "not an autoscaling concept".
  - `TENSOR_PARALLEL_SIZE` and `PIPELINE_PARALLEL_SIZE` cannot be set through environment variables.

**`LLMInferenceService`: tensor, data and expert parallelism.**
- Source: [Configuration Guide](https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/llmisvc/llmisvc-configuration).
- `spec.parallelism` has these fields:
  - `tensor` is the TP degree.
  - `data` is the total number of data-parallel instances ("replicate models for throughput").
  - `dataLocal` is the number of data-parallel instances (GPUs) per node.
  - `expert: true` enables expert parallelism for MoE models such as Mixtral and DeepSeek-R1.
  - `dataRPCPort` sets the data-parallel RPC port.
- Multi-node size is computed as `data / dataLocal`. For example, 16/8 gives a LeaderWorkerSet of size 2.
- Multi-node is built on LeaderWorkerSet, triggered by `spec.worker`.
- The docs' "Distributed Inference" feature list names only TP, DP and EP. I found no pipeline-parallel field in LLMISVC's `spec.parallelism`.
- The 0.18 blog adds LWS-based autoscaling (WVA) for multi-node LLMISVC.

**Plain replication.**
- `replicas: N` in LLMISVC, or normal InferenceService autoscaling, gives separate single-GPU pods behind a load balancer. This is data parallelism at the Kubernetes level rather than inside vLLM.

**Caveat on LLMISVC single-node parallelism.**
- In KServe v0.19, `spec.parallelism.tensor` on a single-node LLMISVC (no `spec.worker`) was silently ignored. The `vllm serve` command received no `--tensor-parallel-size`, and the second GPU sat idle while the resource reported `Ready=True` ([issue #5773](https://github.com/kserve/kserve/issues/5773)).
- A fix PR (#5782) was opened. The issue was auto-closed as stale, "not planned". I did not verify whether the fix merged.
- The working workaround is to pass `--tensor-parallel-size N` explicitly, for example in `VLLM_ADDITIONAL_ARGS`.
- The docs' own single-node examples also pass vLLM args directly.

## 3. How vLLM options are handled

**`InferenceService` (Hugging Face runtime).**
- The runtime accepts its own arguments: `--model_name`, `--model_id`, `--model_dir`, `--backend` (`auto`, `huggingface` or `vllm`), `--task`, `--dtype`, `--max_model_len` and `--trust_remote_code`, among others.
- The docs also say: "The Hugging Face runtime supports **all** vLLM engine arguments", and "vLLM backend engine arguments can also be specified on the command line and will be parsed by the Hugging Face runtime".
- You put them in the predictor container `args`, for example `--tensor_parallel_size`, `--gpu_memory_utilization`, `--quantization` or `--enforce_eager`.
- Environment variables such as `VLLM_CPU_KVCACHE_SPACE` go in `env`.
- Source: [Runtime Overview](https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/overview).

**`LLMInferenceService`.**
- You define the container yourself: `image: vllm/vllm-openai`, `args`, `env` and resources.
- The controller injects well-known preset configs, such as `kserve-config-llm-template` for single-node, and renders a `vllm serve /mnt/models ...` command.
- That command ends with `${VLLM_ADDITIONAL_ARGS} $@`. Extra vLLM flags therefore go in the `VLLM_ADDITIONAL_ARGS` env var or in container `args`.
- The preset commands and `VLLM_ADDITIONAL_ARGS` come from issue #5773. Container `args` appear in the config guide's examples.
- Presets compose through `baseRefs` (`LLMInferenceServiceConfig`), and any field in the service spec overrides them.
- Source: [Configuration Guide](https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/llmisvc/llmisvc-configuration).

**Multi-node `InferenceService`.**
- Parallel sizes must come from `workerSpec`, not environment variables or args.
- Other vLLM options go through the runtime args as above.

## Pitfalls to check on your setup

- In LLMISVC, keep `spec.parallelism` and `resources.limits.nvidia.com/gpu` consistent. They are separate fields and nothing derives one from the other (a commenter on #5773 raised this).
- Multi-node `InferenceService` needs an RWX PVC and cannot autoscale. LLMISVC's LWS path is the more actively developed route.
- vLLM's own docs recommend tensor parallelism within a node and pipeline parallelism across nodes. I only read this from the search snippet (docs.vllm.ai parallelism page), not the full page.

## Confidence and open questions

- Confidence is high on the architecture, the parallelism types, the `workerSpec` semantics and the option passthrough, because the KServe 0.20 docs state them directly.
- It is medium on the exact shell command LLMISVC renders, because that comes from a bug report against v0.19. Check the preset in your own version with `kubectl get llminferenceserviceconfig -n kserve`.
- Not verified:
  - Whether PR #5782 merged.
  - Whether the multi-node docs on the `mp` executor backend (`kserve-vllm-multinode` runtime) were updated in 0.20. Only the 0.18 blog describes it.
  - Whether a pipeline-parallel field exists in LLMISVC beyond the documented `tensor`, `data`, `dataLocal` and `expert`.
- Tell me your KServe version and whether you use `InferenceService` or `LLMInferenceService`. I can then give you an exact manifest for your GPU count.

Compris : vous voulez comprendre comment le routage des experts (MoE, Mixture of Experts) fonctionne lorsque le modèle est réparti sur plusieurs GPU. Je vérifie cela dans des sources de référence.Je lis la documentation vLLM, qui est la source de référence, et un article d'explication.La page vLLM a renvoyé une erreur 429. Je tente le miroir GitHub de la même documentation.Compris : vous demandez comment le routage des experts d'un modèle MoE (Mixture of Experts) se déroule quand les experts sont répartis sur plusieurs GPU.

## Réponse courte

Le routeur ne change pas avec le nombre de GPU. Il reste une petite couche qui note les experts, token par token et couche par couche. Ce qui change avec plusieurs GPU, c'est l'endroit où se trouve l'expert choisi. Si cet expert est sur un autre GPU, le token doit y être envoyé, puis le résultat doit revenir.

Ce mécanisme s'appelle l'expert parallelism (EP). La source principale est un article d'ingénierie de Daily Dose of Data Science (sept. 2026) et la documentation vLLM sur le déploiement EP. La page officielle vLLM a renvoyé une erreur 429. J'ai donc lu un miroir GitHub (fork EasySteer-vllm-v1), dont la version peut différer légèrement de la documentation actuelle.

## Déroulement pour une couche MoE

1. **Routage local.** Chaque GPU possède ses propres tokens. Le routeur calcule un score pour chaque expert. Un top-k garde les experts sélectionnés et leurs poids. Exemple cité : Qwen3-30B-A3B choisit 8 experts parmi 128 par token, sur 48 couches.
2. **Dispatch (envoi).** Les assignations token-expert sont regroupées par GPU de destination. Dans l'exemple de l'article, GPU A possède E1 et E2, GPU B possède E3 et E4. Un token sur A qui choisit E1 et E3 garde son assignation E1 sur A. L'assignation E3 part vers B. Chaque envoi contient le vecteur du token et des métadonnées : identifiant du token, expert cible, GPU source, poids de routage. Avec de nombreux GPU, chacun envoie à plusieurs pairs, ce qui donne un schéma **all-to-all**.
3. **Calcul des experts.** Chaque GPU regroupe les assignations locales et reçues par expert. Il exécute une matrice par expert actif, souvent avec un grouped GEMM (plusieurs matrices en un seul lancement de noyau).
4. **Combine (retour).** Les résultats repartent vers le GPU source. Celui-ci remet les tokens dans l'ordre, applique les poids de routage et somme les contributions des experts sélectionnés.

Ce sont les activations des tokens qui circulent, pas les poids des experts, qui restent en place. Ce schéma se répète à chaque couche MoE. Un petit délai de dispatch s'accumule donc sur tout le modèle (source : article Daily Dose of Data Science).

## Combinaison avec les autres parallélismes (vLLM)

- Avec `--enable-expert-parallel`, la taille EP vaut `EP_SIZE = TP_SIZE × DP_SIZE`.
- Les couches d'experts sont réparties sur tous les rangs EP. L'attention est répliquée entre les rangs DP si TP=1. Si TP>1, elle est répartie en tensor parallelism à l'intérieur de chaque groupe DP.
- Exemple de la documentation : TP=2 et DP=4 sur 8 GPU donnent un groupe EP de taille 8 pour les experts, et TP=2 dans chacun des 4 groupes DP pour l'attention.
- Sans EP, les couches MoE utilisent le tensor parallelism, comme un modèle dense.
- Le backend de communication se choisit avec `--all2all-backend` :
  - `allgather_reducescatter` est le défaut, généraliste.
  - `deepep_high_throughput` convient au prefill multi-nœuds.
  - `deepep_low_latency` convient au decode multi-nœuds.
  - Deux backends FlashInfer ciblent les systèmes NVLink multi-nœuds.

## Le problème principal : le déséquilibre de charge

- Si un expert reçoit beaucoup de tokens, le GPU qui l'héberge devient le goulot d'étranglement de toute la couche. La documentation vLLM le dit ainsi : « the distribution of tokens across experts can be highly skewed ».
- vLLM propose l'EPLB (`--enable-eplb`). Il collecte des statistiques de charge, puis redistribue périodiquement les experts entre les rangs. Valeurs par défaut : fenêtre de 1000 pas, rééquilibrage tous les 3000 pas.
- `num_redundant_experts` permet de dupliquer les experts populaires. Le coût mémoire est d'environ 2,4 Go par expert redondant et par rang pour DeepSeek-V3.
- À l'entraînement, une loss auxiliaire d'équilibrage et une capacité maximale par expert (avec abandon ou débordement des tokens en excès) limitent le déséquilibre. Je n'ai lu que les extraits de recherche sur ce point (papier Switch Transformer, arXiv 2101.03961, et un billet Hugging Face), pas les pages complètes.

## Points de vigilance

- **La topologie compte.** Les transferts entre serveurs (InfiniBand ou Ethernet) coûtent davantage qu'au sein d'un serveur (NVLink ou NVSwitch). Le placement des experts détermine la fréquence des traversées de liens lents.
- **La mémoire reste celle du modèle entier.** Pour Qwen3-30B-A3B, 30,5 milliards de paramètres sont résidents, même si seulement 3,3 milliards sont actifs par token. L'EP répartit ces poids sur les GPU.
- **Le trafic de dispatch peut être estimé.** Sa borne haute vaut T × K × H × b : tokens × experts par token × largeur cachée × octets par valeur.
- **Le decode est pénalisé.** Avec peu de requêtes, chaque expert reçoit une ou deux lignes. Le coût de communication et de lancement des noyaux domine alors le calcul.
- **Les DeepEP kernels sont optimisés pour le serving désagrégé.** La documentation précise qu'ils peuvent être peu performants en charge mixte.
- **Un recouvrement est possible.** `--enable-dbo` (Dual Batch Overlap) recouvre l'all-to-all avec le calcul.

Je n'ai pas vérifié les implémentations hors vLLM, comme Megatron-LM, DeepSpeed-MoE ou SGLang. Les principes sont les mêmes, mais les options diffèrent. Si vous me dites quel framework ou quel modèle vous utilisez, je peux préciser la configuration.

Sources :
- https://blog.dailydoseofds.com/p/moe-inference-engineering-clearly
- https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/EasySteer-vllm-v1/blob/main/docs/serving/expert_parallel_deployment.md (miroir de https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/serving/expert_parallel_deployment/)
- https://arxiv.org/pdf/2101.03961 (extrait de recherche uniquement)

answer:
Understood: you want to know how the NetBird "agent-network" feature (docs.netbird.io/agent-network) integrates with the LiteLLM AI gateway. Specifically: whether NetBird creates groups or teams in LiteLLM, how budgets are handled per team, and whether you are limited to the teams that exist in your identity provider.## Short answer

- NetBird does not create groups or teams in LiteLLM. It forwards the caller's groups as request tags, and LiteLLM uses its tag features to track and cap spend.
- Per-team budgets can be enforced in two places: NetBird policy limits and LiteLLM tag budgets.
- You are not limited to teams from your identity provider (IdP), although IdP sync is the usual source of groups.

## How the integration works

You connect LiteLLM in NetBird as a provider (type "LiteLLM Proxy"). You give NetBird the upstream URL and a LiteLLM virtual key, which NetBird stores server-side. Agents call the NetBird endpoint with no key. A policy must connect a source group to the provider, because by default nothing is allowed ([LiteLLM integration](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/integrations/litellm)).

For each request, NetBird adds the caller's identity before forwarding it to LiteLLM:
- **Groups:** "Groups are written into `metadata.tags` in the JSON body, so LiteLLM can apply tag budgets and rate limits."
- **User:** the identity is sent in the `x-litellm-end-user-id` header. The proxy strips any client-supplied value first, so an app can't spoof it.
- **Opt-out:** you can switch this off per provider with "Forward identity metadata".
- **Required key setting:** the virtual key must have `metadata.allow_client_tags: true`, "otherwise LiteLLM silently drops the forwarded tags."

On the LiteLLM side, each NetBird group shows up as a tag. The page says every forwarded group is listed under Experimental → Tag Management "as a tag passed dynamically in the request". Spend per group appears under Usage → Tag Usage.

## How budgets are handled per team

Budgets are enforced in two layers, in this order ([How it works](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/how-it-works)):

1. **NetBird, before the request reaches LiteLLM.**
   - Account-wide ceilings are checked first.
   - Then policy limits apply: tokens or USD, per user and/or per group, over a fixed window ([limits](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/policies/limits)).
   - Windows are fixed buckets aligned to the Unix epoch, not sliding.
   - The check is `used >= cap` before the request runs, so one request can overshoot the cap and the next is blocked.
   - If several policies match, NetBird attributes the request to the one with uncapped or larger remaining budget.
2. **LiteLLM, on top.** You create tags named after your groups, for example `POST /tag/new` with `name`, `max_budget`, `budget_duration`, `rpm_limit` and `tpm_limit` ([LiteLLM tag budgets](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/tag_budgets)). A request carrying several tags is rejected if any one of them is over budget.

Consequences:
- **Multiple groups:** a user in several groups carries several tags, so the tightest exhausted tag blocks them. This follows from "If any tag exceeds its budget, the request will be rejected". Design group overlap with that in mind.
- **Teams are not populated:** NetBird authenticates to LiteLLM with one stored virtual key. I found no documentation of NetBird creating LiteLLM Teams or mapping users to them. This is my inference: LiteLLM team and key budgets would apply to all NetBird traffic together, so per-group budgeting should use tags.
- **Tag budgets are not created automatically:** the docs only say groups appear as tags. I found nothing saying NetBird creates budgeted tags. You would create `max_budget` on a tag with the same name as the group. LiteLLM's baggage-mapping section says a tag's spend is counted from the first request, and creating the tag later resets its counter. I did not confirm that this applies to `metadata.tags` as well.
- **LiteLLM bug:** there was a bug where tag budgets were silently skipped when tags came via the `x-litellm-tags` header ([issue #27480](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/27480)). It is closed. NetBird uses the body path, which that issue says worked, but pin and test your LiteLLM version.

## Are you limited to IdP teams?

No, with two qualifications.

- **Where groups come from:** policies are written against NetBird groups. For humans, the identity "is tied to your identity provider… so the request carries that user and the groups they belong to". For autonomous agents, "the identity is the agent's own NetBird peer identity and the groups assigned to that peer". Agents therefore get groups from NetBird, not from the IdP.
- **IdP sync is optional and licensed:** it works via the Google Workspace and Entra ID APIs, or via SCIM (Entra, Okta, JumpCloud, Keycloak and generic SCIM). It is available on NetBird Cloud Team plan and above, and on self-hosted with an Enterprise Commercial License, not in the open-source Community Edition ([IdP sync](https://docs.netbird.io/manage/team/idp-sync)).
- **Manual groups:** I did not fetch a page confirming that you can create groups by hand for human users and map them to LiteLLM tags. NetBird groups are generally manageable in NetBird itself, but verify it on your edition.

## Open points

- **Beta status:** Agent Network is labelled Beta, so behaviour may change.
- **Group name format:** the exact format of forwarded tag strings (any prefix, special characters or case handling) is not documented in the pages I read. Check Tag Management after a test call.
- **Tag budget testing:** test that a LiteLLM tag budget actually blocks a NetBird-forwarded group before relying on it.

Understood: you want to know how KServe and vLLM work together. Specifically, you want to know how multiple GPUs are handled, which parallelism modes are used (tensor, data, pipeline), and how vLLM options are passed and handled. I'll treat this as a standard research question and check the official docs.## Verdict

KServe does not parallelise anything itself. It is the Kubernetes control plane (pods, GPU requests, routing, autoscaling). vLLM does all the GPU parallelism inside the pods. KServe only passes the parallelism settings through to vLLM, and how it does that differs between its two APIs.

## 1. How KServe and vLLM fit together

There are two ways to run vLLM under KServe (docs v0.20).

- **`InferenceService` with the Hugging Face runtime.**
  - This is a Python model server that uses vLLM as its backend. The docs say it "uses `vLLM` backend engine" and exposes OpenAI-compatible endpoints under an `openai/` prefix, such as `openai/v1/chat/completions`.
  - If vLLM does not support the model architecture, it falls back to the plain Hugging Face backend.
  - Source: [Runtime Overview](https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/overview).
  - I read the server code in the repo: `__main__.py` and `vllm/utils.py`. It checks whether vLLM supports the model, then adds vLLM's own CLI parser to the server's parser (`make_arg_parser`).
  - Engine arguments are built with `AsyncEngineArgs.from_cli_args(args)`.
- **`LLMInferenceService` (the newer GenAI CRD).**
  - It is built on llm-d and runs a plain `vllm/vllm-openai` container.

Compris : vous voulez savoir comment le routage des experts (MoE, Mixture of Experts) fonctionne quand le modèle est réparti sur plusieurs GPU. Cela couvre le parallélisme d'experts, les échanges all-to-all et l'équilibrage de charge. Je cherche des sources de référence.# Routage MoE sur plusieurs GPU

**En bref.** Le routeur (gating) est une petite couche linéaire qui choisit, pour chaque token, les top-k experts. Avec plusieurs GPU, la question devient où se trouvent ces experts et comment les tokens les rejoignent. La réponse dépend du mode de parallélisme, pas du routeur.

## 1. Étapes de base

1. Chaque GPU calcule l'attention, puis passe ses tokens locaux dans le routeur. Celui-ci produit des scores par expert et retient les top-k. Exemple de la doc Megatron : `--moe-router-topk 2` avec 8 experts.
2. **Expert Parallelism (EP).** Les experts sont répartis entre les GPU. Selon la doc Megatron-Core, chaque worker traite « one or more experts for each MoE layer ».
3. **Dispatch (all-to-all).** Chaque token est envoyé au GPU qui héberge son ou ses experts. Megatron l'active avec `--moe-token-dispatcher-type alltoall`. Les tokens sont d'abord permutés, c'est-à-dire regroupés par expert de destination.
4. Chaque GPU calcule ses experts locaux, avec un GroupedGEMM quand il y a plusieurs experts locaux.
5. **Combine (all-to-all inverse).** Les sorties reviennent au GPU d'origine. Elles y sont dépermutées, puis sommées pondérées par les scores du routeur.

Les deux all-to-all par couche MoE sont le coût principal. Megatron recommande donc de garder EP×TP dans le domaine NVLink. Il propose aussi DeepEP pour un dispatch et un combine efficaces, ainsi que le recouvrement entre communication et calcul.

## 2. Équilibrage de charge

Si le routeur envoie trop de tokens vers quelques experts, les GPU qui les hébergent ralentissent tous les autres. Megatron-Core propose plusieurs mécanismes (même source) :

- Une perte auxiliaire d'équilibrage (`--moe-router-load-balancing-type aux_loss`, avec `--moe-aux-loss-coeff 1e-2` dans l'exemple).
- Sinkhorn.
- Un équilibrage sans perte auxiliaire, à la manière de DeepSeek-V3.
- Un routage limité par nœud (node-limited routing), qui réduit le trafic inter-nœuds.
- Un *capacity factor* : `capacity = num_tokens_per_rank * topk * capacity_factor / num_experts`. Les tokens au-delà de la capacité sont abandonnés avant l'échange entre rangs EP. Par défaut, le mode est *dropless*, sans abandon.

## 3. En inférence avec vLLM

Source : article AMD ROCm sur vLLM (24 nov. 2025). Je n'ai pas pu lire la page officielle vLLM, qui a renvoyé une erreur HTTP 429.

- **EP n'est pas une stratégie autonome.** C'est un drapeau, `--enable-expert-parallel`, à combiner avec TP ou DP. Il n'a d'effet que si `TP_SIZE × DP_SIZE > 1`.
- **Sans EP**, tous les experts sont présents sur chaque GPU, mais leurs poids sont découpés (sharded), avec un AllReduce.
- **Avec EP**, chaque GPU détient des experts complets. Avec 256 experts routés et 8 GPU, cela donne 32 experts par GPU. La formule est `EP_SIZE = TP_SIZE × DP_SIZE`.
- **L'all-to-all n'apparaît qu'avec DP+EP.** Le code cité est `use_all2all_kernels = dp_size > 1 and use_ep`. Avec TP+EP, la communication reste un AllReduce.
- **Experts partagés.** Ils sont toujours actifs, sans routage, et traités comme un MLP dense.
- **Compromis (benchmarks AMD sur MI300X).**
  - TP+EP donne une meilleure latence à faible concurrence. L'article mesure 52 % de débit en plus que DP+EP à 64-128 requêtes.
  - DP+EP passe mieux à l'échelle en débit.
  - Pour les modèles MLA comme DeepSeek, DP+EP évite la duplication du cache KV sur tous les rangs TP.

## 4. Points à vérifier

- Activer `--enable-expert-parallel` ne produit pas toujours un vrai routage inter-GPU par all-to-all. Avec TP seul, le comportement est proche du mode sans EP.
- Le gain de l'EP vient surtout de la bande passante mémoire cumulée pour charger les poids des experts. L'article AMD indique que cela vaut pour la plupart des modèles, sauf les modèles très creux (moins de 1 % d'activation).
- Les chiffres de performance viennent d'un seul fournisseur (AMD) et de matériel MI300X. Ils ne sont pas forcément transposables à d'autres GPU.

## Sources

- NVIDIA Megatron-Core, Mixture of Experts : https://docs.nvidia.com/megatron-core/developer-guide/0.15.0/api-guide/moe.html
- AMD ROCm, *The vLLM MoE Playbook* : https://rocm.blogs.amd.com/software-tools-optimization/vllm-moe-guide/README.html
- Non lue (erreur 429) : https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/serving/expert_parallel_deployment/

Je peux détailler un cadre précis (entraînement avec Megatron, inférence vLLM ou SGLang, multi-nœuds avec DeepEP) si vous voulez.

Understood: you want to know how the NetBird "agent-network" feature integrates with the LiteLLM AI gateway. Specifically, you're asking whether NetBird creates groups in LiteLLM, how budgets are handled per team, and whether you're limited to teams from the identity provider.## Short answer

- NetBird does not create groups, teams or budgets in LiteLLM. It forwards the caller's groups with each request as LiteLLM tags.
- LiteLLM tags are not LiteLLM Teams. The NetBird docs only describe tags (`metadata.tags`) and the end-user ID.
- Per-team budgets can be set in two places: NetBird policy limits, and LiteLLM tag budgets that you create yourself.
- You are not limited to groups that come from your identity provider.

## How the integration works

NetBird sits in front of a self-hosted LiteLLM. You add LiteLLM as a provider, using the upstream URL and a LiteLLM virtual key. NetBird stores that key server-side. A NetBird policy then connects source groups to that provider. ([LiteLLM integration](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/integrations/litellm))

On each request, NetBird identifies the caller from the WireGuard tunnel, so the client holds no key. It then adds identity to the upstream request:

> "**Groups** are written into `metadata.tags` in the JSON body, so LiteLLM can apply tag budgets and rate limits. The **user identity** is sent in the `x-litellm-end-user-id` header."

The proxy removes any client-supplied value first, so a caller cannot spoof its identity. You can switch this off per provider with "Forward identity metadata", which is on by default. The virtual key must have `metadata.allow_client_tags: true`. Otherwise "LiteLLM silently drops the forwarded tags."

## Does NetBird create groups in LiteLLM?

No. NetBird sends group names as tags on each call, and LiteLLM registers them dynamically. They appear in the UI under Experimental → Tag Management as "tag[s] passed dynamically in the request". They also appear in Usage → Tag Usage with their own spend overview. ([source](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/integrations/litellm))

Nothing in the docs says NetBird creates LiteLLM tag objects, budgets, teams or keys. I found no sync from NetBird into LiteLLM.

## How budgets work per team

Budgets are enforced at two layers, in this order ([How It Works](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/how-it-works)):

Confidence is high on the mechanics: tags in the body, the end-user header, no group creation, and the two budget layers. These come from the NetBird and LiteLLM docs I read.

Still unverified:
- Whether manual NetBird groups work as source groups. I did not find an explicit statement.
- How LiteLLM handles a tag that has no existing tag record, for budget enforcement.
- How group names containing special characters or spaces are handled as tags.

Understood: you want an explanation of how KServe serves models with vLLM, how multiple GPUs are handled (tensor, data or pipeline parallelism), and how vLLM options are passed and handled. I'll treat this as a standard research question and verify it against the current KServe and vLLM docs.**Bottom line:** KServe does not run inference. It deploys and routes to a vLLM server, and vLLM does the parallelism. Multi-GPU behaviour depends on which KServe resource you use, and the two paths behave differently.

## 1. How KServe and vLLM fit together

KServe has two ways to run vLLM:

| | `InferenceService` + Hugging Face runtime | `LLMInferenceService` (newer, GenAI-focused) |
|---|---|---|
| Role of vLLM | The Hugging Face runtime server uses vLLM as its backend. It falls back to the plain Hugging Face backend if vLLM doesn't support the model. | You supply a vLLM image (e.g. `vllm/vllm-openai`) and KServe renders the `vllm serve` command. |
| Extras | OpenAI-compatible endpoints under the `openai/` prefix (`openai/v1/completions`, `openai/v1/chat/completions`, embeddings, rerank). | Gateway API routing, an inference-aware scheduler (KV-cache-aware routing), prefill/decode separation, LeaderWorkerSet for multi-node. It is built on llm-d. |
| Scope | KServe's docs say `InferenceService` is for predictive AI, but it can still serve LLMs "only for basic single-node deployments". | Multi-GPU, multi-node and disaggregated serving. |

Sources: [Runtime overview](https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/overview), [LLMInferenceService overview](https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/llmisvc/llmisvc-overview).

KServe v0.18 ships vLLM v0.19.0 ([v0.18 release notes](https://kserve.github.io/website/blog/kserve-0.18-release)).

## 2. How multiple GPUs are handled

All three kinds of parallelism exist, but they sit in different places.

**Single node, one pod with several GPUs (InferenceService):**
- You request `nvidia.com/gpu: N` on the container.
- You enable tensor parallelism yourself with vLLM's `--tensor_parallel_size`, which the docs list as a frequently used vLLM argument.
- KServe does not infer it from the GPU count.

**Multi-node on InferenceService (`workerSpec`, multi-node runtime):**
- **Tensor parallelism:** `workerSpec.tensorParallelSize` shards the weights across GPUs.
- **Pipeline parallelism:** `workerSpec.pipelineParallelSize` splits the layers across stages.
- **GPU count:** KServe computes total GPUs as `tensorParallelSize × pipelineParallelSize`.
- **Pod layout:** it derives the number of pods from `workerSpec.resources.requests.gpu`.
- **Rewrite:** if you ask for TP=16 with 8 GPUs per pod, KServe rewrites it internally to PP=2 × TP=8.
- **Ray head pod:** historically, coordination goes through a Ray head pod, and you must have exactly one.
- **No Ray (v0.18):** a `multinode/executor-backend` annotation on the ServingRuntime switches between `ray` (default) and `mp`. In `mp` mode, the number of nodes comes from PP and the GPUs per node from TP.
- **Restrictions:** the docs list these.
  - Standard (raw Deployment) mode only.
  - No autoscaling.
  - A ReadWriteMany PVC as the only storage option.
  - NCCL only.
  - `TENSOR_PARALLEL_SIZE` and `PIPELINE_PARALLEL_SIZE` cannot be set through environment variables.
  - Do not change PP in production, because it is "not an autoscaling concept".

**`LLMInferenceService` (`spec.parallelism`):**
- **Fields:** `tensor`, `data`, `dataLocal` and `expert: true`. There is no pipeline field in the docs I fetched, only tensor, data and expert.
- **Multi-node sizing:** `spec.worker` triggers a LeaderWorkerSet, and its size is `data / dataLocal`. For example, `data: 16` with `dataLocal: 8` gives 2 nodes.
- **Use cases:** data parallelism for throughput, and data plus expert parallelism for MoE models such as Mixtral and DeepSeek-R1.
- **Replicas versus data parallelism:** `replicas` are independent replicas of the whole workload. `parallelism.data` is vLLM-level data parallelism inside one multi-node group.
- **Pipeline parallelism:** whether it is configurable here is unverified. A bug report ([#5773](https://github.com/kserve/kserve/issues/5773)) refers to "spec.parallelism (tensor/pipeline)", but the docs I fetched list only tensor, data and expert.
- **Autoscaling:** v0.18 allows LeaderWorkerSet as a scaling target for multi-node workloads.

**Pitfall (known bug, KServe v0.19):**
- On a single-node `LLMInferenceService`, with no `spec.worker`, setting `spec.parallelism.tensor: 2` is silently ignored.
- The rendered `vllm serve` command has no `--tensor-parallel-size`, so vLLM runs on one GPU and the resource still reports `Ready=True`.
- The reporter's workaround was to pass `--tensor-parallel-size 2` through `VLLM_ADDITIONAL_ARGS`.
- A fix PR (#5782) was opened, but the issue was auto-closed as stale and I did not verify that the fix merged. Check `nvidia-smi` or the vLLM logs on your version.

## 3. How vLLM options are handled

- **InferenceService, Hugging Face runtime:**
  - Runtime arguments such as `--model_name`, `--model_id`, `--backend` (`auto`, `huggingface` or `vllm`), `--dtype`, `--max_model_len` and `--task` go in the container `args`.
  - The docs state the runtime supports all vLLM engine arguments, which are parsed by the runtime from the same command line.
  - Common examples are `--quantization`, `--tensor_parallel_size`, `--gpu_memory_utilization`, `--max_model_len` and `--enforce_eager`.
  - CPU tuning uses environment variables such as `VLLM_CPU_KVCACHE_SPACE` and `VLLM_CPU_OMP_THREADS_BIND`.
- **Multi-node runtime:** TP and PP must come from `workerSpec`, not from env vars or args.
- **LLMInferenceService:**
  - Options go in `spec.template.containers[].args` or in an env var such as `VLLM_ADDITIONAL_ARGS`, which the issue shows is appended to the generated `vllm serve` command.
  - The documented single-node example passes `--model /mnt/models` as args. The multi-node example adds `--tensor-parallel-size`.
  - Defaults come from preset `LLMInferenceServiceConfig` resources, which are merged with your spec ("config composition"). These are listed in `status.appliedConfigs`.
  - Typed fields like `spec.parallelism` are templated into the command only for the multi-node configs.

## Recommendations

- **Model fits on one GPU:** run several replicas, using `replicas` or data parallelism.
- **Model needs several GPUs on one node:** use tensor parallelism and pass `--tensor-parallel-size` explicitly via args.
- **Model needs several nodes:** use pipeline parallelism across nodes, with tensor parallelism inside each node.

## Gaps and confidence

- Confidence is high for the KServe-side behaviour, which is read directly from the KServe 0.20 docs, the v0.18 release notes and the issue.
- I could not fetch the vLLM parallelism docs (HTTP 429). The vLLM-side statements about TP, PP and DP come from KServe's docs and search snippets, not from a vLLM page I read.
- Unchecked: the actual `kserve-vllm-multinode` ServingRuntime YAML, and whether `LLMInferenceService` has a pipeline field.
- If you tell me your KServe version and GPU topology, I can narrow this to a concrete manifest.

answer:
Compris : vous voulez savoir comment le routage des experts (MoE, Mixture of Experts) fonctionne lorsque le modèle est réparti sur plusieurs GPU, c'est-à-dire l'expert parallelism, les communications all-to-all et l'équilibrage de charge. Le livrable est une explication sourcée.# Routage MoE sur plusieurs GPU

En pratique, le routeur (une petite couche linéaire + top-k) tourne sur chaque GPU. Les experts sont répartis entre les GPU, et les tokens sont envoyés aux experts par un échange all-to-all.

## 1. Principe : le parallélisme d'experts (EP)

- Chaque couche MoE contient E experts (des FFN). Un routeur léger note chaque token contre ces E experts et retient les top-k. Source : [arXiv 2605.20982](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.20982v1).
- Avec l'EP, « different experts are distributed, in whole, across different GPUs. This introduces all-to-all communication as tokens are routed to their GPUs » ([G. Klockwood, expert parallelism](https://www.glennklockwood.com/garden/expert-parallelism)).
- Un expert n'est donc pas découpé entre les GPU. Il réside en entier sur un seul GPU. C'est la différence avec le parallélisme tensoriel (TP).
- Tous les experts doivent rester en mémoire GPU, même s'ils ne sont pas tous actifs pour chaque token (même source).

## 2. Déroulement d'une couche MoE

La séquence suivante est décrite par NVIDIA pour Hybrid-EP ([NVIDIA, 2 fév. 2026](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/optimizing-communication-for-mixture-of-experts-training-with-hybrid-expert-parallel/)) :

1. **Attention**, puis **routage local**. Chaque GPU calcule, pour ses propres tokens, les top-k experts et construit une carte de routage.
2. **Dispatch** : le terme désigne l'opérateur qui « routes the tokens output by the attention operator to the corresponding experts », via un all-to-all. Seuls les tokens nécessaires sont transmis (« to avoid transmitting unwanted token data »).
3. **Calcul des experts** : chaque GPU applique les experts qu'il héberge aux tokens reçus.
4. **Combine** : il renvoie les sorties des experts vers l'attention d'origine. Les contributions des k experts sont accumulées (pondérées par les scores du routeur). Cette accumulation est hiérarchique : d'abord dans le nœud, puis entre nœuds.

En inférence, une configuration courante est « Attention Data Parallel + MoE Expert Parallel » : chaque GPU traite une partie des requêtes pour l'attention, puis les tokens sont échangés pour les experts ([TensorRT-LLM blog](https://nvidia.github.io/TensorRT-LLM/1.3.0rc19/blogs/tech_blog/blog18_Optimizing_MoE_Communication_with_One_Sided_AlltoAll_Over_NVLink.html), d'après l'extrait de recherche, non fetché).

## 3. Coût de communication

Le trafic inter-GPU croît avec le nombre de tokens, la dimension cachée et le nombre d'experts. Klockwood chiffre le cas DeepSeek-V3 (d=7168, 256 experts routés, 8 actifs, 4096 tokens) :

- environ 468 Mo envoyés et 468 Mo reçus par GPU et par couche ;
- environ 54 Go de trafic all-to-all par passe avant, pour 58 couches MoE.

Ces chiffres sont un calcul théorique de l'auteur, pas une mesure.

NVIDIA indique que, sur DeepSeek-V3, la communication peut dépasser 50 % du temps d'entraînement sans optimisation.

## 4. Limiter le trafic : routage limité aux nœuds

DeepSeek-V3 contraint le routage : « the routed experts will be uniformly deployed on 64 GPUs belonging to 8 nodes. As for the node-limited routing, each token will be sent to at most 4 nodes (M=4) » ([DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.19437v2)).

Le lien inter-nœuds (InfiniBand) est le facteur limitant. Au sein d'un nœud, le NVLink est plus rapide (Klockwood). Les bibliothèques comme DeepEP ou Hybrid-EP combinent les deux niveaux : NVLink en intra-nœud, RDMA en inter-nœuds.

## 5. Déséquilibre de charge

- Le routage dynamique crée des « hot experts » qui reçoivent plus de tokens que la moyenne. Les GPU qui les hébergent deviennent des goulots, et les autres attendent (NVIDIA, même article).

  - `window_size` (1000) est le nombre de pas observés.
  - `step_interval` (3000) est la fréquence du rééquilibrage.

- Je n'ai pas traité les alternatives à l'EP pur, comme le TP appliqué aux experts, ni les contraintes de capacité des experts (token dropping) en entraînement.

Si vous me donnez votre matériel (nombre de GPU, NVLink ou PCIe) et le modèle visé (Mixtral, Qwen3-MoE, DeepSeek), je peux préciser la configuration recommandée.

En pratique, le routeur (une petite couche linéaire + top-k) tourne sur chaque GPU. Les experts sont répartis entre les GPU, et les tokens sont envoyés aux experts par un échange all-to-all.

## 1. Principe : le parallélisme d'experts (EP)

- Chaque couche MoE contient E experts (des FFN). Un routeur léger note chaque token contre ces E experts et retient les top-k. Source : [arXiv 2605.20982](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.20982v1).
- Avec l'EP, « different experts are distributed, in whole, across different GPUs. This introduces all-to-all communication as tokens are routed to their GPUs » ([G. Klockwood, expert parallelism](https://www.glennklockwood.com/garden/expert-parallelism)).
- Un expert n'est donc pas découpé entre les GPU. Il réside en entier sur un seul GPU. C'est la différence avec le parallélisme tensoriel (TP).
- Tous les experts doivent rester en mémoire GPU, même s'ils ne sont pas tous actifs pour chaque token (même source).

## 2. Déroulement d'une couche MoE

La séquence suivante est décrite par NVIDIA pour Hybrid-EP ([NVIDIA, 2 fév. 2026](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/optimizing-communication-for-mixture-of-experts-training-with-hybrid-expert-parallel/)) :
