2. **Dispatch** : le terme désigne l'opérateur qui « routes the tokens output by the attention operator to the corresponding experts », via un all-to-all. Seuls les tokens nécessaires sont transmis (« to avoid transmitting unwanted token data »).
3. **Calcul des experts** : chaque GPU applique les experts qu'il héberge aux tokens reçus.
4. **Combine** : il renvoie les sorties des experts vers l'attention d'origine. Les contributions des k experts sont accumulées (pondérées par les scores du routeur). Cette accumulation est hiérarchique : d'abord dans le nœud, puis entre nœuds.

En inférence, une configuration courante est « Attention Data Parallel + MoE Expert Parallel » : chaque GPU traite une partie des requêtes pour l'attention, puis les tokens sont échangés pour les experts ([TensorRT-LLM blog](https://nvidia.github.io/TensorRT-LLM/1.3.0rc19/blogs/tech_blog/blog18_Optimizing_MoE_Communication_with_One_Sided_AlltoAll_Over_NVLink.html), d'après l'extrait de recherche, non fetché).

- environ 468 Mo envoyés et 468 Mo reçus par GPU et par couche ;
- environ 54 Go de trafic all-to-all par passe avant, pour 58 couches MoE.

NVIDIA indique que, sur DeepSeek-V3, la communication peut dépasser 50 % du temps d'entraînement sans optimisation.

DeepSeek-V3 contraint le routage : « the routed experts will be uniformly deployed on 64 GPUs belonging to 8 nodes. As for the node-limited routing, each token will be sent to at most 4 nodes (M=4) » ([DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.19437v2)).

answer:
Understood: you want to know how the NetBird "agent-network" feature (docs.netbird.io/agent-network) integrates with the LiteLLM AI gateway. Specifically, you're asking whether NetBird creates groups in LiteLLM, how budgets are handled per team, and whether teams are limited to those in the identity provider.**Short answer:** NetBird doesn't create anything in LiteLLM. It forwards the caller's identity, and LiteLLM turns the groups into tags, not teams. Budgets can be set in both products. Groups are not limited to the IdP.

## Integration
- You add LiteLLM in NetBird as a provider ("LiteLLM Proxy"). The upstream URL is your self-hosted instance, and you paste a LiteLLM virtual key that NetBird stores server-side. Agents call the NetBird endpoint with no key. ([LiteLLM integration](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/integrations/litellm))
- The NetBird proxy adds the caller's identity to each request:
  - "**Groups** are written into `metadata.tags` in the JSON body, so LiteLLM can apply tag budgets and rate limits."
  - "The **user identity** is sent in the `x-litellm-end-user-id` header."
- The proxy strips any client-supplied value first, so apps can't spoof their identity. Forwarding is on by default. You can turn it off with the provider's "Forward identity metadata" toggle. ([How it works](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/how-it-works))
- The virtual key must have `metadata.allow_client_tags: true`. Otherwise "LiteLLM silently drops the forwarded tags."

## Are groups "created" in LiteLLM?
- No LiteLLM teams are created or synced.
- The groups appear as tags passed dynamically in the request. You can see them under **Experimental → Tag Management** and in **Usage → Tag Usage**, which gives spend and requests per group.
- The docs don't mention LiteLLM Teams or Organizations. If you want budgets on LiteLLM teams, nothing in these docs maps NetBird groups to them. That is my reading of the docs, not something they state.

## Budgets per team
There are two layers, and a request has to pass both.

1. **NetBird policy limits**, enforced first:
   - A policy connects a source group to the LiteLLM provider.
   - You can set token and USD caps per user and per group, over a fixed window.
   - The window is aligned to the Unix epoch, not sliding.
   - The check is `used >= cap` before the request runs, so one request can overshoot the cap. The next one is blocked.
   - Account-wide caps (Global Limits) are checked before any policy.
   - A request is attributed to one policy, chosen among the matching ones. Uncapped policies and larger remaining budgets are preferred.
   - Sources: [limits](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/policies/limits), [how it works](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/how-it-works).
2. **LiteLLM's own budgets**, applied after NetBird: "NetBird enforces your policies, limits, and guardrails first, then LiteLLM applies its own tag and end-user budgets on top." In LiteLLM you set a budget on a tag whose name matches the NetBird group, plus end-user budgets keyed on the email.

A user in several groups sends all of them as tags. I did not check how LiteLLM combines budgets when several tags match one request. Test that before relying on it.

## Limited to the IdP's teams?
No, based on the docs:
- For humans, groups come from the IdP. NetBird can sync them by JWT claim or SCIM ([IdP sync](https://docs.netbird.io/manage/team/idp-sync)).
- For autonomous agents, the identity is "the agent's own NetBird peer identity and the groups assigned to that peer." Those are NetBird groups, so they don't need to exist in the IdP.
- NetBird's own groups can be used in policies and are forwarded as tags. I did not find a page that says explicitly whether NetBird-only groups, as opposed to IdP-synced ones, are forwarded in `metadata.tags`. The how-it-works page does say the request carries "group membership", so I expect they are. Confirm it with a test or in the Agent Network docs.

## Caveats
- Agent Network is in Beta.
- I did not read LiteLLM's own documentation on tag budgets. The LiteLLM-side behaviour above comes from NetBird's docs.

answer:
Understood: you want to know how KServe serves models with vLLM, how multiple GPUs are handled (tensor, data or pipeline parallelism), and how vLLM options are passed and handled. This is a multi-part factual question, so I'll research it in one pass using the official docs.## Summary

KServe doesn't run models itself. It deploys a container that runs vLLM and wraps it with Kubernetes plumbing (pods, GPUs, routing, storage). Multi-GPU parallelism is vLLM's job, and KServe mostly decides how many pods and GPUs to give it and which flags to pass. The behaviour differs between the classic `InferenceService` and the newer `LLMInferenceService`, so I cover both.

## 1. How KServe and vLLM fit together

- **Hugging Face serving runtime.** The `InferenceService` (ISVC) uses the Hugging Face runtime. It "uses `vLLM` backend engine" and exposes OpenAI-compatible endpoints: completions, chat, embeddings and rerank. Routes are prefixed with `openai/`, for example `openai/v1/chat/completions`. (Source: [Runtime Overview](https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/overview))
- **Backend fallback.** "If a model is not supported by the vLLM engine, KServe automatically falls back to the standard Hugging Face backend". `--backend auto|huggingface|vllm` controls this.
- **Image selection.** If the ISVC requests `nvidia.com/gpu`, KServe picks the CUDA image. Otherwise it uses the CPU image.
- **Versions.** KServe v0.18 ships vLLM v0.19.0. (Source: [KServe 0.18 release](https://kserve.github.io/website/blog/kserve-0.18-release))
- **LLMInferenceService (newer CRD).** This is the GenAI-first resource, `serving.kserve.io/v1alpha2`. It adds a router (Gateway API), an llm-d scheduler, prefill/decode disaggregation and LeaderWorkerSet-based multi-node workloads. (Sources: the 0.18 blog above and [LLMInferenceService configuration guide](https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/llmisvc/llmisvc-configuration))

## 2. How multiple GPUs and parallelism are handled

All three forms of parallelism exist, but they are not available everywhere.

| Parallelism | Classic ISVC (HF/vLLM runtime) | LLMInferenceService |
|---|---|---|
| Tensor (TP) | Yes | Yes (`parallelism.tensor`) |
| Pipeline (PP) | Yes, multi-node only | The Go types include it; I found no documented example (see the note below) |
| Data (DP) | No, except by adding replicas | Yes (`data`, `dataLocal`) |
| Expert (EP, for MoE models) | No | Yes (`expert: true`) |

### Classic InferenceService

**Single node.** You request GPUs in `resources` and pass vLLM's `--tensor_parallel_size` as an argument. The runtime overview lists it as a frequently used vLLM option: "Number of GPUs to use for tensor parallelism". Its OOM advice says "Enable tensor parallelism if using multiple GPUs". vLLM's own guidance is that if the model fits on one node, use TP. For example, `tensor_parallel_size=4` on a 4-GPU node. (Source: [vLLM parallelism docs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vllm-project/vllm/main/docs/serving/parallelism_scaling.md))

**Multi-node.** You add a `workerSpec` and use the `kserve-huggingfaceserver-multinode` runtime. Restrictions from the [KServe multi-node guide](https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/multi-node):
- Standard (raw deployment) mode only.
- No autoscaling: the autoscaler class must be `none`.
- A ReadWriteMany PVC is required, and `storageUri` must be `pvc://`.
- NCCL only.
- Exactly one head pod.

```yaml
spec:
  predictor:
    model:
      runtime: kserve-huggingfaceserver-multinode
      modelFormat: {name: huggingface}
      storageUri: pvc://llama-3-8b-pvc/hf/8b_instruction_tuned
    workerSpec:
      pipelineParallelSize: 2
      tensorParallelSize: 1
```

- **GPU math.** Total GPUs = TP × PP. The number of Ray nodes is `ceil(Total GPUs / workerSpec.resources.requests.gpu)`.
- **Mapping.** TP shards the weights across GPUs, and PP splits the layers. The doc says these do not map 1:1 to GPUs or nodes. The vLLM convention is TP = GPUs per node and PP = number of nodes, for example TP=8, PP=2 on 2×8 GPUs.
- **Auto-adjustment.** If you ask for `tensorParallelSize=16` with 8 GPUs per pod, KServe internally rewrites it to PP=2, TP=8.
- **Env vars not allowed.** `TENSOR_PARALLEL_SIZE` and `PIPELINE_PARALLEL_SIZE` cannot be set as environment variables. They must go through `workerSpec`. The runtime defaults for both are 1 and can be overridden by the ISVC.
- **Ray or no Ray.** By default the multi-node runtime uses Ray, with one head pod and worker pods. KServe v0.18 adds a `multinode/executor-backend` annotation on the ServingRuntime to switch between `ray` (default) and `mp` (vLLM multiprocessing, no Ray). In `mp` mode, nodes come from PP and GPUs per node from TP.
- **PP is not for scaling.** The docs warn that "PipelineParallelSize is not an autoscaling concept" and shouldn't be changed in production. Changing PP or TP means recreating the service.

### LLMInferenceService

Parallelism is declarative:

```yaml
spec:
  replicas: 2
  parallelism:
    tensor: 4      # TP
    data: 8        # total DP ranks
    dataLocal: 4   # DP ranks (GPUs) per node
    expert: true   # EP, for MoE models
```

- **Layout.** The multi-node size is `data / dataLocal` (16/8 = 2 nodes). It is deployed as a LeaderWorkerSet, which treats the pods spanning nodes as one unit. A separate `prefill` workload enables prefill/decode disaggregation through llm-d.
- **Scaling.** Since v0.18, LeaderWorkerSet can be an autoscaling target, so whole multi-node replica groups scale up and down together.
- **Pipeline parallelism.** A secondary source says the Go types add `pipeline` and `dataLocal`. I did not find it documented in the config guide.

**Single-node caveat.** [Issue #5773](https://github.com/kserve/kserve/issues/5773), reported against v0.19, says `spec.parallelism.tensor` is silently ignored when there is no `spec.worker`. The rendered `vllm serve` gets no `--tensor-parallel-size`, and the resource still reports `Ready=True`. The workaround is to put `--tensor-parallel-size 2` in `VLLM_ADDITIONAL_ARGS`. The issue was closed as stale and "not planned". A fix PR (#5782) was opened, and I did not verify whether it was merged. Check your KServe version before relying on `parallelism.tensor` on a single node.

**Plain replicas.** For simple data parallelism, run more replicas of the same model. Each replica holds a full copy and the router or autoscaler balances across them.

## 3. How vLLM options are handled

**Classic ISVC.** The Hugging Face runtime takes its own arguments (`--model_name`, `--model_id`, `--model_dir`, `--dtype`, `--task`, `--backend`, `--max_model_len`, `--trust_remote_code` and so on). It also says it "supports **all** vLLM engine arguments", which you "pass directly" on the command line. In the docs, `--quantization`, `--tensor_parallel_size`, `--gpu_memory_utilization`, `--max_model_len` and `--enforce_eager` are given as examples. In practice this means `args:` on the container in the ISVC or the ServingRuntime. The ServingRuntime holds defaults, and the ISVC can override them. I did not fetch a full `args` example page, so that exact YAML form is my inference from these statements.

**Environment variables.** vLLM environment variables such as `VLLM_CPU_KVCACHE_SPACE` and `VLLM_CPU_OMP_THREADS_BIND` go in `env`. KServe also sets defaults such as `SAFETENSORS_FAST_GPU` and `KSERVE_OPENAI_ROUTE_PREFIX`.

**Exceptions.** Parallel sizes in multi-node mode must go through `workerSpec`, not env vars or flags. The controller injects `PIPELINE_PARALLEL_SIZE`, `TENSOR_PARALLEL_SIZE` and `WORKER_SVC` into worker containers in `mp` mode.

**LLMInferenceService.** The container command is a rendered `vllm serve` template. The template fills in model name, port and parallelism from the spec. Everything else goes through `VLLM_ADDITIONAL_ARGS` (for example `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 --max-model-len 8192`) or the container args, as in the issue's manifest.

## Confidence and gaps

- **Confidence.** High on the multi-node ISVC mechanics, `workerSpec` and the TP/PP/DP/EP split. Medium on the exact way args are passed in the ISVC, which is inferred.
- **vLLM docs.** The vLLM `docs.vllm.ai` pages returned HTTP 429. I read vLLM's parallelism guide from its raw GitHub source instead, and did not read the dedicated data-parallel deployment page.
- **Version gaps.** I did not check which KServe version first shipped each feature. The multi-node page is the 0.20 docs, the release blog is 0.18, and the issue is against 0.19.
- **Not covered.** Whether the `mp` backend applies to the Hugging Face multinode runtime or to a separate `kserve-vllm-multinode` runtime. The 0.18 blog example uses `kserve-vllm-multinode`.

(Source: [Runtime Overview](https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/overview))
- **Backend fallback.** "If a model is not supported by the vLLM engine, KServe automatically falls back to the standard Hugging Face backend". `--backend auto|huggingface|vllm` controls this.
- **Image selection.** If the ISVC requests `nvidia.com/gpu`, KServe picks the CUDA image. Otherwise it uses the CPU image.
- **Versions.** KServe v0.18 ships vLLM v0.19.0. (Source: [KServe 0.18 release](https://kserve.github.io/website/blog/kserve-0.18-release))
- **LLMInferenceService (newer CRD).** This is the GenAI-first resource, `serving.kserve.io/v1alpha2`. It adds a router (Gateway API), an llm-d scheduler, prefill/decode disaggregation and LeaderWorkerSet-based multi-node workloads. (Sources: the 0.18 blog above and [LLMInferenceService configuration guide](https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/llmisvc/llmisvc-configuration))

## 2. How multiple GPUs and parallelism are handled

All three forms of parallelism exist, but they are not available everywhere.

| Parallelism | Classic ISVC (HF/vLLM runtime) | LLMInferenceService |
|---|---|---|
| Tensor (TP) | Yes | Yes (`parallelism.tensor`) |
| Pipeline (PP) | Yes, multi-node only | The Go types include it; I found no documented example (see the note below) |
| Data (DP) | No, except by adding replicas | Yes (`data`, `dataLocal`) |
| Expert (EP, for MoE models) | No | Yes (`expert: true`) |

### Classic InferenceService

**Single node.** You request GPUs in `resources` and pass vLLM's `--tensor_parallel_size` as an argument. The runtime overview lists it as a frequently used vLLM option: "Number of GPUs to use for tensor parallelism". Its OOM advice says "Enable tensor parallelism if using multiple GPUs". vLLM's own guidance is that if the model fits on one node, use TP. For example, `tensor_parallel_size=4` on a 4-GPU node. (Source: [vLLM parallelism docs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vllm-project/vllm/main/docs/serving/parallelism_scaling.md))

**Multi-node.** You add a `workerSpec` and use the `kserve-huggingfaceserver-multinode` runtime. Restrictions from the [KServe multi-node guide](https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/multi-node):
- Standard (raw deployment) mode only.
- No autoscaling: the autoscaler class must be `none`.
- A ReadWriteMany PVC is required, and `storageUri` must be `pvc://`.
- NCCL only.
- Exactly one head pod.

```yaml
spec:
  predictor:
    model:
      runtime: kserve-huggingfaceserver-multinode
      modelFormat: {name: huggingface}
      storageUri: pvc://llama-3-8b-pvc/hf/8b_instruction_tuned
    workerSpec:
      pipelineParallelSize: 2
      tensorParallelSize: 1
```

- **GPU math.** Total GPUs = TP × PP. The number of Ray nodes is `ceil(Total GPUs / workerSpec.resources.requests.gpu)`.
- **Mapping.** TP shards the weights across GPUs, and PP splits the layers. The doc says these do not map 1:1 to GPUs or nodes. The vLLM convention is TP = GPUs per node and PP = number of nodes, for example TP=8, PP=2 on 2×8 GPUs.
- **Auto-adjustment.** If you ask for `tensorParallelSize=16` with 8 GPUs per pod, KServe internally rewrites it to PP=2, TP=8.
- **Env vars not allowed.** `TENSOR_PARALLEL_SIZE` and `PIPELINE_PARALLEL_SIZE` cannot be set as environment variables. They must go through `workerSpec`. The runtime defaults for both are 1 and can be overridden by the ISVC.
- **Ray or no Ray.** By default the multi-node runtime uses Ray, with one head pod and worker pods. KServe v0.18 adds a `multinode/executor-backend` annotation on the ServingRuntime to switch between `ray` (default) and `mp` (vLLM multiprocessing, no Ray). In `mp` mode, nodes come from PP and GPUs per node from TP.
- **PP is not for scaling.** The docs warn that "PipelineParallelSize is not an autoscaling concept" and shouldn't be changed in production. Changing PP or TP means recreating the service.

### LLMInferenceService

Parallelism is declarative:

```yaml
spec:
  replicas: 2
  parallelism:
    tensor: 4      # TP
    data: 8        # total DP ranks
    dataLocal: 4   # DP ranks (GPUs) per node
    expert: true   # EP, for MoE models
```

- **Layout.** The multi-node size is `data / dataLocal` (16/8 = 2 nodes). It is deployed as a LeaderWorkerSet, which treats the pods spanning nodes as one unit. A separate `prefill` workload enables prefill/decode disaggregation through llm-d.
- **Scaling.** Since v0.18, LeaderWorkerSet can be an autoscaling target, so whole multi-node replica groups scale up and down together.
- **Pipeline parallelism.** A secondary source says the Go types add `pipeline` and `dataLocal`. I did not find it documented in the config guide.

**Single-node caveat.** [Issue #5773](https://github.com/kserve/kserve/issues/5773), reported against v0.19, says `spec.parallelism.tensor` is silently ignored when there is no `spec.worker`. The rendered `vllm serve` gets no `--tensor-parallel-size`, and the resource still reports `Ready=True`. The workaround is to put `--tensor-parallel-size 2` in `VLLM_ADDITIONAL_ARGS`. The issue was closed as stale and "not planned". A fix PR (#5782) was opened, and I did not verify whether it was merged. Check your KServe version before relying on `parallelism.tensor` on a single node.

**Plain replicas.** For simple data parallelism, run more replicas of the same model. Each replica holds a full copy and the router or autoscaler balances across them.

## 3. How vLLM options are handled

**Classic ISVC.** The Hugging Face runtime takes its own arguments (`--model_name`, `--model_id`, `--model_dir`, `--dtype`, `--task`, `--backend`, `--max_model_len`, `--trust_remote_code` and so on). It also says it "supports **all** vLLM engine arguments", which you "pass directly" on the command line. In the docs, `--quantization`, `--tensor_parallel_size`, `--gpu_memory_utilization`, `--max_model_len` and `--enforce_eager` are given as examples. In practice this means `args:` on the container in the ISVC or the ServingRuntime. The ServingRuntime holds defaults, and the ISVC can override them. I did not fetch a full `args` example page, so that exact YAML form is my inference from these statements.

**Environment variables.** vLLM environment variables such as `VLLM_CPU_KVCACHE_SPACE` and `VLLM_CPU_OMP_THREADS_BIND` go in `env`. KServe also sets defaults such as `SAFETENSORS_FAST_GPU` and `KSERVE_OPENAI_ROUTE_PREFIX`.

**Exceptions.** Parallel sizes in multi-node mode must go through `workerSpec`, not env vars or flags. The controller injects `PIPELINE_PARALLEL_SIZE`, `TENSOR_PARALLEL_SIZE` and `WORKER_SVC` into worker containers in `mp` mode.

**LLMInferenceService.** The container command is a rendered `vllm serve` template. The template fills in model name, port and parallelism from the spec. Everything else goes through `VLLM_ADDITIONAL_ARGS` (for example `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 --max-model-len 8192`) or the container args, as in the issue's manifest.

## Confidence and gaps

- **Confidence.** High on the multi-node ISVC mechanics, `workerSpec` and the TP/PP/DP/EP split. Medium on the exact way args are passed in the ISVC, which is inferred.
- **vLLM docs.** The vLLM `docs.vllm.ai` pages returned HTTP 429. I read vLLM's parallelism guide from its raw GitHub source instead, and did not read the dedicated data-parallel deployment page.
- **Version gaps.** I did not check which KServe version first shipped each feature. The multi-node page is the 0.20 docs, the release blog is 0.18, and the issue is against 0.19.
- **Not covered.** Whether the `mp` backend applies to the Hugging Face multinode runtime or to a separate `kserve-vllm-multinode` runtime. The 0.18 blog example uses `kserve-vllm-multinode`.

Compris : vous voulez savoir comment le routage des experts (MoE, Mixture of Experts) fonctionne lorsque le modèle est réparti sur plusieurs GPU (expert parallelism, communication all-to-all, équilibrage de charge, etc.).## Routage MoE sur plusieurs GPU

**Principe général.** Le routage (le *router*, ou *gate*) est le même qu'avec un seul GPU. Un petit réseau note chaque token face aux E experts, puis l'envoie vers ses top-k experts (résumé de la source arXiv [2605.20982](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.20982v1)). Le multi-GPU ajoute une question: où se trouvent physiquement les experts choisis, et comment les tokens y arrivent.

### 1. Deux façons de répartir les experts (source: [guide vLLM MoE d'AMD](https://rocm.blogs.amd.com/software-tools-optimization/vllm-moe-guide/README.html))

| Mode | Placement des experts | Communication |
|---|---|---|
| **Experts « sharded »** (sans `--enable-expert-parallel`) | Tous les experts sont sur chaque GPU, mais leurs matrices sont découpées entre les GPU. Exemple du guide: 256 experts et TP=8, soit 8 morceaux par expert. | AllReduce |
| **Experts « split »** (avec Expert Parallelism, EP) | Chaque GPU détient des experts complets. Exemple du guide: 256 experts sur 8 GPU, donc 32 experts par GPU (GPU 0: experts 0-31, GPU 1: 32-63, etc.). | AllToAll (avec DP>1) ou AllReduce (DP=1) |

La formule donnée dans le guide est `EP_SIZE = TP_SIZE × DP_SIZE`, puis `experts routés par GPU = total / EP_SIZE`.

### 2. Déroulé d'une couche MoE avec EP
Le guide vLLM ne détaille pas ces étapes une à une. Elles reprennent l'architecture que décrit Megatron-Core (router, token dispatcher, experts, avec « token permutation / unpermutation »):
1. Chaque GPU traite son propre lot de tokens, avec l'attention répliquée ou découpée.
2. Le router calcule les top-k experts de chaque token.
3. **Dispatch**: les tokens sont regroupés par expert de destination, puis envoyés aux GPU qui les hébergent par un **AllToAll**.
4. Chaque GPU applique ses experts locaux aux tokens reçus.
5. **Combine**: un second AllToAll renvoie les sorties vers les GPU d'origine, où elles sont dépermutées. Elles sont ensuite pondérées par les scores du router et sommées.

### 3. Pourquoi faire de l'EP
Selon le guide AMD, ce sont les lectures mémoire des poids d'experts qui limitent la latence, plus que le calcul. Avec 8 GPU en EP, on cumule 8 fois la bande passante mémoire pour charger les experts. Le coût de l'AllToAll est « much smaller » que ce gain pour la plupart des modèles. Le guide cite une exception: les modèles ultra-creux, avec moins de 1 % d'activation.

### 4. Précisions sur vLLM (même source)
- **L'EP n'est pas une stratégie autonome.** C'est un drapeau qui change la communication MoE. Il ne prend effet que si `TP_SIZE × DP_SIZE > 1`.
- **TP+EP n'utilise pas d'AllToAll.** Dans le code vLLM, `use_all2all_kernels` vaut `dp_size > 1 and use_ep`. Seul DP+EP (« DP attention ») déclenche l'AllToAll.
- **Experts partagés** (comme le 1 expert partagé de DeepSeek-R1): ils sont toujours actifs et ne passent pas par le router. Ils sont traités comme un MLP dense.

### 5. Équilibrage de charge
Le router peut envoyer trop de tokens vers quelques experts. Le GPU qui les héberge ralentit alors tous les autres, car l'AllToAll synchronise l'ensemble.
- **À l'entraînement** (Megatron-Core): perte auxiliaire d'équilibrage, Sinkhorn, ou équilibrage sans perte auxiliaire. Côté dispatch, soit « dropless », soit abandon de tokens avec ou sans padding à la capacité (*capacity factor*).
- **À l'inférence** (vLLM): l'EPLB (*Expert Parallel Load Balancer*) redistribue les experts entre les rangs EP. D'après le snippet de la documentation vLLM, il sert à « even the load across experts ». Un test publié sur jarvislabs.ai montre qu'il peut ajouter de la latence au premier token.
- **Multi-nœuds**: Megatron-Core propose DeepEP (dispatch inter-nœuds) et HybridEP (intra-nœud).

### Limites de cette réponse
- La page de la documentation vLLM sur le déploiement EP a renvoyé une erreur HTTP 429. Je n'ai donc pas lu ses détails sur l'EPLB.
- Le déroulé en 5 étapes reste générique. Les implémentations varient (backends all2all, DeepEP, etc.).
- Je n'ai pas vérifié les performances chiffrées, qui dépendent du modèle et du matériel.

Si vous me dites quel cadre vous intéresse (vLLM, Megatron, DeepSpeed) et votre topologie GPU, je peux préciser la configuration.

**Sources**
- [Guide vLLM MoE d'AMD (ROCm)](https://rocm.blogs.amd.com/software-tools-optimization/vllm-moe-guide/README.html)
- [Megatron-Core MoE (NVIDIA)](https://docs.nvidia.com/megatron-core/developer-guide/0.15.0/api-guide/moe.html)
- [vLLM Expert Parallel Deployment](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/serving/expert_parallel_deployment/): snippet de recherche seulement
- [arXiv 2605.20982](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.20982v1): snippet de recherche seulement
- [Jarvislabs: EP et stratégies mixtes dans vLLM](https://jarvislabs.ai/blog/expert-parallelism-mixed-strategies-vllm): snippet de recherche seulement

Understood: you want to know how the NetBird "agent-network" feature (docs.netbird.io/agent-network) integrates with the LiteLLM AI gateway. Specifically: whether NetBird creates groups in LiteLLM, how budgets are handled per team, and whether teams are limited to those in the identity provider. I'll check the docs first.## Short answers

- **Groups in LiteLLM:** NetBird does not create groups, teams or tag objects in LiteLLM. It sends the caller's groups with each request as tags, and LiteLLM picks them up dynamically.
- **Budgets:** Budgets are enforced in two independent places. NetBird applies per-user and per-group caps from its policies. LiteLLM then applies its own tag budgets and end-user budgets. You create the LiteLLM budgets yourself.
- **IdP limit:** You are not strictly limited to IdP teams, but the group-based attribution is only as good as your group hygiene. Details are below.

## How the integration works

You add LiteLLM in NetBird as a provider (Agent Network → Providers → LiteLLM Proxy). You give it the upstream URL and a LiteLLM virtual key, which NetBird stores server-side. A NetBird policy then connects a source group to that provider. Agents call the NetBird endpoint with no key. ([LiteLLM integration](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/integrations/litellm))

For each request, NetBird maps the caller's identity onto it like this:

- **Groups:** written into `metadata.tags` in the JSON body, "so LiteLLM can apply tag budgets and rate limits".
- **User:** sent in the `x-litellm-end-user-id` header. The screenshot caption says this carries the user's email.
- **Spoofing:** the proxy strips any client-supplied values first.
- **Virtual key requirement:** the key must be a LiteLLM virtual key with `metadata.allow_client_tags: true`, "otherwise LiteLLM silently drops the forwarded tags".
- **Opt-out:** the "Forward identity metadata" toggle on the provider is on by default and can be turned off. ([Providers](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/providers#identity-metadata))

In LiteLLM, the forwarded groups appear under Usage → Tag Usage and under Experimental → Tag Management as "a tag passed dynamically in the request". ([source](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/integrations/litellm))

## How budgets work per team

**1. NetBird layer (enforced before the request reaches LiteLLM)**
- A policy can cap tokens and spend per user and per group over a fixed window. Windows are aligned to the Unix epoch, not sliding. ([Limits](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/policies/limits))
- Enforcement is `used >= cap`, checked before the request runs. One request can therefore overshoot the cap, and the next one is blocked.
- Account-wide ceilings are checked first. ([How it works](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/how-it-works))

**2. LiteLLM layer**
- The NetBird docs say LiteLLM then applies "its own tag and end-user budgets on top".
- The budget itself must be defined in LiteLLM. Create a tag whose name matches the NetBird group name exactly, with `max_budget`, `budget_duration` and optionally `rpm_limit` and `tpm_limit`, through `/tag/new` or the Tag Management page. ([LiteLLM tag budgets](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/tag_budgets))
- If a request carries several tags, which is the case when the user is in several groups, "if any tag exceeds its budget, the request will be rejected". A user in `Engineering` and `Contractors` is blocked when either tag is exhausted.
- These are LiteLLM Tags, not LiteLLM Teams. Team-level features in LiteLLM (team keys, team budgets, team members) are not populated by this integration. I found no documentation saying NetBird maps groups to LiteLLM Teams.

## Are you limited to IdP teams?

- **No hard limit in the LiteLLM integration.** NetBird sends the caller's NetBird group membership. For a human user that is tied to the IdP. For an autonomous agent, "the identity is the agent's own NetBird peer identity and the groups assigned to that peer". Such agents therefore get groups assigned in NetBird, not from the IdP. ([How it works](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/how-it-works#identity-and-authentication))
- **IdP group sync is a licensing question.**
  - IdP-Sync, which provisions users and groups through SCIM or the Entra ID and Google APIs, is available on NetBird Cloud Team plan and above, and in self-hosted deployments only with an Enterprise Commercial License. The Community Edition does not include it. ([IdP sync](https://docs.netbird.io/manage/team/idp-sync))
  - Search results also mention JWT group sync, which reads groups from a token claim, and I did not verify its availability by edition. ([Identity providers](https://docs.netbird.io/selfhosted/identity-providers))
- **Group names must match.** A tag only gets a budget if the LiteLLM tag name matches the group name. Renaming a group in the IdP or NetBird silently produces a new, unbudgeted tag.

## Caveats and open questions

- **Manual groups.** The LiteLLM page speaks of "IdP groups", while the architecture page says "the caller's groups". I did not find an explicit statement that manually created NetBird groups are also forwarded. Test this with a manual group and check Tag Management.
- **Unbudgeted tags.** I did not verify what LiteLLM does with a tag that has no budget defined. Spend is tracked but nothing is capped. The doc's own example for baggage-mapped tags says spend is tracked "whether or not the tag has a budget".
- **Spend reset on tag creation.** For tags created after traffic started, LiteLLM documents that `/tag/new` resets the counter. That text is in the baggage-mapping section, so it may not apply to tags sent in `metadata.tags`. Create the budgeted tags before rollout.
- **Beta.** Agent Network is labelled Beta. Behaviour may change.
- **Tag budget rejection code.** Tag budget rejections are HTTP 422 in LiteLLM, while NetBird denials are 403. Your clients and monitoring need to handle both.

## Practical recommendation

Use NetBird policy limits for hard per-group and per-user cost control, since that is enforced at the edge, in USD or tokens. Pre-create matching tags in LiteLLM only if you want LiteLLM-side budgets or reporting. Keep group names stable and make sure users do not belong to overlapping groups with conflicting budgets.

- **Opt-out:** the "Forward identity metadata" toggle on the provider is on by default and can be turned off. ([Providers](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/providers#identity-metadata))

In LiteLLM, the forwarded groups appear under Usage → Tag Usage and under Experimental → Tag Management as "a tag passed dynamically in the request". ([source](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/integrations/litellm))

## How budgets work per team

**1. NetBird layer (enforced before the request reaches LiteLLM)**
- A policy can cap tokens and spend per user and per group over a fixed window. Windows are aligned to the Unix epoch, not sliding. ([Limits](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/policies/limits))
- Enforcement is `used >= cap`, checked before the request runs. One request can therefore overshoot the cap, and the next one is blocked.
- Account-wide ceilings are checked first. ([How it works](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/how-it-works))

**2. LiteLLM layer**
- The NetBird docs say LiteLLM then applies "its own tag and end-user budgets on top".
- The budget itself must be defined in LiteLLM. Create a tag whose name matches the NetBird group name exactly, with `max_budget`, `budget_duration` and optionally `rpm_limit` and `tpm_limit`, through `/tag/new` or the Tag Management page. ([LiteLLM tag budgets](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/tag_budgets))
- If a request carries several tags, which is the case when the user is in several groups, "if any tag exceeds its budget, the request will be rejected". A user in `Engineering` and `Contractors` is blocked when either tag is exhausted.
- These are LiteLLM Tags, not LiteLLM Teams. Team-level features in LiteLLM (team keys, team budgets, team members) are not populated by this integration. I found no documentation saying NetBird maps groups to LiteLLM Teams.

## Are you limited to IdP teams?

- **No hard limit in the LiteLLM integration.** NetBird sends the caller's NetBird group membership. For a human user that is tied to the IdP. For an autonomous agent, "the identity is the agent's own NetBird peer identity and the groups assigned to that peer". Such agents therefore get groups assigned in NetBird, not from the IdP. ([How it works](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/how-it-works#identity-and-authentication))
- **IdP group sync is a licensing question.**
  - IdP-Sync, which provisions users and groups through SCIM or the Entra ID and Google APIs, is available on NetBird Cloud Team plan and above, and in self-hosted deployments only with an Enterprise Commercial License. The Community Edition does not include it. ([IdP sync](https://docs.netbird.io/manage/team/idp-sync))
  - Search results also mention JWT group sync, which reads groups from a token claim, and I did not verify its availability by edition. ([Identity providers](https://docs.netbird.io/selfhosted/identity-providers))
- **Group names must match.** A tag only gets a budget if the LiteLLM tag name matches the group name. Renaming a group in the IdP or NetBird silently produces a new, unbudgeted tag.

## Caveats and open questions

- **Manual groups.** The LiteLLM page speaks of "IdP groups", while the architecture page says "the caller's groups". I did not find an explicit statement that manually created NetBird groups are also forwarded. Test this with a manual group and check Tag Management.
- **Unbudgeted tags.** I did not verify what LiteLLM does with a tag that has no budget defined. Spend is tracked but nothing is capped. The doc's own example for baggage-mapped tags says spend is tracked "whether or not the tag has a budget".
- **Spend reset on tag creation.** For tags created after traffic started, LiteLLM documents that `/tag/new` resets the counter. That text is in the baggage-mapping section, so it may not apply to tags sent in `metadata.tags`. Create the budgeted tags before rollout.
- **Beta.** Agent Network is labelled Beta. Behaviour may change.
- **Tag budget rejection code.** Tag budget rejections are HTTP 422 in LiteLLM, while NetBird denials are 403. Your clients and monitoring need to handle both.

## Practical recommendation

Use NetBird policy limits for hard per-group and per-user cost control, since that is enforced at the edge, in USD or tokens. Pre-create matching tags in LiteLLM only if you want LiteLLM-side budgets or reporting. Keep group names stable and make sure users do not belong to overlapping groups with conflicting budgets.

Understood: you want to know how KServe serves models with vLLM, how multiple GPUs are handled (tensor, pipeline or data parallelism), and how vLLM options are passed and handled. I'll answer from current documentation.**Short answer:** KServe doesn't implement any GPU parallelism itself. It starts vLLM, passes it the parallelism settings, and creates the pods and GPU resources. vLLM does the actual splitting. Tensor and pipeline parallelism are used, and data parallelism is available only on the newer `LLMInferenceService` path.

I could not fetch the vLLM docs pages (HTTP 429), so the vLLM-side statements rest on search snippets. Everything KServe-related comes from pages I fetched.

## 1. How KServe and vLLM fit together

KServe has two ways to serve LLMs with vLLM.

**a) `InferenceService` with the Hugging Face runtime (`kserve-huggingfaceserver`)**
- The runtime is a model server with two backends, vLLM and plain Hugging Face. If vLLM doesn't support a model, KServe falls back to the Hugging Face backend.
- `--backend auto|huggingface|vllm` selects the backend.
- It exposes OpenAI-compatible endpoints under the `openai/` prefix: `openai/v1/completions`, `chat/completions`, `embeddings` and `rerank`.
- KServe picks the CUDA image if the pod requests `nvidia.com/gpu`, and the CPU image otherwise.
- Source: https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/overview

**b) `LLMInferenceService` (`serving.kserve.io/v1alpha2`)**
- This is the newer API and runs `vllm serve` directly. Its configuration guide covers router settings and a `parallelism` spec, and the 0.18 release notes cover llm-d integration.
- Source: https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/llmisvc/llmisvc-configuration

## 2. How multiple GPUs are handled

**Single node, several GPUs (`InferenceService`)**
- You request `nvidia.com/gpu: N` on the container and pass `--tensor_parallel_size N` to vLLM. The overview doc lists `--tensor_parallel_size` as "Number of GPUs to use for tensor parallelism".

**Multi-node (`InferenceService`)**
- Use the `kserve-huggingfaceserver-multinode` runtime and add a `workerSpec` to the InferenceService. Setting `workerSpec` is what turns multi-node on, and it needs the field in both the ServingRuntime and the InferenceService.
- Parallelism is set with `workerSpec.tensorParallelSize` and `workerSpec.pipelineParallelSize`. Both default to 1.
- You cannot set `TENSOR_PARALLEL_SIZE` or `PIPELINE_PARALLEL_SIZE` as environment variables.
- The multi-node guide says KServe sizes the deployment as follows:
  ```
  Total GPUs = tensorParallelSize × pipelineParallelSize
  Ray node count = ceil(Total GPUs / workerSpec.resources.requests.gpu)
  ```
- Example: a `tensor-parallel-size` of 16 with 8 GPUs per pod becomes TP=8 × PP=2 across two pods.
- With Ray, there is exactly one head pod, plus worker pods running the same Ray cluster.
- Restrictions:
  - Standard (raw deployment) mode only.
  - No autoscaling (the autoscaler class must be `none`).
  - A ReadWriteMany PVC is required, and `storageUri` must be `pvc://`.
  - NCCL only.
  - Don't mix GPU types.
  - Source: https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/multi-node
- The 0.18 release adds groundwork for multi-node inference without Ray, using vLLM's `mp` executor backend. It also adds LeaderWorkerSet-based autoscaling for `LLMInferenceService` multi-node workloads. Source: https://kserve.github.io/website/blog/kserve-0.18-release

**`LLMInferenceService`: tensor, data and expert parallelism**
- `spec.parallelism` takes `tensor`, `data`, `dataLocal`, `expert` (boolean) and `dataRPCPort`.
- Multi-node size is `data / dataLocal`, implemented as a LeaderWorkerSet. For example, `data: 16, dataLocal: 8` gives 2 nodes.
- Pipeline parallelism appears as a field in this API's types. The doc sections I read describe only TP, DP and EP.

## 3. Which parallelism is used

| Type | Where in KServe | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Tensor (TP) | Both APIs | Shards weight matrices across GPUs. |
| Pipeline (PP) | `InferenceService` multi-node (`pipelineParallelSize`) | Splits layers across nodes or GPUs. |
| Data (DP) | `LLMInferenceService` (`data`, `dataLocal`) | Runs several full replicas of the model. |
| Expert (EP) | `LLMInferenceService` (`expert: true`) | For mixture-of-experts models. |

- The multi-node page says "PipelineParallelSize is not an autoscaling concept". It sets how many nodes run the model, so don't use it to scale throughput.
- For plain throughput scaling on the `InferenceService` path, use ordinary replicas, which are independent pods and effectively data parallelism. Replicas are not available in multi-node mode.
- vLLM's own docs (snippet only) say it "supports distributed tensor-parallel and pipeline-parallel inference and serving", and that data parallelism is a separate deployment mode.

## 4. How vLLM options are handled

- **Hugging Face runtime:** the runtime's own arguments (`--model_name`, `--model_id`, `--dtype`, `--backend`, `--max_model_len` and so on) are parsed by KServe. The overview doc says vLLM engine arguments "can also be specified on the command line and will be parsed by the Hugging Face runtime". It says "all" engine arguments are supported, for example `--quantization`, `--gpu_memory_utilization` and `--enforce_eager`. You put them in `spec.predictor.model.args`. Environment variables such as `VLLM_CPU_KVCACHE_SPACE` are passed through the container `env`.
- **`LLMInferenceService`:** the vLLM command is rendered from preset config templates. Extra flags go through the `VLLM_ADDITIONAL_ARGS` environment variable, which is expanded into `vllm serve ...`. This comes from a GitHub issue, not from the main docs. The issue is #5773: https://github.com/kserve/kserve/issues/5773
- **Pitfall in `LLMInferenceService`:** issue #5773 reports that on KServe v0.19, `spec.parallelism.tensor` was silently ignored for single-node deployments (no `spec.worker`). The service reported `Ready=True` while vLLM ran with TP=1 and the second GPU sat idle.
  - A fix PR (#5782) was opened, but the issue was auto-closed as stale, so I can't confirm the fix has shipped.
  - The workaround that worked was to put `--tensor-parallel-size 2` in `VLLM_ADDITIONAL_ARGS` instead.
  - Check the rendered pod command (`kubectl get pod -o yaml`) on your version.

## Practical recommendation

- One node with 2 to 8 GPUs: use the Hugging Face runtime with `--tensor_parallel_size N` and `nvidia.com/gpu: N`.
- Models too big for one node: use `workerSpec` multi-node (TP within a node, PP across nodes), or `LLMInferenceService` if you need data or expert parallelism.

**Confidence:** high on the KServe mechanics, medium on the vLLM-side details because of the failed fetches.

**Open questions:**
- Which KServe version you run. The docs I read are 0.20, and `LLMInferenceService` is v1alpha2.
- Whether `pipeline` is honored in `LLMInferenceService`.
- The exact `args` format the runtime expects on your version.

Compris : vous voulez savoir comment fonctionne le routage des experts dans un modèle Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) lorsque le modèle est réparti sur plusieurs GPU (expert parallelism, communications, équilibrage de charge). Je lance une recherche standard.# Routage MoE sur plusieurs GPU

Le routage (le choix des experts) est calculé localement sur chaque GPU. Le coût multi-GPU vient ensuite de l'envoi des tokens vers les GPU qui hébergent les experts choisis. Cet envoi se fait par deux opérations all-to-all par couche MoE.

## 1. Principe : l'expert parallelism (EP)

- Les experts d'une couche MoE sont répartis entre les GPU. Chaque GPU ne stocke que ses experts, pas la couche entière.
- Le routeur (réseau de gating) est une petite couche linéaire suivie d'un top-k. Il est répliqué ou local, donc il ne nécessite aucune communication.
- Les couches d'attention suivent une autre parallélisation : répliquées en data parallel, ou shardées en tensor parallel.

## 2. Déroulé d'une couche MoE (4 phases)

D'après [Brenndoerfer, Expert Parallelism](https://mbrenndoerfer.com/writing/expert-parallelism-distributed-moe-training) :

1. **Décision de routage** : chaque GPU calcule, pour ses propres tokens, les top-k experts et leurs poids.
2. **Dispatch (premier all-to-all)** : les tokens sont envoyés aux GPU qui hébergent leurs experts cibles. Un token qui vise l'expert 42, situé sur le GPU 5, traverse le réseau jusqu'au GPU 5.
3. **Calcul des experts** : chaque GPU traite tous les tokens reçus avec ses experts locaux, sans communication pendant cette phase.
4. **Combine (second all-to-all)** : les résultats retournent au GPU d'origine, où ils sont sommés avec les poids du routeur, puis ajoutés au flux résiduel.

Exemple de la même source : 16 experts sur 4 GPU, top-2. Un token du GPU 0 choisit l'expert 2 (local) et l'expert 11 (GPU 2), avec les poids 0,6 et 0,4. Sa sortie finale vaut 0,6×sortie₂ + 0,4×sortie₁₁. Le routage local ne coûte aucune communication réseau.

## 3. Pourquoi c'est difficile

- **Trafic dynamique** : l'all-to-all dépend du contenu des données. Chaque GPU envoie des volumes différents à chaque autre GPU, avec des messages de taille variable (`all_to_all_single` ou `all_to_allv`). Les compteurs d'envoi doivent d'abord être échangés pour dimensionner les buffers.
- **Coût doublé** : chaque couche MoE paie deux all-to-all.
- **Déséquilibre de charge** : si un expert est très sollicité, son GPU devient le goulot et tous les autres l'attendent.

## 4. Techniques pour limiter le coût et le déséquilibre

- **Node-limited routing (DeepSeek-V3)** : chaque token est envoyé à au plus M nœuds, avec M=4. Les experts routés sont répartis uniformément sur 64 GPU de 8 nœuds. Cela borne le trafic inter-nœuds, plus lent que le NVLink intra-nœud ([rapport technique DeepSeek-V3](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.19437v2)).
- **Équilibrage sans loss auxiliaire (DeepSeek-V3)** : un biais par expert est ajusté pendant l'entraînement (vitesse γ=0,001), avec une petite balance loss (α=0,0001) pour éviter un déséquilibre extrême au sein d'une séquence (même rapport).
- **EPLB en inférence (vLLM)** : en pratique la distribution des tokens par expert peut être très asymétrique. EPLB collecte des statistiques de charge à chaque forward pass et redistribue périodiquement les experts entre rangs EP. Il peut aussi répliquer les experts populaires (`num_redundant_experts`). Réglages par défaut : `window_size` 1000, `step_interval` 3000. Coût mémoire : environ 2,4 Go pour un expert redondant par rang sur DeepSeek-V3 ([doc vLLM Expert Parallel Deployment](https://github.com/inclusionAI/vllm-ling-v3/blob/main/docs/serving/expert_parallel_deployment.md)).
- **Noyaux de communication spécialisés** : vLLM propose plusieurs backends all-to-all (`--all2all-backend`). Le défaut est `allgather_reducescatter`. `deepep_high_throughput` vise le prefill multi-nœuds et `deepep_low_latency` le decode (même doc).
- **Recouvrement calcul/communication** : `--enable-dbo` (Dual Batch Overlap) superpose l'all-to-all au calcul.

## 5. Configuration concrète dans vLLM

- Activation : `--enable-expert-parallel`.
- Taille EP : `EP_SIZE = TP_SIZE × DP_SIZE`, calculée automatiquement.
- Exemple sur 8 GPU : `--tensor-parallel-size 1 --data-parallel-size 8 --enable-expert-parallel`. L'attention est répliquée sur les 8 GPU et les experts sont répartis sur les 8.
- Sans `--enable-expert-parallel`, les couches MoE utilisent du tensor parallel, comme un modèle dense.
- vLLM indique que l'EP est généralement associé au data parallelism, car il est plus efficace dans cette combinaison.

## Limites de cette réponse

- La page officielle `docs.vllm.ai` a renvoyé une erreur 429. J'ai donc lu une copie de la même documentation dans un fork (`inclusionAI/vllm-ling-v3`). Ses options peuvent différer légèrement de la version officielle actuelle.
- Je n'ai pas traité les variantes propres à d'autres frameworks (Megatron-LM, DeepSpeed-MoE, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM) ni les politiques de capacity factor et de suppression de tokens à l'entraînement.
- Les chiffres de DeepSeek-V3 sont spécifiques à ce modèle. Ne les généralisez pas à d'autres.

Je peux détailler un point si vous le souhaitez : choix TP/DP/EP selon votre matériel, EPLB, ou entraînement avec Megatron.

- **Node-limited routing (DeepSeek-V3)** : chaque token est envoyé à au plus M nœuds, avec M=4. Les experts routés sont répartis uniformément sur 64 GPU de 8 nœuds. Cela borne le trafic inter-nœuds, plus lent que le NVLink intra-nœud ([rapport technique DeepSeek-V3](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.19437v2)).
- **Équilibrage sans loss auxiliaire (DeepSeek-V3)** : un biais par expert est ajusté pendant l'entraînement (vitesse γ=0,001), avec une petite balance loss (α=0,0001) pour éviter un déséquilibre extrême au sein d'une séquence (même rapport).
- **EPLB en inférence (vLLM)** : en pratique la distribution des tokens par expert peut être très asymétrique. EPLB collecte des statistiques de charge à chaque forward pass et redistribue périodiquement les experts entre rangs EP. Il peut aussi répliquer les experts populaires (`num_redundant_experts`). Réglages par défaut : `window_size` 1000, `step_interval` 3000. Coût mémoire : environ 2,4 Go pour un expert redondant par rang sur DeepSeek-V3 ([doc vLLM Expert Parallel Deployment](https://github.com/inclusionAI/vllm-ling-v3/blob/main/docs/serving/expert_parallel_deployment.md)).
- **Noyaux de communication spécialisés** : vLLM propose plusieurs backends all-to-all (`--all2all-backend`). Le défaut est `allgather_reducescatter`. `deepep_high_throughput` vise le prefill multi-nœuds et `deepep_low_latency` le decode (même doc).
- **Recouvrement calcul/communication** : `--enable-dbo` (Dual Batch Overlap) superpose l'all-to-all au calcul.

## 5. Configuration concrète dans vLLM

- Activation : `--enable-expert-parallel`.
- Taille EP : `EP_SIZE = TP_SIZE × DP_SIZE`, calculée automatiquement.
- Exemple sur 8 GPU : `--tensor-parallel-size 1 --data-parallel-size 8 --enable-expert-parallel`. L'attention est répliquée sur les 8 GPU et les experts sont répartis sur les 8.
- Sans `--enable-expert-parallel`, les couches MoE utilisent du tensor parallel, comme un modèle dense.
- vLLM indique que l'EP est généralement associé au data parallelism, car il est plus efficace dans cette combinaison.

## Limites de cette réponse

- La page officielle `docs.vllm.ai` a renvoyé une erreur 429. J'ai donc lu une copie de la même documentation dans un fork (`inclusionAI/vllm-ling-v3`). Ses options peuvent différer légèrement de la version officielle actuelle.
- Je n'ai pas traité les variantes propres à d'autres frameworks (Megatron-LM, DeepSpeed-MoE, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM) ni les politiques de capacity factor et de suppression de tokens à l'entraînement.
- Les chiffres de DeepSeek-V3 sont spécifiques à ce modèle. Ne les généralisez pas à d'autres.

Je peux détailler un point si vous le souhaitez : choix TP/DP/EP selon votre matériel, EPLB, ou entraînement avec Megatron.

Understood: you want to know how the NetBird "agent-network" documentation describes integration with the LiteLLM AI gateway. Specifically, you're asking whether NetBird creates groups in LiteLLM, how budgets are handled per team, and whether you're limited to teams that exist in the identity provider.**Short answer:** NetBird does not create groups, teams or budgets inside LiteLLM. It forwards the caller's group names and user identity on each request. LiteLLM then treats the groups as tags and applies its own budgets to them. NetBird also enforces its own, separate budgets before the request reaches LiteLLM.

## How the integration works

- **Provider setup.** You add LiteLLM as a "LiteLLM Proxy" provider with your self-hosted URL and a LiteLLM virtual key. NetBird stores the key server-side, so clients hold no key. A policy must connect a source group to the provider before anyone can use it ([LiteLLM integration](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/integrations/litellm)).
- **Identity forwarding.** On each request NetBird does two things, per the same page:
  - It writes the caller's groups into `metadata.tags` in the JSON body.
  - It sends the user identity in the `x-litellm-end-user-id` header. The screenshot caption says this maps to the user's email.
  - The proxy strips any client-supplied values first, so an app can't spoof its identity.
- **Requirement on the key.** The virtual key must have `metadata.allow_client_tags: true`. Otherwise "LiteLLM silently drops the forwarded tags."
- **Toggle.** Forwarding is on by default. You can turn it off per provider with "Forward identity metadata" ([providers](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/providers#identity-metadata)).

## Are groups "created" in LiteLLM?

Not as teams. They appear as dynamic tags. The doc says "You can see every group forwarded from NetBird under Experimental → Tag Management, where each NetBird IdP group is listed as a tag passed dynamically in the request." Spend per group shows under Usage → Tag Usage.

LiteLLM Teams (its own team and key objects) are not mapped to NetBird groups in the docs I read.

## How budgets are handled

There are two independent layers:

1. **NetBird layer, enforced first.** A policy can set token and USD caps per user and per group over a fixed window, aligned to the Unix epoch ([limits](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/policies/limits)).
   - The check is `used >= cap`, made before the request runs. One request can therefore overshoot the cap, and the next one is blocked.
   - Account-wide caps are checked first ([how it works](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/how-it-works)).
2. **LiteLLM layer, applied afterwards.** The docs say "LiteLLM applies its own tag and end-user budgets on top, driven by the same NetBird identity." You configure these budgets and rate limits in LiteLLM, keyed on the tag (group name) or the end-user ID. NetBird's docs don't describe the LiteLLM-side configuration, so use LiteLLM's tag-budget documentation for that.

In practice, a group budget can be defined in both places. NetBird blocks first, and LiteLLM enforces independently.

## Are you limited to teams from the identity provider?

The docs do not say so explicitly. Here is what they do say:
- Policies are written against NetBird groups. The caller's "group membership" is what gets resolved ([how it works](https://docs.netbird.io/agent-network/how-it-works)).
- For humans, those groups come from the IdP. NetBird can sync them through a JWT groups claim or SCIM ([IdP docs](https://docs.netbird.io/selfhosted/identity-providers)). SCIM is not in the open-source Community Edition.
- For autonomous agents, the identity is the agent's own NetBird peer identity "and the groups assigned to that peer." Those are groups you manage in NetBird, not IdP teams.

**My inference, not stated in the docs:** you are not limited to IdP teams. Native NetBird groups, such as peer groups for agents, are part of the caller's group membership. They should be forwarded in `metadata.tags` like any other group. The LiteLLM page only says "IdP groups," so test it with a non-IdP group and check Tag Management before relying on it.

Two caveats from the IdP docs:
- Groups with the same name in NetBird and the IdP do not sync. You must delete the NetBird one first.
- Without JWT group sync or SCIM, IdP teams won't appear in NetBird at all.

## Open questions

- Whether manually created NetBird groups are forwarded as tags. I inferred this and did not find a doc that states it.
- How tags interact with LiteLLM Teams, or whether tag budgets can be mixed with team budgets. I did not research LiteLLM's side.
- The docs are marked Beta, so behaviour may change.

Understood: you want to know how KServe and vLLM work together, how multiple GPUs are handled (tensor, data or pipeline parallelism), and how vLLM options are passed through KServe. The output is a sourced explanatory answer.## Summary

KServe handles the Kubernetes side: pods, GPU resources, routing, autoscaling and model download. vLLM does the inference and all the GPU parallelism. KServe doesn't implement any parallelism itself. It translates a few CRD fields, or your args, into `vllm serve` flags and lays out the pods so vLLM can use the GPUs.

## 1. How KServe and vLLM fit together

There are two APIs.

**`InferenceService` with the Hugging Face runtime**
- The runtime is a Python model server that uses vLLM as its backend. It exposes OpenAI-compatible endpoints under the `openai/` prefix: `openai/v1/completions`, `chat/completions`, `embeddings` and `rerank`.
- It checks whether vLLM supports the model. If not, "KServe automatically falls back to the standard Hugging Face backend". You can force a backend with `--backend=auto|huggingface|vllm`.
- It picks the CUDA image if the pod requests `nvidia.com/gpu`, and the CPU image otherwise.
- Source: [Runtime Overview](https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/overview)

**`LLMInferenceService` (v1alpha2, newer)**
- This is built for LLMs. It runs `vllm serve` directly and adds a Gateway API and `InferencePool` router, an llm-d scheduler, prefill/decode disaggregation, and LeaderWorkerSet (LWS) for multi-node.
- Source: [KServe 0.18 release](https://kserve.github.io/website/blog/kserve-0.18-release). That release ships vLLM v0.19.0.

## 2. How multiple GPUs are handled

The answer depends on which API you use.

### a) `InferenceService`, single node

Request N GPUs on the pod and pass vLLM's `--tensor_parallel_size N` as an argument. The docs list `--tensor_parallel_size` as "Number of GPUs to use for tensor parallelism" ([Runtime Overview](https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/overview)). This is tensor parallelism inside one pod.

Scaling out by adding replicas (the predictor's min/max replicas) gives you independent copies of the model behind the load balancer. This is request-level data parallelism, but it is plain Kubernetes replication, not vLLM's own `--data-parallel-size`. That last point is my reading, not a quote from the docs.

### b) `InferenceService`, multi-node (`workerSpec`)

This uses the `kserve-huggingfaceserver-multinode` runtime ([multi-node guide](https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/multi-node)).
- It combines **tensor parallelism and pipeline parallelism**. There is no data parallelism in this mode.
- You set `workerSpec.tensorParallelSize` and `workerSpec.pipelineParallelSize`. `TENSOR_PARALLEL_SIZE` and `PIPELINE_PARALLEL_SIZE` "cannot be set via environment variables".
- The GPU arithmetic is:
  ```
  Total GPUs = tensorParallelSize × pipelineParallelSize
  Ray Node Count = ceil(Total GPUs / workerSpec.resources.requests.gpu)
  ```
- Example: TP=8, PP=2 with 8 GPUs per pod gives 2 pods. The equivalent command is `vllm serve ... --tensor-parallel-size 8 --pipeline-parallel-size 2`.
- If you set only TP=16 with 8 GPUs per pod, KServe rewrites it internally to PP=2 and TP=8.
- Restrictions:
  - Standard (raw Deployment) mode only.
  - No autoscaling (the autoscaler class must be `none`).
  - A ReadWriteMany PVC is required, and `pvc://` is the only supported storage protocol.
  - Exactly one head pod.
  - NCCL only.
- The doc says PP size "is not an autoscaling concept" and shouldn't be changed in production.
- Until now this ran on a Ray cluster. KServe 0.18 adds an `mp` (multiprocessing) executor backend, selected with the `multinode/executor-backend` annotation on the ServingRuntime. `ray` stays the default. In `mp` mode, "the number of nodes is derived from pipeline parallelism (PP) and GPUs per node from tensor parallelism (TP)" ([0.18 blog](https://kserve.github.io/website/blog/kserve-0.18-release)). This matches vLLM's recommendation of TP = GPUs per node and PP = number of nodes ([vLLM parallelism docs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vllm-project/vllm/main/docs/serving/parallelism_scaling.md)).

### c) `LLMInferenceService`

This one has all three, plus expert parallelism ([configuration guide](https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/llmisvc/llmisvc-configuration)):
```yaml
spec:
  parallelism:
    tensor: 4       # TP: split the model across 4 GPUs
    data: 8         # DP: total data-parallel instances
    dataLocal: 4    # DP ranks (GPUs) per node
    expert: true    # EP: for MoE models
```
- The LeaderWorkerSet size is `data / dataLocal`. For example, `data: 16` and `dataLocal: 8` gives 2 nodes.
- I found no `pipeline` field in the pages I fetched. A bug report refers to `spec.parallelism` as "tensor/pipeline", so the field may exist, but I couldn't confirm it.
- `spec.replicas` creates multiple LWS replicas, and each replica spans several nodes. These can be autoscaled as a group (KServe 0.18, `spec.scaling` with LWS).

## 3. Summary of the parallelism types

| Type | What is split | Where in KServe |
|---|---|---|
| Tensor (TP) | Weights inside each layer, across GPUs | `--tensor_parallel_size`, `workerSpec.tensorParallelSize`, `parallelism.tensor` |
| Pipeline (PP) | Layers, across GPUs or nodes | `workerSpec.pipelineParallelSize` |
| Data (DP) | Whole model copies, each serving different requests | `parallelism.data` / `dataLocal` in `LLMInferenceService`, or ordinary replicas |
| Expert (EP) | MoE experts | `parallelism.expert` |

vLLM's own guidance is to use TP when the model fits on one node, and TP plus PP when it doesn't. PP also suits GPUs without NVLink, and uneven GPU splits. For MoE models, vLLM supports "Data Parallel attention with Expert or Tensor Parallel MoE layers" ([vLLM docs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vllm-project/vllm/main/docs/serving/parallelism_scaling.md)).

## 4. How vLLM options are handled

- **`InferenceService`:** put them in `spec.predictor.model.args`. The runtime parses its own flags (`--model_name`, `--backend`, `--dtype`, `--max_model_len`, and so on). Per the docs, "The Hugging Face runtime supports **all** vLLM engine arguments". Anything else you list is parsed by vLLM's engine-args parser. Example from the [text-generation guide](https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/tasks/text-generation):
  ```yaml
  model:
    modelFormat: {name: huggingface}
    args: [--model_name=qwen2, --dtype=bfloat16, --max-model-len=2048]
    storageUri: hf://...
  ```
  Both the docs' underscore style and the dash style work. Typical flags are `--quantization`, `--gpu_memory_utilization` and `--enforce_eager`. vLLM CPU settings use environment variables such as `VLLM_CPU_KVCACHE_SPACE`.
- **Multi-node:** the TP and PP values come only from `workerSpec`, never from env vars. KServe injects `PIPELINE_PARALLEL_SIZE`, `TENSOR_PARALLEL_SIZE` and `WORKER_SVC` in `mp` mode.
- **`LLMInferenceService`:** KServe renders a `vllm serve` command template. Extra flags go in the container `args` or in the `VLLM_ADDITIONAL_ARGS` environment variable, which is appended to the command ([issue #5773](https://github.com/kserve/kserve/issues/5773)). `spec.parallelism` turns into flags only in the multi-node templates.

## 5. Caveats

- **Single-node `LLMInferenceService` ignored `spec.parallelism.tensor`** in v0.19. The field was accepted, but `--tensor-parallel-size` was never rendered, so vLLM ran on one GPU while the resource reported Ready ([#5773](https://github.com/kserve/kserve/issues/5773)). The workaround is `--tensor-parallel-size 2` in `VLLM_ADDITIONAL_ARGS`. A fix PR was opened (#5782), but the issue was closed as stale, so I can't confirm the fix has shipped.
- GPU requests don't follow `parallelism` automatically. You must set `resources.limits` to match yourself.
- The multi-node docs say KServe's TP and PP values don't map 1:1 to GPUs and nodes. Check the pod layout against the formula above.

## Confidence and open questions

Confidence is high for the `InferenceService` behaviour, because it comes from the official 0.20 docs and the 0.18 release notes. It is medium for `LLMInferenceService` internals, which come from a configuration guide and an issue report. The vLLM docs page returned errors, so I read the vLLM parallelism content from its raw source on GitHub.

Open questions:
- Is there a `pipeline` field in `LLMInferenceService`?
- Is the single-node TP fix released?
- Which KServe version are you running? The behaviour differs between 0.18, 0.19 and 0.20.

Example from the [text-generation guide](https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/generative-inference/tasks/text-generation):
  ```yaml
  model:
    modelFormat: {name: huggingface}
    args: [--model_name=qwen2, --dtype=bfloat16, --max-model-len=2048]
    storageUri: hf://...
  ```
  Both the docs' underscore style and the dash style work. Typical flags are `--quantization`, `--gpu_memory_utilization` and `--enforce_eager`. vLLM CPU settings use environment variables such as `VLLM_CPU_KVCACHE_SPACE`.
- **Multi-node:** the TP and PP values come only from `workerSpec`, never from env vars. KServe injects `PIPELINE_PARALLEL_SIZE`, `TENSOR_PARALLEL_SIZE` and `WORKER_SVC` in `mp` mode.
- **`LLMInferenceService`:** KServe renders a `vllm serve` command template. Extra flags go in the container `args` or in the `VLLM_ADDITIONAL_ARGS` environment variable, which is appended to the command ([issue #5773](https://github.com/kserve/kserve/issues/5773)). `spec.parallelism` turns into flags only in the multi-node templates.

## 5. Caveats

- **Single-node `LLMInferenceService` ignored `spec.parallelism.tensor`** in v0.19. The field was accepted, but `--tensor-parallel-size` was never rendered, so vLLM ran on one GPU while the resource reported Ready ([#5773](https://github.com/kserve/kserve/issues/5773)). The workaround is `--tensor-parallel-size 2` in `VLLM_ADDITIONAL_ARGS`. A fix PR was opened (#5782), but the issue was closed as stale, so I can't confirm the fix has shipped.
- GPU requests don't follow `parallelism` automatically. You must set `resources.limits` to match yourself.
- The multi-node docs say KServe's TP and PP values don't map 1:1 to GPUs and nodes. Check the pod layout against the formula above.

## Confidence and open questions

Confidence is high for the `InferenceService` behaviour, because it comes from the official 0.20 docs and the 0.18 release notes. It is medium for `LLMInferenceService` internals, which come from a configuration guide and an issue report. The vLLM docs page returned errors, so I read the vLLM parallelism content from its raw source on GitHub.

Open questions:
- Is there a `pipeline` field in `LLMInferenceService`?
- Is the single-node TP fix released?
- Which KServe version are you running? The behaviour differs between 0.18, 0.19 and 0.20.

Compris : vous voulez savoir comment le routage des experts (MoE, Mixture of Experts) fonctionne lorsque le modèle est réparti sur plusieurs GPU. Je pars sur une réponse explicative et sourcée.# Routage MoE sur plusieurs GPU

Le routage lui-même ne change pas quand on ajoute des GPU. Le routeur reste une petite couche de scoring qui choisit les top-k experts de chaque token. Ce qui change, c'est que les experts sont répartis entre les GPU. Les tokens doivent donc être envoyés vers le GPU qui héberge l'expert choisi, puis les résultats doivent revenir.

## 1. Répartition des poids

- **Parties partagées.** L'attention, les embeddings, la tête LM et le KV cache restent disponibles sur chaque GPU. Avec EP seul (TP=1), ils sont répliqués. Avec EP+TP, ils sont partitionnés entre les rangs TP (source : blog JarvisLabs).
- **Experts.** Ils sont répartis entre les GPU au lieu d'être copiés partout. Exemple de la source : GPU 0 stocke les experts 0–127 et GPU 1 les experts 128–255. vLLM gère aussi un placement round-robin selon la configuration (JarvisLabs).

## 2. Flux d'un token dans une couche MoE

D'après la description de vLLM par JarvisLabs :

1. **Routage.** Après l'attention, un réseau de gating score tous les experts et retient les top-k pour chaque token.
2. **Dispatch (all-to-all).** Chaque token est envoyé au GPU qui possède l'expert choisi. S'il a plusieurs experts, il est envoyé à plusieurs GPU.
3. **Calcul local.** Chaque GPU n'exécute que les FFN des experts qu'il héberge, sur les tokens reçus.
4. **Combine (all-to-all).** Les sorties retournent au GPU d'origine, sont pondérées par les scores du routeur et sont sommées avant la couche suivante.

Le principal surcoût est ce double échange all-to-all, un par sens. Il dépend fortement de l'interconnexion (NVLink, InfiniBand). NVIDIA a publié une bibliothèque de communication dédiée, Hybrid-EP, qui combine NVLink et RDMA pour approcher la bande passante matérielle.

## 3. Expert Parallel ou Tensor Parallel pour les experts

La documentation TensorRT-LLM distingue deux approches :

- **TP sur les experts.** Le poids de chaque expert est découpé entre les GPU. Chaque GPU reçoit les hidden states de tous les tokens pour tous les experts et calcule avec des poids partiels.
- **EP.** Chaque GPU détient des experts complets. Il ne reçoit que les tokens destinés à ses experts et calcule avec les poids complets.
- **Hybride.** Les deux sont combinés pour mieux équilibrer la charge. La contrainte est `moe_tp_size × moe_ep_size = tp_size`.

## 4. Équilibrage de charge

Si le routeur envoie trop de tokens vers quelques experts, les GPU qui les hébergent deviennent des goulots d'étranglement. Les approches courantes :

- **Switch Transformer.** Une perte auxiliaire d'équilibrage et une capacité maximale par expert. Au-delà de cette capacité, le token est abandonné, c'est-à-dire qu'aucun expert ne le traite (apxml.com, résumé du papier Switch). Je n'ai pas relu ce point dans le papier original.
- **DeepSeek-V3.** Un biais par expert ajusté pendant l'entraînement, sans perte auxiliaire, plus une petite perte d'équilibrage au niveau séquence. Le routage est aussi limité par nœud pour réduire le trafic inter-nœuds. Dans leur configuration, les experts d'une couche sont répartis sur 64 GPU de 8 nœuds, et chaque token est envoyé à 4 nœuds au maximum (arXiv 2412.19437).
- **En inférence.** vLLM propose l'EPLB (Expert Parallel Load Balancer), qui rééquilibre les experts entre GPU. Le blog JarvisLabs le teste, mais je n'ai pas détaillé son mécanisme ici.

## À retenir pour le choix de configuration

- L'EP réduit la mémoire de poids d'experts par GPU. Elle coûte deux all-to-all par couche MoE.
- Sur des GPU reliés seulement par PCIe, ce coût peut annuler le gain. Je n'ai pas vérifié ce point par une mesure.
- Le déséquilibre du routage (experts « chauds ») est le risque pratique principal.

## Limites

La page de documentation vLLM (`docs.vllm.ai`) a renvoyé une erreur 429 et je ne l'ai pas lue. Les détails vLLM viennent donc d'un blog tiers. Si vous voulez une réponse pour un modèle et un matériel précis (par exemple Mixtral ou Qwen sur 2 à 8 GPU), dites-le-moi.

Sources :
- https://jarvislabs.ai/blog/expert-parallelism-mixed-strategies-vllm
- https://nvidia.github.io/TensorRT-LLM/advanced/expert-parallelism.html
- https://arxiv.org/html/2412.19437v2
- https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/optimizing-communication-for-mixture-of-experts-training-with-hybrid-expert-parallel/
- https://apxml.com/courses/mixture-of-experts-advanced-implementation/chapter-2-advanced-routing-mechanisms/switch-transformers-routing

---

## Default Value: `0.9` (90%)

The `--gpu-memory-utilization` CLI option defaults to **0.9**, meaning vLLM will reserve 90% of each GPU's total VRAM by default.

### What It Controls

The parameter controls **the fraction of GPU memory to be used for the model executor** — which includes:

- **Model weights**
- **Activations**  
- **KV cache**

From vLLM's official EngineArgs documentation:

> "The fraction of GPU memory to be used for the model executor, which can range from 0 to 1. For example, a value of 0.5 would imply 50% GPU memory utilization."

### Practical Example

If you have a GPU with 80 GB of VRAM and use the default value:
- vLLM will use up to **72 GB** (0.9 × 80 GB) for model weights and KV cache
- The remaining ~8 GB is left for the OS and other processes

### Why It Matters

- **Higher values** → More KV cache space → Higher throughput (more requests can be served in parallel)
- **Too high** → Risk of out-of-memory (OOM) errors

---

### Source References

1. **vLLM Docs — Engine Arguments** (docs.vllm.ai):
   > "The fraction of GPU memory to be used for the model executor, which can range from 0 to 1. For example, a value of 0.5 would imply 50% GPU memory utilization."
   - URL: https://docs.vllm.ai/en/v0.6.4/models/engine_args.html

2. **vLLM Source Code** (`EngineArgs` dataclass):
   The CLI argument maps to the `CacheConfig` dataclass field:
   ```python
   gpu_memory_utilization: float | None = CacheConfig.gpu_memory_utilization
   ```
   Where `CacheConfig.gpu_memory_utilization` is defined as `0.9` by default.
   - URL: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/engine/arg_utils.py
   - Config definition: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/config/cache.py
