---

## 1. What Each One Caches

### vLLM's Automatic Prefix Caching (APC)

APC caches **KV cache blocks** (key-value tensors from attention layers) on a per-block basis. Each complete KV cache block is assigned a content-based hash computed from the prefix tokens and the block's own tokens:

> "Every block in the KV cache can be uniquely identified by `hash(prefix tokens, tokens in this block)`... we can add another indirection in vLLM's KV cache management: `Logical block table --> hash table --> physical block table`"
> — [vLLM APC RFC](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/2614)

Each cached block tracks: block hash, reference count, last accessed time, total access count, and prefix length. Blocks are only fully cached once they reach their complete size (e.g., 16 tokens for block_size=16). Partially-filled blocks are not stored in the hash table.

APC is prefix-bound: a new query reuses blocks only if they share the same prefix alignment with previously cached blocks. It works within vLLM's PagedAttention framework.

### LMCache

LMCache also caches **KV cache chunks** (block-aligned KV tensors), but with a wider scope:

> "LMCache extends an LLM inference engine (e.g., vLLM) with a multi-tier KV cache storage system spanning GPU memory, CPU memory, and disk/remote backends"
> — [LMCache Architecture Overview](https://docs.lmcache.ai/developer_guide/architecture.html)

LMCache chunks KV data into configurable sizes (default 256 tokens) and maintains an internal index mapping token sequences to cached KV entries. Beyond prefix caching, LMCache supports:

- **CacheBlend (non-prefix KV reuse):** Reuses cached KV blocks at any position in the prompt, not just at the prefix:
  > "Extend KV reuse beyond prefix caching by reusing cached KV blocks at any position in the prompt. This leverages CacheBlend to selectively recompute tokens for quality recovery."
  > — [LMCache GitHub README](https://github.com/lmcache/lmcache)

- **Cross-engine sharing:** LMCache stores are engine-independent:
  > "LMCache, as a standalone daemon process, manages KV cache independently from the inference engine process, so that KV cache will not be lost even if the inference engine crashes"
  > — [LMCache GitHub README](https://github.com/lmcache/lmcache)

LMCache also supports **KV cache compression** via CacheGen (SERDE interface for token dropping and custom serialization):
> "Pluggable KV transformation: A simple interface for researchers to write compression, token dropping, and custom serialization through a flexible SERDE interface."
> — [LMCache GitHub README](https://github.com/lmcache/lmcache)

---

## 2. Where the Cache Is Stored

### vLLM's APC (GPU-only)

By default, APC stores everything in **GPU memory only**, within the vLLM process:

> "vLLM turns automatic prefix caching on by default because the lookup adds near-zero overhead... APC only reduces the time of processing the queries (the prefilling phase)"
> — [vLLM APC docs](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/features/automatic_prefix_caching/)

GPU memory is finite. When the cache fills up, blocks are evicted using LRU with tie-breaking on reference count and prefix length. Cached data is **ephemeral** — it lives only as long as the vLLM process and GPU memory allows:

> "Because vLLM's prefix cache and CPU offload both live inside the vLLM process, restarting vLLM wipes them out entirely"
> — [MindStudio: LMCache vs vLLM Caching](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents)

### vLLM's Native CPU Offloading (extension to APC)

vLLM supports offloading evicted blocks to **CPU memory** as a secondary tier:

> "vLLM's native backend moves evicted KV blocks to CPU memory instead of discarding them, then reloads them on a later cache hit... kv_offloading_backend: Set to 'native' for vLLM's built-in CPU offloading"
> — [Ray Serve KV Cache Offloading](https://docs.ray.io/en/latest/serve/llm/user-guides/kv-cache-offloading.html)

This is still **within the vLLM process**. The CPU tier has no persistence beyond the process lifetime.

### LMCache (Multi-Tier: L1 + L2)

LMCache implements a **hierarchical storage system** with distinct tiers:

**L1 Cache (CPU RAM or NVMe):**
- **`L1MemoryManager`** (default): pinned CPU DRAM, lazy growth up to `--l1-size-gb`
- **`DevDaxL1MemoryManager`**: Device-DAX-backed L1 slab (via `--l1-devdax-path`)
- **`GDSL1MemoryManager`**: NVMe slab file via GPUDirect Storage (via `--gds-l1-path`), with DMA directly between GPU staging buffer and slab

> "The underlying memory allocation is handled by one of three interchangeable tiers selected at startup"
> — [LMCache MP Mode](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/index.html)

**L2 Storage (Remote/Persistent):**
LMCache supports a large set of backends for persistent secondary storage:

> "Through this interface, LMCache supports storage backends including CPU RAM, local disk (SSD), Redis/Valkey, Mooncake, InfiniStore, S3-compatible object storage, NIXL, and GDS"
> — [LMCache GitHub README](https://github.com/lmcache/lmcache)

> "NIXL, Native NIXL, File & Block, Remote & Distributed (Bigtable, SageMaker HyperPod, S3, HF Bucket, Mooncake Store, RESP/Redis/Valkey, Valkey, Aerospike, Hf3fs, WQS), DAX, Mock, Fault Inject, Plugin (Custom/External)"
> — [LMCache L2 Supported Storages](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/l2_storage/supported_storages.html)

**Process Isolation:**
LMCache runs as a **standalone daemon process** (`lmcache server`) separate from vLLM. This means:

> "LMCache, as a standalone daemon process, manages KV cache independently from the inference engine process"
> — [LMCache GitHub README](https://github.com/lmcache/lmcache)

> "By running LMCache in a separate process, its Python GIL and CPU work (hashing, memory management, L2 I/O) do not compete with vLLM's inference threads"
> — [LMCache MP Mode](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/index.html)

---

## 3. When LMCache Is Worth Adding Over vLLM's Built-in Prefix Caching

### 3.1 LMCache is NOT worth it for single-instance, single-GPU setups where everything fits in GPU/CPU memory

> "In steady-state serving, with everything fitting in GPU memory or RAM, LMCache performs roughly on par with vLLM's own CPU offload. In one comparison, LMCache measured around 140 milliseconds against vLLM's offload at 164 milliseconds, essentially a tie"
> — [MindStudio: LMCache vs vLLM Caching](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents)

> "LMCache's real advantage shows up after a restart... in steady-state, not automatically worth the added complexity"
> — [MindStudio: LMCache vs vLLM Caching](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents)

### 3.2 When LMCache IS worth it

#### A. Cache must survive vLLM restarts or crashes

> "In testing, both [vLLM GPU cache and CPU offload] fell back to full, uncached latency (around 1.35 seconds) immediately after a restart. LMCache, because its cache lives in a separate server that keeps running independently, reconnected after the restart and immediately resumed near-instant responses (around 141 milliseconds with a 99.9% hit rate)"
> — [MindStudio: LMCache vs vLLM Caching](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents)

#### B. Multi-turn agent workloads or long conversations where conversation history is a shared prefix

> "Every turn in an agent session makes the model reread the entire conversation so far, unless something is cached... scaling to eight agents sharing one GPU made the gap larger... With caching on, throughput climbed to nearly 60 turns per minute from roughly eight turns per minute"
> — [MindStudio: LMCache vs vLLM Caching](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents)

> "Testing showed up to roughly 5.6x to 7.5x more completed turns per minute with eight agents running cached versus uncached"
> — [MindStudio: LMCache vs vLLM Caching](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents)

#### C. Workloads exceeding GPU memory, where vLLM's native CPU offloading is insufficient and you need disk-backed persistence

> "When the workload was scaled up to overflow available GPU cache (48 large documents against a GPU that could hold notes for far fewer), vLLM's GPU-only prefix cache saw its hit rate collapse to 0%, performing about as poorly as no caching at all. Switching on CPU offload fixed that, recovering hit rates above 99%"
> — [MindStudio: LMCache vs vLLM Caching](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents)

> "LMCache becomes worth the added complexity mainly when you need the cache to survive a vLLM restart or crash, or when your workload outgrows available RAM and needs disk-backed storage"
> — [MindStudio: LMCache vs vLLM Caching](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents)

#### D. Cross-instance KV cache sharing (multiple vLLM workers on the same node or across machines)

> "LMCache adds a distributed cache layer so multiple vLLM workers on different machines share the same KV cache over Ethernet, RDMA, or NVLink"
> — [Spheron Network: Deploy LMCache on GPU Cloud](https://www.spheron.network/blog/deploy-lmcache-vllm-kv-cache-sharing-gpu-cloud/)

> "One LMCache server per node can serve multiple vLLM pods, providing process isolation, shared caching, and independent resource scaling"
> — [LMCache MP Mode](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/index.html)

> "LMCache allows unlimited amount of KV caches to be stored on cheap disks and be shared across multiple vLLM instances. It is in contrast with vLLM APC which is single-instance only"
> — [LMCache Blog: Turboboosting vLLM](https://blog.lmcache.ai/en/2024/09/17/lmcache-turboboosting-vllm-with-7x-faster-access-to-100x-more-kv-caches/)

#### E. Prefill/decode disaggregation

> "Support KV cache transfer from prefill workers to decode workers over NVLink, RDMA, or TCP through transport layers such as NIXL"
> — [LMCache GitHub README](https://github.com/lmcache/lmcache)

APC caches **KV cache blocks** (key-value tensors from attention layers) on a per-block basis. Each complete KV cache block is assigned a content-based hash computed from the prefix tokens and the block's own tokens:

> "Every block in the KV cache can be uniquely identified by `hash(prefix tokens, tokens in this block)`... we can add another indirection in vLLM's KV cache management: `Logical block table --> hash table --> physical block table`"
> — [vLLM APC RFC](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/2614)

Each cached block tracks: block hash, reference count, last accessed time, total access count, and prefix length. Blocks are only fully cached once they reach their complete size (e.g., 16 tokens for block_size=16). Partially-filled blocks are not stored in the hash table.

APC is prefix-bound: a new query reuses blocks only if they share the same prefix alignment with previously cached blocks. It works within vLLM's PagedAttention framework.

### LMCache

LMCache also caches **KV cache chunks** (block-aligned KV tensors), but with a wider scope:

> "LMCache extends an LLM inference engine (e.g., vLLM) with a multi-tier KV cache storage system spanning GPU memory, CPU memory, and disk/remote backends"
> — [LMCache Architecture Overview](https://docs.lmcache.ai/developer_guide/architecture.html)

GPU memory is finite. When the cache fills up, blocks are evicted using LRU with tie-breaking on reference count and prefix length. Cached data is **ephemeral** — it lives only as long as the vLLM process and GPU memory allows:

> "Through this interface, LMCache supports storage backends including CPU RAM, local disk (SSD), Redis/Valkey, Mooncake, InfiniStore, S3-compatible object storage, NIXL, and GDS"

> "NIXL, Native NIXL, File & Block, Remote & Distributed (Bigtable, SageMaker HyperPod, S3, HF Bucket, Mooncake Store, RESP/Redis/Valkey, Valkey, Aerospike, Hf3fs, WQS), DAX, Mock, Fault Inject, Plugin (Custom/External)"

> — [LMCache GitHub README](https://github.com/lmcache/lmcache)

## REPEATABLE READ vs SERIALIZABLE in PostgreSQL

Based on the [PostgreSQL 18 documentation — Section 13.2: Transaction Isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html) and [Section 13.5: Serialization Failure Handling](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/mvcc-serialization-failure-handling.html).

### Anomalies Prevented (from Table 13.1)

| Isolation Level | Dirty Read | Nonrepeatable Read | Phantom Read | Serialization Anomaly |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Repeatable Read** | ❌ Not possible | ❌ Not possible | ❌ Allowed, but not in PG | ⚠️ **Possible** |
| **Serializable** | ❌ Not possible | ❌ Not possible | ❌ Not possible | ❌ Not possible |

**Key distinction:** Repeatable Read and Serializable behave identically with respect to dirty reads, nonrepeatable reads, and phantom reads — PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read implementation goes *above* the SQL standard minimum by also preventing phantom reads. The **sole difference** is that **Serializable also prevents serialization anomalies**, while Repeatable Read does not.

### What is a Serialization Anomaly?

The documentation defines it as:

> "The result of successfully committing a group of transactions is inconsistent with all possible orderings of running those transactions one at a time."

**Concrete example from the docs** (Section 13.2.3): Consider a table `mytab` with rows `{class=1, value=10}, {class=1, value=20}, {class=2, value=100}, {class=2, value=200}`. Transaction A computes `SUM(value)` for `class=1` (gets 30) and inserts it as a new row with `class=2`. Concurrently, transaction B computes `SUM(value)` for `class=2` (gets 300) and inserts it as a new row with `class=1`. If either transaction ran at Repeatable Read, both commits would be allowed — but there is **no serial order** of execution that would produce the same result, making it a serialization anomaly. Serializable detects this and aborts one of them.

### How the Levels Differ Internally

- **Repeatable Read** is implemented via **Snapshot Isolation**: the transaction sees a stable snapshot as of the start of the first non-transaction-control statement. It prevents reads of uncommitted or concurrently-committed data, and will reject any attempt to update/delete rows changed by another committed transaction after the snapshot was taken, raising:
  ```
  ERROR: could not serialize access due to concurrent update
  ```

- **Serializable** is implemented via **Serializable Snapshot Isolation** (predicate locking): it works "exactly the same as Repeatable Read except that it also monitors for conditions which could make execution of a concurrent set of serializable transactions behave in a manner inconsistent with all possible serial executions." It uses **predicate locks** (visible in `pg_locks` with mode `SIReadLock`) to detect read/write dependencies among concurrent transactions:
  ```
  ERROR: could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions
  ```

### SQLSTATE for Serialization Failures

From the official docs (Section 13.2.3 and Section 13.5):

> "it is important that an environment which uses this technique have a generalized way of handling serialization failures (**which always return with an SQLSTATE value of '40001'**)..."

> "Such an error's message text will vary according to the precise circumstances, but it will always have the SQLSTATE code **`40001`** (`serialization_failure`)."

**Both** Repeatable Read and Serializable isolation levels can raise this `40001` error, and applications using either level **must be prepared to retry the complete transaction from the beginning** when they receive it.

### Sources

1. PostgreSQL 18, *13.2. Transaction Isolation* — https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html
2. PostgreSQL 18, *13.5. Serialization Failure Handling* — https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/mvcc-serialization-failure-handling.html

## Findings

**Summary**: As of vLLM's current versions (0.29+), the default value of `--gpu-memory-utilization` (also `--gpu-memory-utilzation` as a typo alias) is **0.92** (i.e. 92%). In older versions it was 0.9 (90%).

**What it controls**: The parameter sets the fraction of each GPU's total memory to be reserved for vLLM's model executor. The memory is split between:
- Model weights (loaded onto the GPU)
- Non-Torch memory (e.g. CUDA graph overhead)
- Peak activation memory during inference
- **KV cache** (the remaining budget is allocated as cache space for tokens)

Specifically, `total_GPU_memory × gpu_memory_utilization` = total memory budget per GPU. vLLM then subtracts weights + activations + CUDA-graph memory to determine how much remains for the KV cache.

**What it does NOT control**: The KV cache is *not* pre-allocated up to this full budget; instead this value determines the maximum memory vLLM *may use*, and the KV cache gets whatever is left after model weights and other overheads are accounted for.

---

### Sources

**1. Official docs — Engine Arguments (v0.6.4):**

> "The fraction of GPU memory to be used for the model executor, which can range from 0 to 1. For example, a value of 0.5 would imply 50% GPU memory utilization. If unspecified, will use the default value of **0.9**."

URL: https://docs.vllm.ai/en/v0.6.4/models/engine_args.html

**2. Official docs — Engine Arguments (current stable):**

> "If unspecified, will use the default value of **0.92**. This is a per-instance limit, and only applies to the current vLLM instance."

URL: https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/configuration/engine_args/

**3. Source code (quoted in GitHub issue #56830):**

The parameter is defined in vLLM's Python source as:
```python
gpu_memory_utilization: float = Field(default=0.92, gt=0, le=1)
"""The fraction of GPU memory to be used for the model executor, which can range from 0 to 1. ... This is a per-instance limit, and only applies to the current vLLM instance."""
```

URL: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/56830

**4. Optimization guide (what it controls):**

> "Increase `gpu_memory_utilization`. vLLM pre-allocates GPU cache using this percentage of memory. By increasing utilization, you can provide more KV cache space."

URL: https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/configuration/optimization.md

**5. Historical change (0.95 → 0.9):**

> "The gpu-memory-utilization argument was originally set to 0.95 by default but changed to 0.9, mainly because the memory profiling at the [startup]..."

URL: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/1018

---

### Key takeaways

| Aspect | Value |
|---|---|
| **Current default** | **0.92** (92% of GPU VRAM) |
| **Previous default** | 0.9 (90%) in older versions |
| **Accepted range** | 0 to 1 (float) |
| **What it sets** | Max memory budget for model executor + KV cache |
| **Per-GPU** | Yes, applies independently per GPU |
| **Per-instance** | Yes, if two vLLM instances share one GPU, each can set its own value (e.g. 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.0) |

### Open questions

- The exact file path in the vLLM repo where this default is defined (`default=0.92` was confirmed via a GitHub issue quote, but I could not directly fetch the source file due to rate limiting). The documentation at `docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/configuration/engine_args/` confirms 0.92 for the current `stable` branch, and the issue #56830 confirms the `Field(default=0.92)` definition in the codebase.

# LMCache vs. vLLM Built-in Prefix Caching — Detailed Comparison

## 1. What Does LMCache Cache?

**LMCache caches KV cache (key-value attention tensors)** — specifically, the intermediate K and V tensors that the model has already computed for tokens in a prompt and the tokens generated so far. From the architecture documentation:

> "LMCache extends an LLM inference engine (e.g., vLLM) with a multi-tier KV cache storage system spanning GPU memory, CPU memory, and disk/remote backends."

— [LMCache Architecture Overview](https://docs.lmcache.ai/developer_guide/architecture.html)

The cached data is organized into **chunks** (configurable chunk size, default 256 tokens), where each chunk contains the KV tensors for a contiguous span of tokens. When LMCache detects a cache hit for a sequence of tokens, it loads the precomputed KV chunks and plugs them into vLLM's paged attention memory manager so that the model can skip the prefill computation for those tokens entirely.

> "During prompt processing, it checks if token sequences were seen before: Cache hit: Fetches precomputed KV cache chunks from LMCache, bypassing computation"

— [LMCache Architecture Overview](https://docs.lmcache.ai/developer_guide/architecture.html)

**Additionally, LMCache supports non-KV caching capabilities** through its SERDE interface, including:
- **Hidden states** — for encoder caching or blending ([LMCache Non-KV Caching](https://docs.lmcache.ai/non_kv_cache/index.html))
- **Encodings** — token-level embeddings

It also supports **KV cache compression** via CacheGen for efficient remote storage ([LMCache SERDE](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/serde.html)).

## 2. What Does vLLM's Built-in Prefix Caching Cache?

**vLLM's built-in Automatic Prefix Caching (APC) caches KV cache blocks** — the same K and V tensors, but at the granularity of vLLM's paged attention blocks (typically 16–64 KB per block, e.g., 62.5 KB for Llama-3.1-8B). From the vLLM documentation:

> "Prefix caching kv-cache blocks is a popular optimization in LLM inference to avoid redundant prompt computations. The core idea is simple – we cache the kv-cache blocks of processed requests, and reuse these blocks when a new request comes in with the same prefix as a previous request."

— [vLLM Automatic Prefix Caching](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/design/prefix_caching/)

vLLM indexes each block by a **content hash** of its tokens. When a new request arrives with a prefix matching a cached block's hash, vLLM skips the prefill computation for those blocks. This is enabled by default in the V1 engine and can be disabled with `--no-enable-prefix-caching` ([ScaleOps blog](https://scaleops.com/blog/vllm-kv-cache-prefix-cache-gpu-memory/)).

**Key limitation: vLLM's prefix cache is strictly within-GPU memory.** Every unique prefix, including one-off RAG queries and completed chat turns, is stored in GPU memory until memory is full. LRU eviction starts only then, and there is no shrink-on-idle. There is **no mechanism to persist cached prefixes to CPU, disk, or remote storage** across process restarts or to share them across vLLM instances.

— [ScaleOps blog on vLLM KV Cache and Prefix Cache](https://scaleops.com/blog/vllm-kv-cache-prefix-cache-gpu-memory/)

## 3. Where is LMCache's Cache Stored?

**LMCache uses a multi-tier, hierarchical storage system** with the following backends:

### Tier 1: GPU Memory
Holds the active working set of KV caches currently being used by the model.

— [LMCache Architecture Overview](https://docs.lmcache.ai/developer_guide/architecture.html)

### Tier 2: CPU DRAM
Acts as a "hot cache" for recently used KV chunks, using pinned memory for efficient GPU-CPU transfers. Configurable via `max_local_cpu_size` (default 5.0 GB).

> "When LMCACHE_LOCAL_CPU=True is used in conjunction with the disk backend or a remote backend… we can think of the CPU RAM as a 'hot cache' that will contain the 'hottest' (most recently accessed) subset of KV caches from Disk and Remote storage."

— [LMCache CPU RAM Storage](https://docs.lmcache.ai/legacy/kv_cache/storage_backends/cpu_ram.html)

Supports Linux hugepages (2 MiB) for reduced TLB pressure:

> "enabling Linux hugepages (2 MiB pages) can reduce TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer) pressure and improve memory access performance"

— [LMCache CPU RAM Storage](https://docs.lmcache.ai/legacy/kv_cache/storage_backends/cpu_ram.html)

### Tier 3: Local Disk (SSD/NVMe)
Stores KV cache chunks as individual `.pt` files with LRU/LFU/FIFO/MRU eviction policies. Configurable via `local_disk` and `max_local_disk_size`. Supports multi-path NVMe sharding.

> "The disk backend will create one file per KV cache chunk as they are stored, evicting if capacity is exceeded (LRU currently)"

— [LMCache Local Storage](https://docs.lmcache.ai/legacy/kv_cache/storage_backends/local_storage.html)

### Tier 4: Remote Storage
LMCache supports a wide range of remote/distributed backends through pluggable connectors:

- **Redis / Valkey** — in-memory key-value store
- **S3-compatible object storage**
- **NVIDIA NIXL** — peer-to-peer GPU transfer (NVLink, RDMA, TCP)
- **Mooncake** — distributed KV cache sharing
- **InfiniStore**
- **Google Cloud Bigtable**
- **Azure Blob Storage**
- **Aerospike**
- **Hugging Face Buckets**
- **WQS**
- **DAX**

> "Through this interface, LMCache supports storage backends including CPU RAM, local disk (SSD), Redis/Valkey, Mooncake, InfiniStore, S3-compatible object storage, NIXL, and GDS."

— [LMCache GitHub README](https://github.com/lmcache/lmcache)

### Cross-Instance Coordination
LMCache includes a centralized **KV cache controller** (standalone process) for global metadata management, enabling cache lookups and sharing across multiple vLLM instances on different nodes:

> "LMCache operates as a distributed caching system built around a centralized KV cache controller responsible for global metadata management, cache manipulation, and request routing."

— [LMCache arXiv Paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.09665v2)

## 4. Where is vLLM's Built-in Prefix Caching Stored?

**vLLM's prefix cache lives entirely in GPU memory.** The KV cache blocks are stored in the GPU memory pool managed by vLLM's paged attention allocator.

From the ScaleOps analysis:

> "The KV cache (key-value cache) stores the attention keys and values computed for every input and output token during inference… The cache lives in GPU memory and scales with prompt length, output length, quantization, and the number of concurrent requests."

> "vLLM splits GPU memory into distinct pools… 2. KV Cache: Memory used for inference… 3. Prefix Cache: KV cache blocks from earlier requests, kept so later requests can reuse them instead of recomputing them."

— [ScaleOps blog on vLLM KV Cache and Prefix Cache](https://scaleops.com/blog/vllm-kv-cache-prefix-cache-gpu-memory/)

There is **no built-in CPU or disk backing** for vLLM's prefix cache. When GPU memory fills up, LRU eviction discards the least-recently-used blocks with no ability to persist them elsewhere.

Some external tools (like ScaleOps) can profile and right-size the GPU reservation, but this does not change where the cache is stored:

> "GPU Memory Optimization profiles each vLLM workload's GPU memory in production, split into model weights, active KV cache, and reusable prefix cache."

— [ScaleOps blog on vLLM KV Cache and Prefix Cache](https://scaleops.com/blog/vllm-kv-cache-prefix-cache-gpu-memory/)

## 5. Key Architectural Differences

| Aspect | vLLM Built-in Prefix Caching | LMCache |
|---|---|---|
| **Scope** | Single vLLM instance/process only | Cross-instance, cross-node via centralized coordinator |
| **Storage tiers** | GPU memory only (LRU eviction) | GPU → CPU RAM → Local Disk → Remote (Redis, S3, NIXL, etc.) |
| **Persistence across restarts** | No — cache is lost when vLLM restarts | Yes — when backed by disk or remote storage |
| **Fate-sharing with engines** | Yes — cache lives in the inference engine process | No — LMCache runs as a **standalone daemon** process |
> "LMCache, as a standalone daemon process, manages KV cache independently from the inference engine process, so that KV cache will not be lost even if the inference engine crashes (i.e., no fate-sharing with engines)."

— [LMCache GitHub README](https://github.com/lmcache/lmcache) |
| **Granularity** | vLLM paged attention blocks (16–64 KB) | Configurable chunks (default 256 tokens; often much larger) |
| **Compression** | None built-in | Yes — CacheGen compression and custom SERDE interface |
| **Non-prefix reuse** | Prefix-only (tokens must share a contiguous prefix from the start) | **CacheBlend** enables non-prefix KV reuse — selective recomputation for quality recovery |
> "Extend KV reuse beyond prefix caching by reusing cached KV blocks at any position in the prompt. This leverages CacheBlend to selectively recompute tokens for quality recovery."

— [LMCache GitHub README](https://github.com/lmcache/lmcache) |
| **PD disaggregation** | Not built-in for cross-engine transfer | Full support — prefill-decode disaggregation with KV transfer over NVLink, RDMA, or TCP via NIXL |
> "Support KV cache transfer from prefill workers to decode workers over NVLink, RDMA, or TCP through transport layers such as NIXL."

— [LMCache GitHub README](https://github.com/lmcache/lmcache) |
| **Management APIs** | Limited — no programmatic cache pinning, compression, or location lookup | Rich controller API: `lookup`, `pin/unpin`, `compress/decompress`, `move`, `clear` |
> "LMCache exposes APIs that allow developers and operators to locate, move, pin, and even compress KV cache extracted from inference engines."

— [LMCache arXiv Paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.09665v2) |
| **Observability** | Prefix cache hit rate metrics only | Rich KV-cache-specific metrics: request-level and token-level prefix cache hits, lifecycle, performance, health monitoring, KV cache events |
> "LMCache provides a rich set of KV cache observability metrics, including typical Kubernetes metrics (health monitoring, performance diagnostics), KV-cache-specific metrics (request-level and token-level prefix cache hits, lifecycle, request-level KV cache performance), management metrics (user-specific usage), and more."

— [LMCache GitHub README](https://github.com/lmcache/lmcache) |
| **Engine compatibility** | Tightly coupled to vLLM V1 engine | Engine-independent — connector interface supports vLLM and SGLang, and is vendor-neutral |
> "LMCache, as a standalone daemon process, manages KV cache independently from the inference engine process"
> "LMCache is vendor-neutral. It can be used as a KV cache layer for a range of mainstream open-source serving engines"

— [LMCache GitHub README](https://github.com/lmcache/lmcache) |
| **Adoption by others** | Native to vLLM | Integrated into NVIDIA Dynamo, llm-d, AIBrix, vLLM Production Stack |
> "Open-source adoptions, including NVIDIA dynamo project, llm-d project from RedHat, AIBrix project from ByteDance, and vLLM production stack project."

— [LMCache arXiv Paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.09665v2) |

## 6. When is LMCache Worth Adding Over vLLM's Built-in Prefix Caching?

### Scenarios where LMCache provides significant value:

**a) Multi-instance / multi-node deployments with shared prefixes**

vLLM's prefix cache only works within a single process. When you run multiple vLLM pods/replicas behind a load balancer, each instance maintains its own independent prefix cache, so shared prompts (system instructions, common RAG documents) are recomputed on every pod that receives the request.

> "vLLM's prefix caching breaks in distributed deployments"

— [llm-d blog on KV-Cache Wins](https://llm-d.ai/blog/kvcache-wins-you-can-see)

LMCache's coordinator enables cross-instance cache sharing — requests can be routed to the node that already holds the needed KV chunks.

**b) Contexts larger than GPU memory**

> "We observe that the required size of KV cache is now far exceeding the GPU memory capacity… the portion of KV cache that no longer fits in GPU memory has increased significantly over time, showing that GPU memory alone is insufficient for storing all caches."

— [LMCache arXiv Paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.09665v2)

When prompt + output lengths exceed available GPU KV cache memory, vLLM evicts prefixes via LRU with no fallback. LMCache offloads evicted chunks to CPU RAM or disk, so they can be reloaded when the same context is reused later.

**c) Long-running workloads requiring cache persistence across engine restarts**

Because LMCache can persist to disk or remote storage and its daemon process is separate from vLLM, cache survives vLLM crashes or restarts. vLLM's prefix cache is lost on every restart.

> "LMCache, as a standalone daemon process, manages KV cache independently from the inference engine process, so that KV cache will not be lost even if the inference engine crashes (i.e., no fate-sharing with engines)."

— [LMCache GitHub README](https://github.com/lmcache/lmcache)

**d) Prefill-decode disaggregation**

LMCache supports moving KV caches between separate prefill and decode nodes over NVLink/RDMA/Ethernet. vLLM does not have a built-in mechanism for this.

> "Prefill–decode (PD) disaggregation (i.e.,cross-engine KV cache transfer) splits inference into a prefill stage and a decode stage across different GPUs or nodes."

— [LMCache arXiv Paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.09665v2)

**e) Agentic workflows with structured/repeated tool calls**

> "LMCache consistently outperforms both built-in KV caching mechanisms in open-source inference frameworks and commercial inference APIs, delivering up to 15× higher throughput and at least 2× lower latency across diverse settings, including local prefix caching, distributed prefix reuse, and PD disaggregation."

— [LMCache arXiv Paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.09665v2)

Agentic workloads often involve the same system prompts, tool definitions, and previously retrieved documents being reused across many turns. LMCache's non-prefix reuse (CacheBlend) also allows reusing cached blocks that appear in the middle of a prompt, not just at the start.

**f) When GPU memory is a bottleneck and you need to reclaim it**

LMCache offloads unused KV blocks out of GPU memory to CPU/disk, freeing GPU memory for more active requests. vLLM's prefix cache competes with active KV cache for the same GPU memory pool.

> "LMCache incorporates a series of performance optimizations that make storing and loading KV cache efficient and practical in real deployments… LMCache stores/loads KV cache at a configurable chunk size, often much larger than page size, to fully utilize the bandwidth between storage devices and GPU memory."

— [LMCache arXiv Paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.09665v2)

### Scenarios where vLLM's built-in prefix caching is sufficient:

- **Single-instance deployment** with moderate context lengths that fit in GPU memory
- **Short-lived workloads** where cache persistence across restarts is not needed
- **Simple prompt patterns** where prefix-only reuse is adequate
- **When you want zero operational overhead** — LMCache adds a separate daemon, coordinator, and configuration surface

---

## Open Questions

1. **Direct benchmark comparisons**: I found references to LMCache outperforming built-in caching (the arXiv paper claims up to 15× throughput improvement and 2× lower latency), but did not fetch the full benchmark tables from that paper. A direct side-by-side benchmark under identical workloads would be valuable for quantifying the gains.

2. **vLLM's CPU offload API**: There is evidence of a native Python CPU DRAM cache implementation with ARC/LRU eviction policy in vLLM for general KV offload:
   > "vLLM's KV Offload API includes a native Python implementation with a CPU DRAM cache managed by an ARC or LRU eviction policy"

   — [arXiv paper on External KV Caching](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.11744v1)

   However, this appears to be a separate feature from prefix caching and its relationship to APC (whether it also serves as a prefix cache fallback) was not fully clarified. This warrants further investigation.

3. **Performance overhead of LMCache coordinator**: The latency impact of the centralized coordinator for cache lookups at high QPS was not benchmarked in the fetched sources.

4. **LMCache's multiprocess (MP) architecture specifics**: LMCache recently released a new MP architecture (2026/04) with claimed 10× Moe performance improvements. The detailed performance characteristics of the MP mode versus the legacy in-process mode were not fully explored.

   — [LMCache blog on MP architecture](https://blog.lmcache.ai/en/2026/04/03/lmcaches-new-architecture-boosts-moe-inference-performance-by-10x/)

- **Hidden states** — for encoder caching or blending ([LMCache Non-KV Caching](https://docs.lmcache.ai/non_kv_cache/index.html))
- **Encodings** — token-level embeddings

## 2. What Does vLLM's Built-in Prefix Caching Cache?

**vLLM's built-in Automatic Prefix Caching (APC) caches KV cache blocks** — the same K and V tensors, but at the granularity of vLLM's paged attention blocks (typically 16–64 KB per block, e.g., 62.5 KB for Llama-3.1-8B). From the vLLM documentation:

> "Prefix caching kv-cache blocks is a popular optimization in LLM inference to avoid redundant prompt computations. The core idea is simple – we cache the kv-cache blocks of processed requests, and reuse these blocks when a new request comes in with the same prefix as a previous request."

— [vLLM Automatic Prefix Caching](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/design/prefix_caching/)

vLLM indexes each block by a **content hash** of its tokens. When a new request arrives with a prefix matching a cached block's hash, vLLM skips the prefill computation for those blocks. This is enabled by default in the V1 engine and can be disabled with `--no-enable-prefix-caching` ([ScaleOps blog](https://scaleops.com/blog/vllm-kv-cache-prefix-cache-gpu-memory/)).

**Key limitation: vLLM's prefix cache is strictly within-GPU memory.** Every unique prefix, including one-off RAG queries and completed chat turns, is stored in GPU memory until memory is full. LRU eviction starts only then, and there is no shrink-on-idle. There is **no mechanism to persist cached prefixes to CPU, disk, or remote storage** across process restarts or to share them across vLLM instances.

— [ScaleOps blog on vLLM KV Cache and Prefix Cache](https://scaleops.com/blog/vllm-kv-cache-prefix-cache-gpu-memory/)

## 3. Where is LMCache's Cache Stored?

**LMCache uses a multi-tier, hierarchical storage system** with the following backends:

### Tier 1: GPU Memory
Holds the active working set of KV caches currently being used by the model.

— [LMCache Architecture Overview](https://docs.lmcache.ai/developer_guide/architecture.html)

### Tier 2: CPU DRAM
Acts as a "hot cache" for recently used KV chunks, using pinned memory for efficient GPU-CPU transfers. Configurable via `max_local_cpu_size` (default 5.0 GB).

> "When LMCACHE_LOCAL_CPU=True is used in conjunction with the disk backend or a remote backend… we can think of the CPU RAM as a 'hot cache' that will contain the 'hottest' (most recently accessed) subset of KV caches from Disk and Remote storage."

— [LMCache CPU RAM Storage](https://docs.lmcache.ai/legacy/kv_cache/storage_backends/cpu_ram.html)

Supports Linux hugepages (2 MiB) for reduced TLB pressure:

> "enabling Linux hugepages (2 MiB pages) can reduce TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer) pressure and improve memory access performance"

— [LMCache CPU RAM Storage](https://docs.lmcache.ai/legacy/kv_cache/storage_backends/cpu_ram.html)

### Tier 3: Local Disk (SSD/NVMe)
Stores KV cache chunks as individual `.pt` files with LRU/LFU/FIFO/MRU eviction policies. Configurable via `local_disk` and `max_local_disk_size`. Supports multi-path NVMe sharding.

> "The disk backend will create one file per KV cache chunk as they are stored, evicting if capacity is exceeded (LRU currently)"

— [LMCache Local Storage](https://docs.lmcache.ai/legacy/kv_cache/storage_backends/local_storage.html)

### Tier 4: Remote Storage
LMCache supports a wide range of remote/distributed backends through pluggable connectors:

- **Redis / Valkey** — in-memory key-value store
- **S3-compatible object storage**
- **NVIDIA NIXL** — peer-to-peer GPU transfer (NVLink, RDMA, TCP)
- **Mooncake** — distributed KV cache sharing
- **InfiniStore**
- **Google Cloud Bigtable**
- **Azure Blob Storage**
- **Aerospike**
- **Hugging Face Buckets**
- **WQS**
- **DAX**

> "Through this interface, LMCache supports storage backends including CPU RAM, local disk (SSD), Redis/Valkey, Mooncake, InfiniStore, S3-compatible object storage, NIXL, and GDS."

— [LMCache GitHub README](https://github.com/lmcache/lmcache)

### Cross-Instance Coordination
LMCache includes a centralized **KV cache controller** (standalone process) for global metadata management, enabling cache lookups and sharing across multiple vLLM instances on different nodes:

> "LMCache operates as a distributed caching system built around a centralized KV cache controller responsible for global metadata management, cache manipulation, and request routing."

— [LMCache arXiv Paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.09665v2)

## 4. Where is vLLM's Built-in Prefix Caching Stored?

**vLLM's prefix cache lives entirely in GPU memory.** The KV cache blocks are stored in the GPU memory pool managed by vLLM's paged attention allocator.

From the ScaleOps analysis:

> "The KV cache (key-value cache) stores the attention keys and values computed for every input and output token during inference… The cache lives in GPU memory and scales with prompt length, output length, quantization, and the number of concurrent requests."

> "vLLM splits GPU memory into distinct pools… 2. KV Cache: Memory used for inference… 3. Prefix Cache: KV cache blocks from earlier requests, kept so later requests can reuse them instead of recomputing them."

— [ScaleOps blog on vLLM KV Cache and Prefix Cache](https://scaleops.com/blog/vllm-kv-cache-prefix-cache-gpu-memory/)

There is **no built-in CPU or disk backing** for vLLM's prefix cache. When GPU memory fills up, LRU eviction discards the least-recently-used blocks with no ability to persist them elsewhere.

Some external tools (like ScaleOps) can profile and right-size the GPU reservation, but this does not change where the cache is stored:

> "GPU Memory Optimization profiles each vLLM workload's GPU memory in production, split into model weights, active KV cache, and reusable prefix cache."

— [ScaleOps blog on vLLM KV Cache and Prefix Cache](https://scaleops.com/blog/vllm-kv-cache-prefix-cache-gpu-memory/)

| Aspect | vLLM Built-in Prefix Caching | LMCache |
|---|---|---|
| **Scope** | Single vLLM instance/process only | Cross-instance, cross-node via centralized coordinator |
| **Storage tiers** | GPU memory only (LRU eviction) | GPU → CPU RAM → Local Disk → Remote (Redis, S3, NIXL, etc.) |
| **Persistence across restarts** | No — cache is lost when vLLM restarts | Yes — when backed by disk or remote storage |
| **Fate-sharing with engines** | Yes — cache lives in the inference engine process | No — LMCache runs as a **standalone daemon** process |
> "LMCache, as a standalone daemon process, manages KV cache independently from the inference engine process, so that KV cache will not be lost even if the inference engine crashes (i.e., no fate-sharing with engines)."

— [LMCache GitHub README](https://github.com/lmcache/lmcache) |
| **Granularity** | vLLM paged attention blocks (16–64 KB) | Configurable chunks (default 256 tokens; often much larger) |
| **Compression** | None built-in | Yes — CacheGen compression and custom SERDE interface |

> "LMCache exposes APIs that allow developers and operators to locate, move, pin, and even compress KV cache extracted from inference engines."

— [LMCache arXiv Paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.09665v2) |
| **Observability** | Prefix cache hit rate metrics only | Rich KV-cache-specific metrics: request-level and token-level prefix cache hits, lifecycle, performance, health monitoring, KV cache events |
> "LMCache provides a rich set of KV cache observability metrics, including typical Kubernetes metrics (health monitoring, performance diagnostics), KV-cache-specific metrics (request-level and token-level prefix cache hits, lifecycle, request-level KV cache performance), management metrics (user-specific usage), and more."

— [LMCache GitHub README](https://github.com/lmcache/lmcache) |
| **Engine compatibility** | Tightly coupled to vLLM V1 engine | Engine-independent — connector interface supports vLLM and SGLang, and is vendor-neutral |
> "LMCache, as a standalone daemon process, manages KV cache independently from the inference engine process"
> "LMCache is vendor-neutral. It can be used as a KV cache layer for a range of mainstream open-source serving engines"

— [LMCache GitHub README](https://github.com/lmcache/lmcache) |
| **Adoption by others** | Native to vLLM | Integrated into NVIDIA Dynamo, llm-d, AIBrix, vLLM Production Stack |
> "Open-source adoptions, including NVIDIA dynamo project, llm-d project from RedHat, AIBrix project from ByteDance, and vLLM production stack project."

— [LMCache arXiv Paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.09665v2) |

## 6. When is LMCache Worth Adding Over vLLM's Built-in Prefix Caching?

### Scenarios where LMCache provides significant value:

**a) Multi-instance / multi-node deployments with shared prefixes**

vLLM's prefix cache only works within a single process. When you run multiple vLLM pods/replicas behind a load balancer, each instance maintains its own independent prefix cache, so shared prompts (system instructions, common RAG documents) are recomputed on every pod that receives the request.

> "vLLM's prefix caching breaks in distributed deployments"

— [llm-d blog on KV-Cache Wins](https://llm-d.ai/blog/kvcache-wins-you-can-see)

LMCache's coordinator enables cross-instance cache sharing — requests can be routed to the node that already holds the needed KV chunks.

**b) Contexts larger than GPU memory**

> "We observe that the required size of KV cache is now far exceeding the GPU memory capacity… the portion of KV cache that no longer fits in GPU memory has increased significantly over time, showing that GPU memory alone is insufficient for storing all caches."

— [LMCache arXiv Paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.09665v2)

When prompt + output lengths exceed available GPU KV cache memory, vLLM evicts prefixes via LRU with no fallback. LMCache offloads evicted chunks to CPU RAM or disk, so they can be reloaded when the same context is reused later.

**c) Long-running workloads requiring cache persistence across engine restarts**

Because LMCache can persist to disk or remote storage and its daemon process is separate from vLLM, cache survives vLLM crashes or restarts. vLLM's prefix cache is lost on every restart.

> "LMCache, as a standalone daemon process, manages KV cache independently from the inference engine process, so that KV cache will not be lost even if the inference engine crashes (i.e., no fate-sharing with engines)."

— [LMCache GitHub README](https://github.com/lmcache/lmcache)

**d) Prefill-decode disaggregation**

LMCache supports moving KV caches between separate prefill and decode nodes over NVLink/RDMA/Ethernet. vLLM does not have a built-in mechanism for this.

> "Prefill–decode (PD) disaggregation (i.e.,cross-engine KV cache transfer) splits inference into a prefill stage and a decode stage across different GPUs or nodes."

— [LMCache arXiv Paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.09665v2)

**e) Agentic workflows with structured/repeated tool calls**

> "LMCache consistently outperforms both built-in KV caching mechanisms in open-source inference frameworks and commercial inference APIs, delivering up to 15× higher throughput and at least 2× lower latency across diverse settings, including local prefix caching, distributed prefix reuse, and PD disaggregation."

— [LMCache arXiv Paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.09665v2)

Agentic workloads often involve the same system prompts, tool definitions, and previously retrieved documents being reused across many turns. LMCache's non-prefix reuse (CacheBlend) also allows reusing cached blocks that appear in the middle of a prompt, not just at the start.

**f) When GPU memory is a bottleneck and you need to reclaim it**

LMCache offloads unused KV blocks out of GPU memory to CPU/disk, freeing GPU memory for more active requests. vLLM's prefix cache competes with active KV cache for the same GPU memory pool.

> "LMCache incorporates a series of performance optimizations that make storing and loading KV cache efficient and practical in real deployments… LMCache stores/loads KV cache at a configurable chunk size, often much larger than page size, to fully utilize the bandwidth between storage devices and GPU memory."

— [LMCache arXiv Paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.09665v2)

### Scenarios where vLLM's built-in prefix caching is sufficient:

- **Single-instance deployment** with moderate context lengths that fit in GPU memory
- **Short-lived workloads** where cache persistence across restarts is not needed
- **Simple prompt patterns** where prefix-only reuse is adequate
- **When you want zero operational overhead** — LMCache adds a separate daemon, coordinator, and configuration surface

## PostgreSQL: REPEATABLE READ vs. SERIALIZABLE Isolation Levels

### Source

PostgreSQL 18 Documentation, Section 13.2 — [Transaction Isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html)

### The Core Difference

Both levels build on PostgreSQL's **Snapshot Isolation** (MVCC), meaning that both only see data committed before the transaction began — never uncommitted data, and never changes committed by concurrent transactions during their own execution. Every query within a single transaction sees the same stable snapshot (unlike `READ COMMITTED`, which takes a fresh snapshot per statement).

The critical distinction is that **`SERIALIZABLE` adds monitoring for serialization anomalies**, while `REPEATABLE READ` does not. The documentation puts it plainly:

> "This isolation level [Serializable] works exactly the same as Repeatable Read except that it also monitors for conditions which could make execution of a concurrent set of serializable transactions behave in a manner inconsistent with all possible serial (one at a time) executions of those transactions."

In other words:

| Isolation Level | Dirty Read | Nonrepeatable Read | Phantom Read | **Serialization Anomaly** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `REPEATABLE READ` | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ (PostgreSQL goes beyond the standard) | ✅ **Allowed** |
| `SERIALIZABLE` | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ **Prevented** (via rollback) |

> "The table also shows that PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read implementation does not allow phantom reads. This is acceptable under the SQL standard because the standard specifies which anomalies must *not* occur at certain isolation levels; higher guarantees are acceptable."

### What Is a Serialization Anomaly?

The documentation defines it precisely:

> "The result of successfully committing a group of transactions is inconsistent with all possible orderings of running those transactions one at a time."

### Concrete Example (from the docs)

Consider a table `mytab`:

```
 class | value
-------+-------
     1 |    10
     1 |    20
     2 |   100
     2 |   200
```

Transaction A computes `SELECT SUM(value) FROM mytab WHERE class = 1;` → gets **30**, then inserts 30 as a new row with `class = 2`. Concurrently, Transaction B computes `SELECT SUM(value) FROM mytab WHERE class = 2;` → gets **300**, and inserts 300 as a new row with `class = 1`. Both try to commit.

At **REPEATABLE READ**, **both would be allowed to commit** — but there is no serial order that produces this result. At **SERIALIZABLE**, one is rolled back with:

> `ERROR:  could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions`

The rationale: "if A had executed before B, B would have computed the sum 330, not 300, and similarly the other order would have resulted in a different sum computed by A."

### What Is Prevented at Each Level

**REPEATABLE READ prevents:**
- **Dirty reads** — reading uncommitted data.
- **Nonrepeatable reads** — a row's value changing between two reads in the same transaction.
- **Phantom reads** — PostgreSQL goes beyond the SQL standard here; a query's result set is stable for the entire transaction.

The documentation notes:

> "This is a stronger guarantee than is required by the SQL standard for this isolation level, and prevents all of the phenomena described in Table 13.1 except for serialization anomalies."

**SERIALIZABLE additionally prevents:**
- **Serialization anomalies** — the only anomaly `REPEATABLE READ` permits. This means the committed result of concurrent transactions is always equivalent to some serial (one-at-a-time) execution order.

The documentation emphasizes:

> "The guarantee that any set of successfully committed concurrent Serializable transactions will have the same effect as if they were run one at a time means that if you can demonstrate that a single transaction, as written, will do the right thing when run by itself, you can have confidence that it will do the right thing in any mix of Serializable transactions, even without any information about what those other transactions might do, or it will not successfully commit."

### SQLSTATE for Serialization Failure

Serialization failures always return SQLSTATE **'40001'**:

> "It is important that an environment which uses this technique have a generalized way of handling serialization failures (which always return with an SQLSTATE value of **'40001'**)"

### How SERIALIZABLE Works Under the Hood

The documentation explains:

> "To guarantee true serializability PostgreSQL uses *predicate locking*, which means that it keeps locks which allow it to determine when a write would have had an impact on the result of a previous read from a concurrent transaction, had it run first."

These predicate locks appear in `pg_locks` with mode `SIReadLock`. They **do not cause blocking** but impose overhead and may trigger serialization failures when read/write dependencies among concurrent transactions are detected.

### What Happens on a Serialization Failure

Applications must be prepared to retry:

> "When an application receives this error message, it should abort the current transaction and retry the whole transaction from the beginning."

There are two possible error messages:

1. **`ERROR: could not serialize access due to concurrent update`** — arises at `REPEATABLE READ` when the transaction tries to update/delete a row that was modified by another committed transaction.
2. **`ERROR: could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions`** — arises at `SERIALIZABLE` when a serialization anomaly is detected.

### Implementation Notes

- **REPEATABLE READ** = **Snapshot Isolation** (as named in academic literature).
- **SERIALIZABLE** = **Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)** — Snapshot Isolation plus anomaly detection. The docs cite: *"Some differences in behavior and performance may be observed when compared with other systems that use a traditional locking technique. Please see [ports12] for detailed information."*

Prior to PostgreSQL 9.1, `SERIALIZABLE` behaved identically to the current `REPEATABLE READ`. The legacy behavior is what `REPEATABLE READ` maps to today, and `SERIALIZABLE` was upgraded to true SSI.

<acknowledgement>: Understood. I will search the official vLLM documentation to find the default value and purpose of the `--gpu-memory-utilization` option.



## Findings: `--gpu-memory-utilization` in vLLM

### Default value: **0.92** (92%)

This is defined in the `CacheConfig` dataclass in vLLM's source code:

**Source:** [`vllm/config/cache.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/config/cache.py)
```python
@config
class CacheConfig:
    DEFAULT_GPU_MEMORY_UTILIZATION: ClassVar[float] = 0.92
```

The `gpu_memory_utilization` field itself is declared as:
```python
gpu_memory_utilization: float | None = Field(default=None, gt=0, le=1)
```

### What it controls

From the source code docstring:

> "The **fraction of GPU memory to be used for the model executor**, which can range from 0 to 1. For example, a value of 0.5 would imply 50% GPU memory utilization. This is a **per-instance limit**, and only applies to the current vLLM instance."

In practice, this fraction determines the **total GPU VRAM budget** available to vLLM. From that budget, vLLM:
1. Sets aside memory for the **model weights** (loaded into GPU VRAM)
2. Uses the remainder to pre-allocate the **KV cache** (via the PagedAttention block allocator)

So the higher the value, the more KV cache space is available — which directly impacts throughput and the number of concurrent requests. Conversely, lowering it leaves more VRAM for other processes on the same GPU.

### Resolved value (dynamic default)

The *effective* default depends on whether the **extensible KV cache** feature is enabled. The `resolved_gpu_memory_utilization` property in `CacheConfig` shows:

```python
@property
def resolved_gpu_memory_utilization(self -> float:
    if self.gpu_memory_utilization is not None:
        return self.gpu_memory_utilization          # user-set value
    if self.enable_extensible_kv_cache:
        return 1.0                                    # extensible mode
    return self.DEFAULT_GPU_MEMORY_UTILIZATION        # 0.92 — standard mode
```

- **Standard mode** (extensible KV cache disabled): defaults to **0.92**
- **Extensible KV cache mode** (enabled by default on CUDA/ROCm): defaults to **1.0** (100%), because the KV cache is dynamically sized from actual free memory rather than a fixed pre-allocation.

### Historical note

vLLM's original default was **0.95** but was changed to **0.9** (later updated to **0.92**) due to memory profiling edge cases — see [GitHub Issue #1018](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/1018). The current default of 0.92 is the value in the main branch as of this writing.

### References

| Source | URL |
|--------|-----|
| Source code (`CacheConfig`) | https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/config/cache.py |
| Engine args (CLI docstring) | https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/configuration/engine_args/ |
| Issue on default value change | https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/1018 |

---

**Assumption:** This brief compares vLLM's built-in Automatic Prefix Caching (APC) with LMCache as standalone daemon, based on official docs, the vLLM design doc, the LMCache MP architecture doc, and independently published benchmarks.

---

## 1. What Each One Caches

### vLLM Built-in Automatic Prefix Caching

- **Data cached:** KV cache *blocks* (key-value tensors produced by the attention layers). vLLM breaks the prompt into fixed-size blocks and caches only *full* blocks. Each block is identified by a hash computed from the block's own token IDs, its parent hash (the prefix chain), and extra context such as LoRA IDs, multi-modal input hashes (images), and optional per-request `cache_salt` for tenant isolation [vLLM Prefix Caching Design](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/docs/design/prefix_caching.md).
- **Scope:** Prefix-only — a cached block is reused only when a new request's prefix *starts with* the same token sequence.
- **Granularity:** Block-level (fixed size, typically 16–32 tokens for full-attention models). Partial matches within a block force full recompute [vLLM Prefix Caching Design](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/docs/design/prefix_caching.md).
- **Hashing:** Default SHA256 (since v0.11), or faster `xxhash`/`xxhash_cbor`/`sha256_cbor` via `--prefix-caching-hash-algo` [vLLM Prefix Caching Design](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/docs/design/prefix_caching.md).

### LMCache

- **Data cached:** KV cache tensors (the same key-value state), stored and retrieved via a standalone daemon process [LMCache README](https://github.com/lmcache/lmcache) · [LMCache MP Overview](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/index.html).
- **Scope:** Prefix reuse (like vLLM's APC) **plus** non-prefix KV reuse. With the `BlendModule` (opt-in via `--engine-type blend`), LMCache can match and retrieve cached KV blocks at *any position* in the prompt, not just at the prefix boundary, using a paged-aware sparse-prefetch pipeline [LMCache MP Overview](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/index.html).
- **Compression:** Pluggable SERDE layer — CacheGen, TurboQuant, encryption, and custom compression are supported to reduce the storage footprint [LMCache MP Overview](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/index.html).
- **Disaggregated PD transfer:** LMCache can transfer KV cache directly from prefill workers to decode workers over NVLink, RDMA, or TCP — a different use case from caching across requests but built on the same KV storage layer [LMCache README](https://github.com/lmcache/lmcache) · [LMCache MP Overview](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/index.html).

---

## 2. Where the Cache Is Stored

### vLLM

| Tier | Medium | Scope |
|------|--------|-------|
| L1 | **GPU memory** (PagedAttention blocks) | In-process, per-vLLM-server |
| L2 (optional) | **CPU RAM** (via `kv_offloading_backend` / `OffloadingConnector`) | Still in-process, per-vLLM-server |

- **Scope:** The cache is *ephemeral and in-process*. It lives inside the vLLM process and is **lost entirely on restart or crash** [vLLM Prefix Caching Design](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/docs/design/prefix_caching.md) · [vLLM KV Offloading Usage](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/features/kv_offloading_usage/).
- **Sharing:** No cross-server or cross-node sharing. Each vLLM instance has its own private cache [vLLM Prefix Caching Design](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/docs/design/prefix_caching.md).

### LMCache

| Tier | Medium | Description |
|------|--------|-------------|
| L1 | CPU DRAM (default), Device-DAX / CXL, or NVMe via GPUDirect Storage (GDS) | Managed by `L1Manager` with state machine; lazy-growth up to `--l1-size-gb` [LMCache MP Overview](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/index.html) |
| L2 | Redis/Valkey, S3, Mooncake, Bigtable, Aerospike, Hf3fs, NIXL (GDS, POSIX, HF3FS), and more | Async push/pull via `L2Adapter` pluggable interface; multi-tier cascade supported [LMCache MP Overview](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/l2_storage/index.html) |

- **Scope:** **Standalone daemon process** (`lmcache server`). vLLM connects via ZMQ or gRPC. This process isolation means LMCache and vLLM have *no fate-sharing* — a vLLM crash does not invalidate LMCache's storage, and vice-versa [LMCache README](https://github.com/lmcache/lmcache) · [LMCache MP Overview](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/index.html).
- **Sharing:** Multiple vLLM pods on one node can share a single LMCache server's L1. Cross-node sharing is supported via **P2P KV cache sharing** (RDMA/NIXL or Mooncake Transfer Engine) with a coordinator for peer discovery [LMCache P2P](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/p2p.html).
- **Observability:** Built-in Prometheus metrics, OTel tracing, and telemetry events for cache hits, evictions, and lifecycle [LMCache MP Overview](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/index.html).

---

## 3. When LMCache Is Worth Adding Over vLLM APC

### LMCache provides clear value when one or more of the following applies:

**a. Cache must survive vLLM restarts or crashes.**
This is the single most-cited differentiator. vLLM's cache — whether GPU-only or CPU-offloaded — is wiped on restart. LMCache's daemon persists independently. In head-to-head testing, a vLLM restart dropped TTFT from ~112 ms back to ~1.35 s (full recomputation), while LMCache immediately resumed at ~141 ms with a 99.9% hit rate after vLLM rebooted [MindStudio blog](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents).

**b. The working set exceeds GPU memory *and* available CPU RAM.**
vLLM CPU offload handles the GPU→CPU spill path but not beyond. LMCache's L2 adapters (Redis, S3, NVMe, etc.) provide disk-backed or remote storage for when the cache no longer fits in RAM [LMCache MP Overview](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/index.html).

**c. You need cross-node KV sharing.**
vLLM APC is strictly single-node. In multi-replica deployments (Kubernetes, cloud), the same prefix may hit different worker nodes and be recomputed from scratch. LMCache's P2P mode lets any node's LMCache server read KV directly from a peer's memory over RDMA [LMCache P2P](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/p2p.html).

**d. You need non-prefix KV reuse (CacheBlend).**
For RAG workloads where retrieved document chunks appear in *arbitrary* positions within the prompt — not just as a common prefix — LMCache's `BlendModule` can match and retrieve cached KV at any offset and selectively recompute the surrounding tokens [LMCache README](https://github.com/lmcache/lmcache) · [LMCache MP Overview](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/index.html).

**e. Disaggregated prefill-decode or multi-engine setups.**
If your architecture separates the prefill and decode stages onto different GPUs, LMCache can transfer KV from the prefill worker to the decode worker, or share KV across heterogeneous serving engines (vLLM, SGLang) — something vLLM's internal APC cannot do [LMCache README](https://github.com/lmcache/lmcache) · [LMCache MP Overview](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/index.html).

**f. KV cache compression is needed.**
LMCache's SERDE pluggable interface supports CacheGen and TurboQuant compression, reducing storage footprint and transfer bandwidth — not natively available in vLLM's APC [LMCache MP Overview](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/index.html).

### When vLLM APC alone is sufficient (LMCache adds complexity for little gain):

- **Single-node, steady-state serving** where the cache fits in GPU memory or CPU RAM. In testing, LMCache performed roughly on par with vLLM's CPU-offloaded mode (140 ms vs 164 ms mean TTFT) but added operational overhead [MindStudio blog](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents).
- **Workloads with low prefix overlap** (e.g., diverse conversational prompts). LMCache showed worse TTFT and throughput than vLLM alone on ShareGPT-like workloads because the overhead outweighed the sparse reuse benefits [LMCache vs vLLM experiment](https://github.com/aneeshp10/LMCache-and-vLLM-Prefix-Caching).
- **Low-to-moderate memory pressure.** An independent Colab experiment found LMCache was *consistently worse* than vLLM APC alone until extreme memory pressure with highly repeated prefixes was reached; under those conditions, LMCache's offload/retrieval overhead degraded ITL even when TTFT improved [LMCache vs vLLM experiment](https://github.com/aneeshp10/LMCache-and-vLLM-Prefix-Caching).

### Concrete benchmark numbers from the LMCache docs (long-doc-qa workload on Qwen3-8B, one A100 node):

| Metric | vLLM alone | vLLM + LMCache |
|--------|-----------|----------------|
| Mean TTFT | 757 ms | **185 ms** (75% reduction) |
| Benchmark duration | 23.47 s | **13.79 s** (41% reduction) |

LMCache improved TTFT because evicted blocks were restored from CPU RAM instead of recomputed [LMCache Benchmarking](https://docs.lmcache.ai/getting_started/benchmarking.html).

---

## 4. Known Limitations

### vLLM APC

- **Ephemeral cache:** Lost on restart/crash. No persistence [vLLM Prefix Caching Design](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/docs/design/prefix_caching.md).
- **Single-node only:** No cross-server or cross-node sharing [vLLM Prefix Caching Design](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/docs/design/prefix_caching.md).
- **Prefix-only reuse:** Cannot reuse KV blocks appearing mid-prompt [vLLM Prefix Caching Design](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/docs/design/prefix_caching.md).
- **Block-boundary matching:** Partial matches within a block force full recompute [vLLM Prefix Caching Design](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/docs/design/prefix_caching.md).
- **Potential duplication:** In v1, append-only block tables can create redundant cached blocks (same hash, separate IDs) until the request is freed, slightly wasting GPU memory [vLLM Prefix Caching Design](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/docs/design/prefix_caching.md).

### LMCache

- **Added operational complexity:** A separate daemon process with its own memory, configuration, and lifecycle; restart coordination is non-trivial [MindStudio blog](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents).
- **Can degrade ITL:** Even when TTFT improves, the offload/retrieval path adds latency to the decode phase, and end-to-end throughput may not improve [LMCache vs vLLM experiment](https://github.com/aneeshp10/LMCache-and-vLLM-Prefix-Caching).
- **Memory release delays during restart:** Dead vLLM GPU memory must be released before a new vLLM instance starts; LMCache enforces a 30-second minimum wait, slowing overall restart time [MindStudio blog](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents).
- **Model support gaps:** Newer or non-standard architectures may lack vLLM/LMCache integration at test time; hybrid models (Mamba + attention) caused offload to fail in one test [MindStudio blog](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents).
- **P2P limitations:** Read-only (a node never writes into a peer's memory); one-hop only (reads are not chained across multiple peers) [LMCache P2P](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/p2p.html).

---

## 5. Open Questions

- **vLLM's latest native KV offloading capabilities:** The vLLM docs were rate-limited (HTTP 429), so some details of the latest `OffloadingConnector` / hybrid KV cache manager (from the `kv_offloading_usage/` guide) could not be fully fetched. The claims above are based on the MindStudio blog and the `kv_offloading_usage/` snippet; a full re-check against the live docs is recommended.
- **Multi-tenant cache isolation in LMCache:** LMCache supports `cache_salt` via `IsolatedLRU` eviction and per-tenant quotas, but the exact security posture and cross-tenant attack surface has not been independently audited in the sources reviewed.
- **Cross-engine compatibility breadth:** LMCache claims support for vLLM, SGLang, and others, but real-world testing across all supported engines and model families (especially MoE and linear-attention hybrids) is still limited to a subset documented on the LMCache docs page [LMCache MP Overview](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/index.html).

---

- **vLLM KV Offloading Usage (official):** https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/features/kv_offloading_usage/
