With the `BlendModule` (opt-in via `--engine-type blend`), LMCache can match and retrieve cached KV blocks at *any position* in the prompt, not just at the prefix boundary, using a paged-aware sparse-prefetch pipeline [LMCache MP Overview](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/index.html).
- **Compression:** Pluggable SERDE layer — CacheGen, TurboQuant, encryption, and custom compression are supported to reduce the storage footprint [LMCache MP Overview](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/index.html).
- **Disaggregated PD transfer:** LMCache can transfer KV cache directly from prefill workers to decode workers over NVLink, RDMA, or TCP — a different use case from caching across requests but built on the same KV storage layer [LMCache README](https://github.com/lmcache/lmcache) · [LMCache MP Overview](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/index.html).

---

## 2. Where the Cache Is Stored

### vLLM

| Tier | Medium | Scope |
|------|--------|-------|
| L1 | **GPU memory** (PagedAttention blocks) | In-process, per-vLLM-server |
| L2 (optional) | **CPU RAM** (via `kv_offloading_backend` / `OffloadingConnector`) | Still in-process, per-vLLM-server |

- **Scope:** The cache is *ephemeral and in-process*. It lives inside the vLLM process and is **lost entirely on restart or crash** [vLLM Prefix Caching Design](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/docs/design/prefix_caching.md) · [vLLM KV Offloading Usage](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/features/kv_offloading_usage/).
- **Sharing:** No cross-server or cross-node sharing. Each vLLM instance has its own private cache [vLLM Prefix Caching Design](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/docs/design/prefix_caching.md).

### LMCache

| Tier | Medium | Description |
|------|--------|-------------|
| L1 | CPU DRAM (default), Device-DAX / CXL, or NVMe via GPUDirect Storage (GDS) | Managed by `L1Manager` with state machine; lazy-growth up to `--l1-size-gb` [LMCache MP Overview](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/index.html) |
| L2 | Redis/Valkey, S3, Mooncake, Bigtable, Aerospike, Hf3fs, NIXL (GDS, POSIX, HF3FS), and more | Async push/pull via `L2Adapter` pluggable interface; multi-tier cascade supported [LMCache MP Overview](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/l2_storage/index.html) |

- **Scope:** **Standalone daemon process** (`lmcache server`). vLLM connects via ZMQ or gRPC. This process isolation means LMCache and vLLM have *no fate-sharing* — a vLLM crash does not invalidate LMCache's storage, and vice-versa [LMCache README](https://github.com/lmcache/lmcache) · [LMCache MP Overview](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/index.html).
- **Sharing:** Multiple vLLM pods on one node can share a single LMCache server's L1. Cross-node sharing is supported via **P2P KV cache sharing** (RDMA/NIXL or Mooncake Transfer Engine) with a coordinator for peer discovery [LMCache P2P](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/p2p.html).
- **Observability:** Built-in Prometheus metrics, OTel tracing, and telemetry events for cache hits, evictions, and lifecycle [LMCache MP Overview](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/index.html).

---

## 3. When LMCache Is Worth Adding Over vLLM APC

### LMCache provides clear value when one or more of the following applies:

**a. Cache must survive vLLM restarts or crashes.**
This is the single most-cited differentiator. vLLM's cache — whether GPU-only or CPU-offloaded — is wiped on restart. LMCache's daemon persists independently. In head-to-head testing, a vLLM restart dropped TTFT from ~112 ms back to ~1.35 s (full recomputation), while LMCache immediately resumed at ~141 ms with a 99.9% hit rate after vLLM rebooted [MindStudio blog](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents).

**b. The working set exceeds GPU memory *and* available CPU RAM.**
vLLM CPU offload handles the GPU→CPU spill path but not beyond. LMCache's L2 adapters (Redis, S3, NVMe, etc.) provide disk-backed or remote storage for when the cache no longer fits in RAM [LMCache MP Overview](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/index.html).

**c. You need cross-node KV sharing.**
vLLM APC is strictly single-node. In multi-replica deployments (Kubernetes, cloud), the same prefix may hit different worker nodes and be recomputed from scratch. LMCache's P2P mode lets any node's LMCache server read KV directly from a peer's memory over RDMA [LMCache P2P](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/p2p.html).

**d. You need non-prefix KV reuse (CacheBlend).**
For RAG workloads where retrieved document chunks appear in *arbitrary* positions within the prompt — not just as a common prefix — LMCache's `BlendModule` can match and retrieve cached KV at any offset and selectively recompute the surrounding tokens [LMCache README](https://github.com/lmcache/lmcache) · [LMCache MP Overview](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/index.html).

**e. Disaggregated prefill-decode or multi-engine setups.**
If your architecture separates the prefill and decode stages onto different GPUs, LMCache can transfer KV from the prefill worker to the decode worker, or share KV across heterogeneous serving engines (vLLM, SGLang) — something vLLM's internal APC cannot do [LMCache README](https://github.com/lmcache/lmcache) · [LMCache MP Overview](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/index.html).

**f. KV cache compression is needed.**
LMCache's SERDE pluggable interface supports CacheGen and TurboQuant compression, reducing storage footprint and transfer bandwidth — not natively available in vLLM's APC [LMCache MP Overview](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/index.html).

### When vLLM APC alone is sufficient (LMCache adds complexity for little gain):

- **Single-node, steady-state serving** where the cache fits in GPU memory or CPU RAM. In testing, LMCache performed roughly on par with vLLM's CPU-offloaded mode (140 ms vs 164 ms mean TTFT) but added operational overhead [MindStudio blog](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents).
- **Workloads with low prefix overlap** (e.g., diverse conversational prompts). LMCache showed worse TTFT and throughput than vLLM alone on ShareGPT-like workloads because the overhead outweighed the sparse reuse benefits [LMCache vs vLLM experiment](https://github.com/aneeshp10/LMCache-and-vLLM-Prefix-Caching).
- **Low-to-moderate memory pressure.** An independent Colab experiment found LMCache was *consistently worse* than vLLM APC alone until extreme memory pressure with highly repeated prefixes was reached; under those conditions, LMCache's offload/retrieval overhead degraded ITL even when TTFT improved [LMCache vs vLLM experiment](https://github.com/aneeshp10/LMCache-and-vLLM-Prefix-Caching).

### Concrete benchmark numbers from the LMCache docs (long-doc-qa workload on Qwen3-8B, one A100 node):

| Metric | vLLM alone | vLLM + LMCache |
|--------|-----------|----------------|
| Mean TTFT | 757 ms | **185 ms** (75% reduction) |
| Benchmark duration | 23.47 s | **13.79 s** (41% reduction) |

LMCache improved TTFT because evicted blocks were restored from CPU RAM instead of recomputed [LMCache Benchmarking](https://docs.lmcache.ai/getting_started/benchmarking.html).

---

## 4. Known Limitations

### vLLM APC

- **Ephemeral cache:** Lost on restart/crash. No persistence [vLLM Prefix Caching Design](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/docs/design/prefix_caching.md).
- **Single-node only:** No cross-server or cross-node sharing [vLLM Prefix Caching Design](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/docs/design/prefix_caching.md).
- **Prefix-only reuse:** Cannot reuse KV blocks appearing mid-prompt [vLLM Prefix Caching Design](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/docs/design/prefix_caching.md).
- **Block-boundary matching:** Partial matches within a block force full recompute [vLLM Prefix Caching Design](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/docs/design/prefix_caching.md).
- **Potential duplication:** In v1, append-only block tables can create redundant cached blocks (same hash, separate IDs) until the request is freed, slightly wasting GPU memory [vLLM Prefix Caching Design](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/docs/design/prefix_caching.md).

### LMCache

- **Added operational complexity:** A separate daemon process with its own memory, configuration, and lifecycle; restart coordination is non-trivial [MindStudio blog](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents).
- **Can degrade ITL:** Even when TTFT improves, the offload/retrieval path adds latency to the decode phase, and end-to-end throughput may not improve [LMCache vs vLLM experiment](https://github.com/aneeshp10/LMCache-and-vLLM-Prefix-Caching).
- **Memory release delays during restart:** Dead vLLM GPU memory must be released before a new vLLM instance starts; LMCache enforces a 30-second minimum wait, slowing overall restart time [MindStudio blog](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents).
- **Model support gaps:** Newer or non-standard architectures may lack vLLM/LMCache integration at test time; hybrid models (Mamba + attention) caused offload to fail in one test [MindStudio blog](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents).
- **P2P limitations:** Read-only (a node never writes into a peer's memory); one-hop only (reads are not chained across multiple peers) [LMCache P2P](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/p2p.html).

---

## 5. Open Questions

- **vLLM's latest native KV offloading capabilities:** The vLLM docs were rate-limited (HTTP 429), so some details of the latest `OffloadingConnector` / hybrid KV cache manager (from the `kv_offloading_usage/` guide) could not be fully fetched. The claims above are based on the MindStudio blog and the `kv_offloading_usage/` snippet; a full re-check against the live docs is recommended.
- **Multi-tenant cache isolation in LMCache:** LMCache supports `cache_salt` via `IsolatedLRU` eviction and per-tenant quotas, but the exact security posture and cross-tenant attack surface has not been independently audited in the sources reviewed.
- **Cross-engine compatibility breadth:** LMCache claims support for vLLM, SGLang, and others, but real-world testing across all supported engines and model families (especially MoE and linear-attention hybrids) is still limited to a subset documented on the LMCache docs page [LMCache MP Overview](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/index.html).

## REPEATABLE READ vs. SERIALIZABLE in PostgreSQL

### What each level prevents (from Table 13.1)

| Phenomenon | REPEATABLE READ | SERIALIZABLE |
|---|---|---|
| Dirty read | ✅ Prevented | ✅ Prevented |
| Non-repeatable read | ✅ Prevented | ✅ Prevented |
| Phantom read | ✅ Prevented (*in PostgreSQL* — the standard only guarantees prevention of dirty reads and non-repeatable reads at this level, and PostgreSQL goes further) | ✅ Prevented |
| **Serialization anomaly** | ❌ **Allowed** | ✅ **Prevented** |

The **one thing that differs** between the two levels is **serialization anomalies**.

### Serialization anomaly (the key differentiator)

From the docs, a **serialization anomaly** is defined as:

> "The result of successfully committing a group of transactions is inconsistent with all possible orderings of running those transactions one at a time."

**REPEATABLE READ** is implemented using *Snapshot Isolation*. It gives each transaction a stable, consistent snapshot from the start of the transaction, preventing all classic read anomalies — but it does **not** detect serialization anomalies. The docs give a concrete example:

> "Attempts to enforce business rules by transactions running at this isolation level are not likely to work correctly without careful use of explicit locks to block conflicting transactions."

**SERIALIZABLE** is implemented using *Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)*, which builds on Snapshot Isolation by **adding monitoring for serialization anomalies** via predicate locks. As the docs state:

> "This level emulates serial transaction execution for all committed transactions; as if transactions had been executed one after another, serially, rather than concurrently."

### How conflicts are detected and what SQLSTATE is raised

Both levels require applications to be prepared to **retry** on serialization failures. However, the mechanisms and messages differ:

1. **REPEATABLE READ** — If a transaction tries to update/delete a row that was modified by another concurrent transaction after its own start, it is rolled back:
   ```
   ERROR:  could not serialize access due to concurrent update
   ```
   This happens because Repeatable Read transactions cannot modify rows changed by others after the transaction began.

2. **SERIALIZABLE** — Predicate locking monitors for read/write dependencies among concurrent transactions. If a serialization anomaly is detected (even in read-only transactions that don't modify anything), one of the conflicting transactions is rolled back:
   ```
   ERROR:  could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions
   ```

**The SQLSTATE for both is `40001`** — the standard SQLSTATE for "serialization failure". The docs state this explicitly:

> "…it will be very hard to predict exactly which transactions might contribute to the read/write dependencies and need to be rolled back to prevent serialization anomalies. The monitoring of read/write dependencies has a cost, as does the restart of transactions which are terminated with a serialization failure…"
>
> "(which always return with an SQLSTATE value of **'40001'…")**

### Summary

| Aspect | REPEATABLE READ | SERIALIZABLE |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | Snapshot Isolation | Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI) + predicate locking |
| Dirty reads | Prevented | Prevented |
| Non-repeatable reads | Prevented | Prevented |
| Phantom reads | Prevented (PostgreSQL-specific) | Prevented |
| Serialization anomalies | **Not prevented** | **Prevented** |
| Can read-only txns be affected? | No ("read-only transactions will never have serialization conflicts") | Yes — unless `SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE` |
| SQLSTATE on failure | `40001` | `40001` |
| Blocking? | No | No (except for `SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE`, which blocks until it can guarantee no anomalies) |

### Source

- PostgreSQL 18 Documentation, Section 13.2 — [Transaction Isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html)
  - Table 13.1: "Transaction Isolation Levels" (anomaly prevention matrix)
  - Section 13.2.2: "Repeatable Read Isolation Level"
  - Section 13.2.3: "Serializable Isolation Level"

## Claim: "PostgreSQL's default transaction isolation level is REPEATABLE READ, and at that level phantom reads can occur."

### Part 1: "PostgreSQL's default transaction isolation level is REPEATABLE READ"

**Unable to verify.** The web call to find PostgreSQL's default isolation level was not returned before the tool budget was reached. (From general knowledge, PostgreSQL's default is **READ COMMITTED**, but I could not confirm this from the official docs with the available tool calls.)

### Part 2: "At that level phantom reads can occur"

**Contradicted by the official PostgreSQL documentation.** From https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html (Section 13.2):

- **Definition of phantom read:** "A transaction re-executes a query returning a set of rows that satisfy a search condition and finds that the set of rows satisfying the condition has changed due to another recently-committed transaction."

- **Table 13.1. Transaction Isolation Levels:**

  | Isolation Level | Phantom Read |
  |---|---|
  | Read committed | Possible |
  | Repeatable read | *Allowed, but not in PG* |
  | Serializable | Not possible |

- **Direct statement:** "The table also shows that **PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read implementation does not allow phantom reads.** This is acceptable under the SQL standard because the standard specifies which anomalies must *not* occur at certain isolation levels; higher guarantees are acceptable."

- **Section 13.2.2. Repeatable Read Isolation Level:** "The Repeatable Read isolation level only sees data committed before the transaction began; it never sees either uncommitted data or changes committed by concurrent transactions during the transaction's execution. … **This is a stronger guarantee than is required by the SQL standard for this isolation level, and prevents all of the phenomena described in Table 13.1 except for serialization anomalies.**"

The default value of vLLM's `--gpu-memory-utilization` option depends on whether the extensible KV cache is enabled:

| Condition | Effective default |
|---|---|
| `--extensible-kv-cache` is **enabled** (default on CUDA & ROCm) | **1.0** (100%) |
| Extensible KV cache is **disabled** or unavailable | **0.92** (92%) |

### What the option controls

The option sets the fraction of GPU memory to be used for the model executor (ranging from 0 to 1). Specifically, it reserves that fraction of GPU memory for the model weights, activations, and KV cache. A higher value increases the KV cache size and thus improves throughput, but if set too high it may cause out-of-memory (OOM) errors.

<acknowledgement>: Understood: You want a detailed explanation of the differences between REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE isolation levels in PostgreSQL, the anomalies each prevents, the SQLSTATE for serialization failures, with citations from the official PostgreSQL documentation.



Here are the findings, all sourced from the official PostgreSQL 18 documentation.

---

## 1. The Core Difference

Both levels are built on PostgreSQL's MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control), but **SERIALIZABLE builds on top of REPEATABLE READ** by adding monitoring for conditions that could make the concurrent execution produce results inconsistent with *any* serial (one-at-a-time) ordering.

From §13.2.3 (Serializable Isolation Level):

> *This level works exactly the same as Repeatable Read except that it also monitors for conditions which could make execution of a concurrent set of serializable transactions behave in a manner inconsistent with all possible serial (one at a time) executions of those transactions.*

REPEATABLE READ implements what the academic literature calls **Snapshot Isolation**. It guarantees every transaction sees a stable snapshot as of the start of the first non-control statement, but does **not** detect serialization anomalies.

SERIALIZABLE implements **Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)**. It adds predicate-locking-style monitoring to detect read/write dependencies among concurrent transactions that would create a serialization anomaly, and will abort one of them.

---

## 2. Anomalies Prevented (from Table 13.1 in §13.2)

| Anomaly | Read Committed | Repeatable Read | Serializable |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dirty read | Not possible | Not possible | Not possible |
| Nonrepeatable read | Possible | **Not possible** | **Not possible** |
| Phantom read | Possible | **Not possible** (PostgreSQL goes beyond the standard) | **Not possible** |
| Serialization anomaly | Possible | **Possible** | **Not possible** |

Key distinction: **only a serialization anomaly can still occur at REPEATABLE READ**. All four other phenomena (dirty read, nonrepeatable read, phantom read, and serialization anomaly) are prevented at SERIALIZABLE.

### What is a serialization anomaly? (§13.2)

> *The result of successfully committing a group of transactions is inconsistent with all possible orderings of running those transactions one at a time.*

**Classic example from §13.2.3:**

A table `mytab` initially contains:

```
 class | value
-------+-------
     1 |    10
     1 |    20
     2 |   100
     2 |   200
```

- Transaction A computes `SELECT SUM(value) FROM mytab WHERE class = 1;` → 30, then inserts that as a new row with `class = 2`.
- Transaction B concurrently computes `SELECT SUM(value) FROM mytab WHERE class = 2;` → 300, then inserts that as a new row with `class = 1`.

> If either transaction were running at the Repeatable Read isolation level, both would be allowed to commit; but since there is no serial order of execution consistent with the result, using Serializable transactions will allow one transaction to commit and will roll the other back.

---

## 3. SQLSTATE for Serialization Failure

From §13.5 (Serialization Failure Handling):

> Both Repeatable Read and Serializable isolation levels can produce errors that are designed to prevent serialization anomalies. [...] Such an error's message text will vary according to the precise circumstances, but it will **always have the SQLSTATE code `40001` (`serialization_failure`)**.

Applications using either level **must be prepared to retry the entire transaction** when they receive this error. The documentation explicitly notes:

> It is important to retry the complete transaction, including all logic that decides which SQL to issue and/or which values to use. Therefore, PostgreSQL does not offer an automatic retry facility, since it cannot do so with any guarantee of correctness.

---

## 4. Summary of Key Mechanisms

| Aspect | REPEATABLE READ | SERIALIZABLE |
|---|---|---|
| Underlying technique | Snapshot Isolation | Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI) |
| Snapshot | Fixed at start of first query | Same snapshot guarantee |

| SQLSTATE on failure | `40001` (`serialization_failure`) | `40001` (`serialization_failure`) |
| Blocking | No additional blocking beyond standard MVCC waits | No additional blocking (predicate locks are non-blocking), except for `SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE` which *does* block until it can prove no conflicts are possible |

---

<acknowledgement>: Understood — you want a sourced comparison of LMCache vs vLLM's built-in prefix caching: what each caches, where the cache lives, and when LMCache adds value.

I'll use the web agent to research both systems and compile the comparison with citations.



## LMCache vs vLLM Built-in Prefix Cache — Comparative Brief

> **Assumption:** This comparison assumes vLLM's V1 engine (the current default), where Automatic Prefix Caching (APC) is enabled by default.

---

### 1. vLLM's Built-in Prefix Cache

**What it caches:** KV cache tensors (key and value tensors from the attention mechanism) computed during the prefill phase. It does *not* cache attention output, hidden states, or model weights — only the KV tensors for processed prompt tokens.

**How it's keyed:** vLLM hashes each KV cache block by the tokens in that block *and* the tokens in the prefix before it, using a hash chain approach:

> "vLLM's Automatic Prefix Caching (APC) hashes KV cache blocks automatically and evicts the least-recently-used block when the cache fills." — [Spheron Blog](https://www.spheron.network/blog/prefix-caching-explained-why-repeated-prompts-get-cheaper-to/)

Each block (default size: **16 tokens**) gets a SHA-256 hash that incorporates the content of every preceding block. Matching is exact on token sequences — two requests sharing tokens 1–3000 but diverging at token 3001 will share nothing from block 3001 onward.

**Where it's stored:** Entirely within GPU memory of the vLLM process, managed via PagedAttention. vLLM also offers CPU offload (`--kv-cache-dtype=fp8` or explicit CPU offloading) which spills KV cache from GPU into system RAM when GPU memory fills, but this is still within the same vLLM process:

> "vLLM also offers a CPU offload mode, which lets cached data spill out of GPU memory into regular system RAM when the GPU runs out of room, while still being managed entirely within the vLLM process." — [MindStudio](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents)

**Shared across workers?** No. vLLM's prefix cache is process-local. Multiple vLLM worker processes or replicas do *not* share KV cache with each other — there is no cross-instance sharing. Each vLLM instance maintains its own independent prefix cache.

**Limitations:**
- **Single process / single node only** — KV cache dies when the vLLM process dies.
- **No cross-instance sharing** — different vLLM instances (even on the same machine) cannot share cached KV blocks.
- **LRU eviction under memory pressure** — if the prefix cache fills and new unique prompts arrive, blocks are evicted, leading to near-zero hit rates:

> "When the workload was scaled up to overflow available GPU cache (48 large documents against a GPU that could hold notes for far fewer), vLLM's GPU-only prefix cache saw its hit rate collapse to 0%." — [MindStudio](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents)

- **No persistence across restarts** — a vLLM restart or crash wipes the entire cache:

> "Because vLLM's prefix cache and CPU offload both live inside the vLLM process, restarting vLLM wipes them out entirely." — [MindStudio](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents)

- **Prefix-bound only** — reuse is strictly limited to exact leading prefixes. Content that appears at different positions (e.g., retrieved documents in different order in RAG) produces no reuse:

> "Reuse follows exact prefix structure." — [Momento Blog](https://www.gomomento.com/blog/prefix-caching-is-still-prefix-caching/)

---

### 2. LMCache

**What it caches:** KV cache (the same KV tensors vLLM computes), plus non-KV caching features like hidden states and encodings.

> "LMCache is a **KV cache management layer** for LLM inference. It turns KV cache from a temporary state into reusable *AI-native knowledge* that can be *stored* persistently, *reused* across multiple serving engines, *monitored* with an observability stack, and *transformed* for better generation quality." — [LMCache README](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache)

> "LMCache supports non-prefix KV reuse via CacheBlend, which can selectively recompute tokens for quality recovery." — [LMCache README](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache)

**Where it's stored — Multi-tier architecture:** LMCache uses a hierarchical storage system spanning multiple layers:

> "LMCache implements a hierarchical storage system with three distinct tiers: GPU Memory (active working set), CPU DRAM (hot cache for recently used KV chunks, using pinned memory), Local storage (e.g. local disk, NVMe GDS) for large-tier caching, Remote storage (e.g. Redis, Mooncake, InfiniStore) for persistent storage." — [LMCache Architecture Docs](https://docs.lmcache.ai/developer_guide/architecture.html)

Pluggable storage backends include: CPU RAM, local disk (SSD), Redis/Valkey, Mooncake, InfiniStore, S3-compatible object storage, NIXL, GDS, Bigtable, Aerospike, and more:

> "Through this interface, LMCache supports storage backends including CPU RAM, local disk (SSD), Redis/Valkey, Mooncake, InfiniStore, S3-compatible object storage, NIXL, and GDS." — [LMCache README](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache)

**Architecture — Standalone daemon, not tied to vLLM process:** LMCache runs as a separate process (daemon server) that integrates with vLLM via a connector module.

> "LMCache, as a standalone daemon process, manages KV cache independently from the inference engine process, so that KV cache will not be lost even if the inference engine crashes (i.e., no fate-sharing with engines)." — [LMCache README](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache)

It integrates into vLLM (and other engines) by tapping into the paged KV memory manager. The connector checks at prefill time whether token sequences were seen before, and fetches precomputed KV chunks on cache hit.

**How it's keyed:** LMCache maintains a cache index mapping token sequences to cached KV entries using a configurable chunking strategy (default **256 tokens** per chunk) and a hashing scheme, with the requirement that multiple processes share the same `PYTHONHASHSEED`:

> "For centralized cache sharing (which is cross-process cases), ensure all processes use the same PYTHONHASHSEED to keep the hash of the KV cache consistent across processes." — [LMCache Docs](https://docs.lmcache.ai/getting_started/quickstart/share_kv_cache.html)

**Cross-instance sharing modes:** LMCache supports multiple KV cache sharing strategies:

- **Centralized sharing via Redis** — a shared Redis server acts as the cache store that multiple vLLM instances connect to.
- **P2P KV cache sharing** — peer-to-peer transfer between instances using NIXL over NVLink, RDMA, or TCP.

> "This section demonstrates how to share KV cache across multiple vLLM instances using peer-to-peer transfer." — [LMCache Docs](https://docs.lmcache.ai/getting_started/quickstart/share_kv_cache.html)

**Disaggregated prefill support:** LMCache also supports PD (prefill-decode) disaggregation, routing KV cache from prefill workers to decode workers:

> "Support KV cache transfer from prefill workers to decode workers over NVLink, RDMA, or TCP through transport layers such as NIXL." — [LMCache README](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache)

---

### 3. When is LMCache Worth Adding Over vLLM's Built-in Prefix Caching?

Based on comparative evidence:

| Scenario | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| **Single vLLM instance, cache fits in GPU** | vLLM prefix cache is sufficient and simpler. LMCache adds negligible benefit. |
| **Multiple vLLM instances / replicas sharing workload** | **LMCache is clearly superior.** vLLM's prefix cache does not cross instance boundaries. LMCache's centralized (Redis) or P2P sharing enables cross-instance KV reuse. |
| **Cache must survive vLLM restarts/crashes** | **LMCache wins decisively.** vLLM's cache (GPU or CPU offload) is wiped on restart. LMCache's standalone server retains cache: |

> "In steady-state serving... LMCache measures around 140 milliseconds against vLLM's offload at 164 milliseconds, essentially a tie. But the real separation appears after a restart. LMCache, because its cache lives in a separate server that keeps running independently, reconnected after the restart and immediately resumed near-instant responses (around 141 milliseconds with a 99.9% hit rate)." — [MindStudio](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents)

| **Cache outgrows GPU memory significantly** | LMCache's tiered offload to CPU RAM, NVMe, and remote backends (Redis, S3) provides much larger capacity than vLLM's CPU offload alone. |
| **RAG with document chunks in varying order** | vLLM's prefix-bound matching misses entirely. LMCache's CacheBlend can do non-prefix KV reuse: |

> "A RAG pipeline that retrieves the same three document chunks in a different order on the next call produces a different token sequence from position one, and the match breaks immediately... LMCache extends its turbo-boost to multimodal models... non-prefix KV reuse via CacheBlend." — [MindStudio](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents) / [LMCache Blog](https://blog.lmcache.ai/en/2025/07/03/lmcache-extends-its-turbo-boost-to-multimodal-models-in-vllm-v1/)

| **Prefill-decode disaggregation** | LMCache natively supports PD disaggregation; vLLM's prefix cache does not. |
| **KV cache compression (CacheGen)** | LMCache supports lossy KV cache compression to reduce memory footprint; vLLM does not. |

## LMCache vs vLLM Built-in Prefix Cache — Comparative Brief

> **Assumption:** This comparison assumes vLLM's V1 engine (the current default), where Automatic Prefix Caching (APC) is enabled by default.

### 1. vLLM's Built-in Prefix Cache

**What it caches:** KV cache tensors (key and value tensors from the attention mechanism) computed during the prefill phase. It does *not* cache attention output, hidden states, or model weights — only the KV tensors for processed prompt tokens.

**How it's keyed:** vLLM hashes each KV cache block by the tokens in that block *and* the tokens in the prefix before it, using a hash chain approach:

> "vLLM's Automatic Prefix Caching (APC) hashes KV cache blocks automatically and evicts the least-recently-used block when the cache fills." — [Spheron Blog](https://www.spheron.network/blog/prefix-caching-explained-why-repeated-prompts-get-cheaper-to/)

Each block (default size: **16 tokens**) gets a SHA-256 hash that incorporates the content of every preceding block. Matching is exact on token sequences — two requests sharing tokens 1–3000 but diverging at token 3001 will share nothing from block 3001 onward.

**Where it's stored:** Entirely within GPU memory of the vLLM process, managed via PagedAttention. vLLM also offers CPU offload (`--kv-cache-dtype=fp8` or explicit CPU offloading) which spills KV cache from GPU into system RAM when GPU memory fills, but this is still within the same vLLM process:

> "vLLM also offers a CPU offload mode, which lets cached data spill out of GPU memory into regular system RAM when the GPU runs out of room, while still being managed entirely within the vLLM process." — [MindStudio](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents)

**Shared across workers?** No. vLLM's prefix cache is process-local. Multiple vLLM worker processes or replicas do *not* share KV cache with each other — there is no cross-instance sharing. Each vLLM instance maintains its own independent prefix cache.

**Limitations:**
- **Single process / single node only** — KV cache dies when the vLLM process dies.
- **No cross-instance sharing** — different vLLM instances (even on the same machine) cannot share cached KV blocks.
- **LRU eviction under memory pressure** — if the prefix cache fills and new unique prompts arrive, blocks are evicted, leading to near-zero hit rates:

> "When the workload was scaled up to overflow available GPU cache (48 large documents against a GPU that could hold notes for far fewer), vLLM's GPU-only prefix cache saw its hit rate collapse to 0%." — [MindStudio](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents)

- **No persistence across restarts** — a vLLM restart or crash wipes the entire cache:

> "Because vLLM's prefix cache and CPU offload both live inside the vLLM process, restarting vLLM wipes them out entirely." — [MindStudio](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents)

- **Prefix-bound only** — reuse is strictly limited to exact leading prefixes. Content that appears at different positions (e.g., retrieved documents in different order in RAG) produces no reuse:

> "Reuse follows exact prefix structure." — [Momento Blog](https://www.gomomento.com/blog/prefix-caching-is-still-prefix-caching/)

---

### 2. LMCache

**What it caches:** KV cache (the same KV tensors vLLM computes), plus non-KV caching features like hidden states and encodings.

> "LMCache is a **KV cache management layer** for LLM inference. It turns KV cache from a temporary state into reusable *AI-native knowledge* that can be *stored* persistently, *reused* across multiple serving engines, *monitored* with an observability stack, and *transformed* for better generation quality." — [LMCache README](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache)

> "LMCache supports non-prefix KV reuse via CacheBlend, which can selectively recompute tokens for quality recovery." — [LMCache README](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache)

**Where it's stored — Multi-tier architecture:** LMCache uses a hierarchical storage system spanning multiple layers:

> "LMCache implements a hierarchical storage system with three distinct tiers: GPU Memory (active working set), CPU DRAM (hot cache for recently used KV chunks, using pinned memory), Local storage (e.g. local disk, NVMe GDS) for large-tier caching, Remote storage (e.g. Redis, Mooncake, InfiniStore) for persistent storage." — [LMCache Architecture Docs](https://docs.lmcache.ai/developer_guide/architecture.html)

Pluggable storage backends include: CPU RAM, local disk (SSD), Redis/Valkey, Mooncake, InfiniStore, S3-compatible object storage, NIXL, GDS, Bigtable, Aerospike, and more:

> "Through this interface, LMCache supports storage backends including CPU RAM, local disk (SSD), Redis/Valkey, Mooncake, InfiniStore, S3-compatible object storage, NIXL, and GDS." — [LMCache README](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache)

**Architecture — Standalone daemon, not tied to vLLM process:** LMCache runs as a separate process (daemon server) that integrates with vLLM via a connector module.

> "LMCache, as a standalone daemon process, manages KV cache independently from the inference engine process, so that KV cache will not be lost even if the inference engine crashes (i.e., no fate-sharing with engines)." — [LMCache README](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache)

It integrates into vLLM (and other engines) by tapping into the paged KV memory manager. The connector checks at prefill time whether token sequences were seen before, and fetches precomputed KV chunks on cache hit.

**How it's keyed:** LMCache maintains a cache index mapping token sequences to cached KV entries using a configurable chunking strategy (default **256 tokens** per chunk) and a hashing scheme, with the requirement that multiple processes share the same `PYTHONHASHSEED`:

> "For centralized cache sharing (which is cross-process cases), ensure all processes use the same PYTHONHASHSEED to keep the hash of the KV cache consistent across processes." — [LMCache Docs](https://docs.lmcache.ai/getting_started/quickstart/share_kv_cache.html)

**Cross-instance sharing modes:** LMCache supports multiple KV cache sharing strategies:

- **Centralized sharing via Redis** — a shared Redis server acts as the cache store that multiple vLLM instances connect to.
- **P2P KV cache sharing** — peer-to-peer transfer between instances using NIXL over NVLink, RDMA, or TCP.

> "This section demonstrates how to share KV cache across multiple vLLM instances using peer-to-peer transfer." — [LMCache Docs](https://docs.lmcache.ai/getting_started/quickstart/share_kv_cache.html)

**Disaggregated prefill support:** LMCache also supports PD (prefill-decode) disaggregation, routing KV cache from prefill workers to decode workers:

> "Support KV cache transfer from prefill workers to decode workers over NVLink, RDMA, or TCP through transport layers such as NIXL." — [LMCache README](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache)

---

## Default Value

The default value of `--gpu-memory-utilization` is **0.92** (i.e., 92% of GPU memory).

This is defined in the `CacheConfig` class in vLLM's source code at `vllm/config/cache.py`:

```python
@config
class CacheConfig:
    """Configuration for the KV cache."""

    DEFAULT_BLOCK_SIZE: ClassVar[int] = 64
    DEFAULT_GPU_MEMORY_UTILIZATION: ClassVar[float] = 0.92

    gpu_memory_utilization: float | None = Field(default=None, gt=0, le=1)
```

The field's default is `None` — when unspecified, the `resolved_gpu_memory_utilization` property returns `0.92`:

```python
@property
def resolved_gpu_memory_utilization(self) -> float:
    """`gpu_memory_utilization`, or its default given the sizing mode."""
    if self.gpu_memory_utilization is not None:
        return self.gpu_memory_utilization
    if self.enable_extensible_kv_cache:
        return 1.0
    return self.DEFAULT_GPU_MEMORY_UTILIZATION
```

> **Important nuance**: Since v0.8+, vLLM defaults to **extensible KV cache** on CUDA/ROCm (enabled unless you set `--kv-cache-memory-bytes`). In that mode, the effective `gpu_memory_utilization` becomes **1.0** (not 0.92), because the cache is sized from the memory actually free after CUDA graph capture rather than from a profiling estimate. See the `enable_extensible_kv_cache` field in the same file.

Understood: I need to compare LMCache vs vLLM's built-in prefix caching — covering what each caches, storage location, and when LMCache is worth adding — with sourced information.

Calling the web_agent now.



Here is the sourced comparison:

---

## 1. What Does Each One Cache?

**vLLM Built-in Prefix Caching (Automatic Prefix Caching — APC):**
- Caches **KV cache blocks** (the key and value tensors computed by the attention layers for each token).
- Uses content-based hashing: each fixed-size block (default 16 tokens) is hashed, and hashes are stored in an in-memory map for O(1) lookups.
- Reuse is **block-aligned only** — a hit matches an entire 16-token block; partial overlaps at non-block boundaries are missed.
- As of vLLM v0.6, APC is **enabled by default**; in the V1 engine it is on by default.

**LMCache:**
- Also caches **KV cache tensors** (the same underlying data — attention key/value state).
- Operates at **chunk granularity** (configurable, default 256 tokens) and supports **non-prefix KV reuse** via CacheBlend, meaning it can reuse cached KV blocks at any position in the prompt (not just at the prefix head), selectively recomputing only the tokens needed for quality recovery.

**Key distinction:** Both cache KV cache data. LMCache extends vLLM's approach with non-prefix reuse, configurable chunk sizes, and a pluggable SERDE/compression layer (CacheGen).

---

## 2. Where Is the Cache Stored?

**vLLM Built-in Prefix Caching:**
- **Scope:** Single vLLM process, single GPU / single node. No cross-instance sharing.
- **Storage medium:** **GPU memory only** — part of the GPU memory pool managed by PagedAttention.
- **Persistence:** Survives as long as the vLLM process lives. Lost on crash, restart, or rolling deployment.
- **Eviction:** LRU within the GPU memory pool when full; no shrink-on-idle.

**LMCache:**
- **Architecture:** Standalone daemon process (`lmcache server`) — decoupled from the inference engine, so cache survives engine crashes (no fate-sharing).
- **L1 tier:** CPU RAM (configurable via `--l1-size-gb`). Acts as the fast local tier.
- **L2 tier:** Pluggable remote/distributed backends — Redis/Valkey, S3, Bigtable, Aerospike, Mooncake, NIXL, FileSystem/SSD, SageMaker HyperPod, and more.
- **Scope:** Cross-instance, cross-node. Multiple vLLM (or SGLang, or TensorRT-LLM) instances can connect to the same LMCache server and share KV caches.
- **Persistence:** Persisted to L2 storage (disk/S3/Redis/etc.), survives engine restarts and rolling upgrades.
- **Disaggregation:** Supports prefill/decode KV cache transfer between workers over NVLink, RDMA, or TCP.

---

## 3. When Is LMCache Worth Adding Over vLLM's Built-in Prefix Caching?

LMCache is worth adding when **any** of these conditions apply:

### a) You need cross-instance KV cache sharing
vLLM's prefix cache only works within a single process/GPU. If you run multiple vLLM replicas behind a load balancer that serve the same model and share prompt prefixes (system prompts, RAG documents, conversation history), LMCache provides a centralized KV cache server all replicas can query.

### b) Your KV cache needs to survive engine restarts or crashes
vLLM's prefix cache is lost when the process dies. LMCache's standalone daemon decouples cache from engine lifecycle — KV data stored in CPU/L2 tier survives vLLM restarts, rolling deployments, and crashes.

### c) GPU memory is tight and you need KV offloading
vLLM's prefix cache is limited to available GPU memory. LMCache offloads KV to CPU RAM and then to L2 storage (SSD, Redis, S3, etc.), freeing GPU memory for more active KV cache and higher concurrency.

### d) You need prefill/decode disaggregation
If your architecture separates prefill workers (processing prompts) from decode workers (generating tokens), LMCache can transfer KV cache from prefill → decode over NVLink, RDMA, or TCP.

### e) You want non-prefix KV reuse
LMCache's CacheBlend can reuse cached KV blocks that appear **anywhere** in a prompt (not just at the prefix head), useful for RAG where retrieved documents may be interspersed with the query.

### f) Engine-agnostic caching
LMCache integrates with vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM. If your platform uses multiple serving engines, a single LMCache instance can serve all of them.

### g) Production observability and management
LMCache provides K8s-native metrics, request-level and token-level prefix cache hits, lifecycle tracking, and per-user usage metrics. vLLM exposes basic counters but lacks the management surface.

**When vLLM's built-in prefix caching is sufficient:**
- Single vLLM instance, single GPU
- Workload has strong prefix overlap (agent system prompts, RAG with stable documents, multi-turn chat)
- You do not need cache persistence across restarts
- You do not need offloading beyond GPU memory
- You do not need cross-engine or cross-instance sharing

---

### Summary Table

| Feature | vLLM APC | LMCache |
|---|---|---|
| **Caches** | KV cache blocks (16 tokens/block) | KV cache chunks (configurable, default 256); non-prefix reuse via CacheBlend |
| **Match granularity** | Block-aligned (exact block match) | Chunk-aligned + CacheBlend (any position) |
| **Storage medium** | GPU memory only | CPU RAM (L1) + pluggable L2 (Redis, S3, SSD, Bigtable, Mooncake, NIXL, etc.) |
| **Process scope** | In-process (single vLLM worker) | Standalone daemon, cross-process, cross-node |
| **Cross-instance sharing** | No | Yes (multiple vLLM/SGLang/TRT-LLM instances) |
| **Survives engine crash** | No | Yes (no fate-sharing) |
| **KV offloading** | No | Yes (GPU → CPU → disk/remote) |
| **PD disaggregation** | No (experimental in vLLM core) | Yes (via NIXL, Mooncake, etc.) |
| **Compression** | No (quantization handled separately by vLLM) | Yes (pluggable SERDE, CacheGen) |
| **Observability** | Basic counters | Full metrics dashboard, K8s-native, per-request tracking |
| **Default** | On since v0.6 | Off (must configure) |

---

### References
- vLLM docs, "Automatic Prefix Caching": https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/design/prefix_caching/
- LMCache GitHub: https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache
- LMCache docs, "Supported Backends": https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/l2_storage/supported_storages.html
- LMCache Quickstart: https://docs.lmcache.ai/getting_started/quickstart.html
- LMCache paper (arXiv:2510.09665): https://arxiv.org/html/2510.09665v2
- ScaleOps, "vLLM KV Cache and Prefix Cache": https://scaleops.com/blog/vllm-kv-cache-prefix-cache-gpu-memory/
- LLM Academy, "Prefix Caching in vLLM & SGLang": https://llm-academy.dev/optimization/prefix-caching/

## 1. Differences Between REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE in PostgreSQL

Both levels prevent **dirty reads**, **non-repeatable reads**, and **phantom reads**. The key distinction:

| Isolation Level | Dirty Read | Nonrepeatable Read | Phantom Read | Serialization Anomaly |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Repeatable Read** | Not possible | Not possible | **Not possible** | **Possible** |
| **Serializable** | Not possible | Not possible | Not possible | **Not possible** |

- **REPEATABLE READ** uses **Snapshot Isolation** — the transaction sees a consistent snapshot taken at the start of its first non-transaction-control statement. It only sees data committed before the transaction began.
- **SERIALIZABLE** uses **Serializable Snapshot Isolation** — Snapshot Isolation + additional monitoring via **predicate locks** to detect conditions that would make concurrent execution behave inconsistently with any serial ordering.

From the docs:
> *"The Serializable isolation level works exactly the same as Repeatable Read except that it also monitors for conditions which could make execution of a concurrent set of serializable transactions behave in a manner inconsistent with all possible serial (one at a time) executions of those transactions."*

Predicate locks are visible in `pg_locks` with mode `SIReadLock` and **do not cause blocking** — they exist solely to flag read/write dependency conflicts.

### Serialization Anomaly Example

> *"Suppose that serializable transaction A computes: `SELECT SUM(value) FROM mytab WHERE class = 1;` and then inserts the result (30) as the value in a new row with class = 2. Concurrently, serializable transaction B computes: `SELECT SUM(value) FROM mytab WHERE class = 2;` and obtains the result 300, which it inserts in a new row with class = 1. Then both transactions try to commit. If either transaction were running at the Repeatable Read isolation level, both would be allowed to commit; but since there is no serial order of execution consistent with the result, using Serializable transactions will allow one transaction to commit and will roll the other back."*

---

## 2. SQLSTATE for Serialization Failure

The SQLSTATE error code is **'40001'** (`serialization_failure`).

Two possible error messages, both with SQLSTATE '40001':

1. **At REPEATABLE READ** — when trying to update/delete a row changed by another concurrent transaction:
   > `ERROR: could not serialize access due to concurrent update`

2. **At SERIALIZABLE** — when predicate lock monitoring detects a read/write dependency conflict:
   > `ERROR: could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions`

From the docs:
> *"It is important that an environment which uses this technique have a generalized way of handling serialization failures (which always return with an SQLSTATE value of '40001'), because it will very hard to predict exactly which transactions might contribute to the read/write dependencies and need to be rolled back to prevent serialization anomalies."*

---

## 3. Required Handling

Applications using either level must be prepared to **retry transactions** on receiving SQLSTATE '40001':

> *"Applications using this level must be prepared to retry transactions due to serialization failures."*
> *"When an application receives this error message, it should abort the current transaction and retry the whole transaction from the beginning."*

Only updating transactions need retries; read-only transactions generally won't conflict.

---

**Source:** PostgreSQL 18 Documentation, Chapter 13: Concurrency Control, Section 13.2 "Transaction Isolation" — https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html

The claim is **confirmed** by the official LMCache documentation. Here are the key passages:

**From the LMCache home page (https://docs.lmcache.ai/):**

> "Persistent, tiered KV cache offloading and reuse: Move KV caches out of GPU memory into a tiered storage hierarchy spanning CPU memory, local storage, and ..."

> "Pluggable storage and transport backends: ... enabling KV cache offloading and sharing across storage providers. Through this interface, LMCache supports storage backends including CPU RAM, local disk (SSD), Redis/Valkey, Mooncake, InfiniStore, S3-compatible object storage, NIXL, and GDS."

**From the CPU RAM documentation (https://docs.lmcache.ai/kv_cache/cpu_ram.html):**

> "CPU RAM and Local Storage are the two ways of offloading KV cache onto non-GPU memory of the same machine that is running inference."

> "When LMCACHE_LOCAL_CPU=True is used in conjunction with the disk backend or a remote backend... we can think of the CPU RAM as a 'hot cache' that will contain the 'hottest' (most recently accessed) subset of KV caches from Disk and Remote storage."

**From the Local Storage documentation (https://docs.lmcache.ai/kv_cache/local_storage.html):**

|---|---|---|
| Default = REPEATABLE READ | **False** — default is READ COMMITTED | §13.2.1 |
| Phantom reads at REPEATABLE READ | **False** — PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ prevents phantom reads | §13.2, Table 13.1 |

(At the *actual* default, READ COMMITTED, phantom reads **are** possible — but that is not the level the claim identifies.)

# vLLM's `--gpu-memory-utilization` Option

## Default Value

The default value of `--gpu-memory-utilization` is **0.92** (i.e., 92% of total GPU memory).

This is defined in vLLM's own source code:

> https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/config/cache.py
>
> `DEFAULT_GPU_MEMORY_UTILIZATION: ClassVar[float] = 0.92`

And confirmed in the official docs, for example:

> https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/api/vllm/config/cache/
>
> `( float , default: 0.92 ) –. The ratio (between 0 and 1) of GPU memory to reserve for the model executor...`

> https://docs.vllm.ai/en/v0.21.0/configuration/engine_args/
>
> `Default: 0.92. ... For example, a value of 0.5 would imply 50% GPU memory utilization.`

## What It Controls

`--gpu-memory-utilization` sets the **fraction of each GPU's total memory that vLLM reserves for three things combined**:

1. **Model weights** — the model parameters loaded in FP16/bfloat16
2. **Activations** — intermediate tensor values computed during inference
3. **KV cache** — the key-value cache used by vLLM's PagedAttention mechanism to store past token states for efficient autoregressive generation

As the docs state:

> https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/api/vllm/config/cache/
>
> `gpu_memory_utilization: ( float , default: 0.92 ) – The ratio (between 0 and 1) of GPU memory to reserve for the model weights, activations, and KV cache.`

> https://discuss.vllm.ai/t/what-is-included-in-gpu-memory-utilization/2559
>
> `The gpu_memory_utilization parameter in vLLM controls the fraction of total GPU memory reserved for model weights, KV cache, ...`

### Practical implications

- The value must be between 0 and 1 (e.g., `0.5` = 50%, `0.92` = 92%).
- At the default of **0.92**, vLLM reserves 92% of the GPU for model + KV cache, leaving ~8% for the OS, CUDA overhead, and other system processes.
- If the model weights alone (in their precision) exceed the reserved memory (e.g., a very large model on a small GPU with the default 0.92), vLLM will fail to load. In that case users typically **lower** `--gpu-memory-utilization` (or reduce `--max-model-len`, `--max-num-seqs`, etc.) to free enough memory for weights.
- If KV cache space is insufficient and you see slow performance or out-of-memory errors during generation, you can **increase** it toward 1.0 — but never to 1.0, as vLLM needs some memory for the CUDA context and system overhead.

## Open Questions

- **Version-specific defaults:** The v0.4.3 docs referenced by an early search result mentioned a default of 0.92. Earlier historical versions may have used 0.90 or 0.95. If you need the default for a specific vLLM version older than the current `main` branch, a search against that version's tags/releases would be needed.
- **Per-GPU vs. multi-GPU semantics:** On multi-GPU deployments, the parameter is **per-GPU** (each GPU reserves its own fraction). This is noted in the docs but not fetched verbatim.

# LMCache vs. vLLM Built-in Prefix Caching: Detailed Comparison

**Assumption:** This comparison focuses on vLLM's standard Automatic Prefix Caching (APC) as of its current stable release, against LMCache (v0.3.x+ / MP mode) as the primary external KV cache management layer. All facts are sourced from live pages fetched during this task.

---

## 1. What Each One Caches

Both systems cache the same fundamental unit: **KV cache** (Key/Value tensors computed during the prefill phase). However, LMCache extends the *scope* of what can be reused.

### vLLM Built-in Prefix Caching
- **Caches KV cache blocks** for sequences that share identical token prefixes. It uses hash-based block matching to identify reusable prefixes.
- Caching is **prefix-only**: reuse is limited to the beginning of the prompt. If the same document chunk appears later in the sequence, it is *not* reused.
- Quote from the vLLM docs: *"Prefix caching kv-cache blocks is a popular optimization in LLM inference to avoid redundant prompt computations. The core idea is simple — we cache the kv-cache blocks and reuse them if a new query has the same prefix as a previous one."*
  - Source: https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/design/prefix_caching/

- In practice, this is extremely effective for conversational AI (where the entire chat history is a growing prefix) and agentic workflows (where tool definitions, goals, and past actions form a massive static prefix).

### LMCache
- **Also caches KV cache blocks**, but extends reuse beyond the prefix through a feature called **CacheBlend**.
- CacheBlend allows reuse of KV blocks **at any position in the prompt**, not just the beginning. Retrieved RAG chunks can be recognized and reused even if they appear in a different order than before.
  - Quote from the LMCache blog: *"CacheBlend changes the game by allowing for the reuse of pre-computed KV caches regardless of their position in the input sequence."*
  - Source: https://www.reddit.com/r/LocalLLaMA/comments/1lp653l/reuse_nonprefix_kv_cache_and_speed_up_rag_by_3x/
  - Source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.16444 (CacheBlend paper)
- This makes LMCache significantly more effective for **RAG workloads**, where the same knowledge-base documents appear across many queries but in varying orders and combinations. The blog reports up to **4.5× faster RAG** with LMCache compared to prefix-only approaches.
  - Source: https://blog.lmcache.ai/en/2024/10/09/beyond-prefix-caching-how-lmcache-speeds-up-rag-by-4-5x-by-one-line-of-change/

---

## 2. Where the Cache is Stored

### vLLM Built-in Prefix Caching
| Storage Tier | Location | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| GPU memory (primary) | VRAM, within the vLLM process | Single replica only |
| CPU RAM (optional offload) | System RAM, still within the vLLM process | Single replica only |

- Both GPU and CPU offload are managed entirely **inside the vLLM process**. The cache is ephemeral — it exists only as long as the vLLM process is running and the memory pool is not evicted.
- Quote from the vLLM design docs: *"Automatic Prefix Caching (APC in short) caches the KV cache of existing queries, so that a new query can directly reuse the KV cache if it shares the same prefix."*
  - Source: https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/features/automatic_prefix_caching/

- When the GPU memory pool fills up, the **oldest cached entries are evicted** with no persistence.
  - Source: https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents

### LMCache
| Storage Tier | Location | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| CPU RAM (DRAM) | System RAM on the same machine | Tier 1 offload |
| Local disk (SSD/NVMe) | Filesystem (.pt files per chunk) | LRU/LFU/FIFO/MRU eviction; O_DIRECT support; async write |
| Redis / Valkey | Remote in-memory store | Shared across machines |
| S3-compatible object storage | Cloud object storage | For long-term archival reuse |
| Mooncake, InfiniStore, NIXL, GDS | Various remote/cluster storage backends | Distributed KV transfer |

- Quote from the LMCache GitHub: *"Through this interface, LMCache supports storage backends including CPU RAM, local disk (SSD), Redis/Valkey, Mooncake, InfiniStore, S3-compatible object storage, NIXL, and GDS."*
  - Source: https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache
- LMCache also operates as a **standalone daemon process**, completely independent of the inference engine process.
  - Quote from the GitHub README: *"LMCache, as a standalone daemon process, manages KV cache independently from the inference engine process, so that KV cache will not be lost even if the inference engine crashes (i.e., no fate-sharing with engines)."*
  - Source: https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache

---

## 3. When LMCache Is Worth Adding Over vLLM's Built-in Prefix Caching

### When LMCache adds clear value:

#### a) Cache persistence across engine restarts/crashes
- vLLM's prefix cache and CPU offload are both **wiped on restart** because they live inside the vLLM process.
- LMCache survives vLLM crashes and restarts because it runs as a separate process with persistent storage.
  - Quote from the MindStudio comparison: *"LMCache's real advantage shows up after a restart. Because it stores notes in a separate process, it survives a vLLM crash or reboot, while vLLM's own cache (GPU or CPU offload) is wiped clean and has to rebuild from scratch."* In testing, LMCache resumed near-instant responses (~141ms, 99.9% hit rate) after restart while vLLM fell back to full uncached latency (~1.35 seconds).
  - Source: https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents

#### b) RAG workloads with document chunks in varying positions
- vLLM's prefix cache only reuses at the prompt beginning. If RAG chunks appear at different positions or orders across queries, prefix caching misses them.
- LMCache's CacheBlend reuses KV blocks at **any position**, making it dramatically faster for RAG.
  - Source: https://blog.lmcache.ai/en/2024/10/09/beyond-prefix-caching-how-lmcache-speeds-up-rag-by-4-5x-by-one-line-of-change/
  - Source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.16444

#### c) Workloads exceeding GPU cache capacity
- When the KV cache demand exceeds what fits in GPU memory, vLLM's GPU-only prefix cache **hit rate collapses to 0%**.
- LMCache's tiered storage (CPU RAM → disk → remote backends) allows the cache to scale beyond GPU/DRAM limits.
  - Quote from the MindStudio testing: *"When the workload was scaled up to overflow available GPU cache (48 large documents against a GPU that could hold notes for far fewer), vLLM's GPU-only prefix cache saw its hit rate collapse to 0%, performing about as poorly as no caching at all. Switching on CPU offload fixed that, recovering hit rates above 99%."* Even then, LMCache with disk offload can exceed local RAM capacity entirely.
  - Source: https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents

#### d) Cross-engine or cross-replica KV cache sharing
- vLLM's prefix cache is **replica-scoped** — each vLLM pod manages its own cache in isolation.
- LMCache with Redis/S3/Mooncake backends enables a **shared cache pool** across multiple vLLM instances or even across different serving engines (vendor-neutral).
  - Source: https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache (engine-independent deployment, vendor-neutral)
  - Source: https://redis.io/blog/get-faster-llm-inference-and-cheaper-responses-with-lmcache-and-redis/

#### e) Prefill/Decode (P/D) disaggregation
- LMCache supports KV cache transfer from prefill workers to decode workers over NVLink, RDMA, or TCP.
  - Source: https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache

### When vLLM's built-in prefix caching is sufficient:

- **Single-instance deployments** where the KV cache fits within GPU memory. vLLM's prefix caching reduces TTFT dramatically (e.g., from 4.3 seconds to 0.6 seconds for repeat prompts) with zero added infrastructure cost.
- **Conversational AI / multi-turn agents** where the entire conversation history forms a natural growing prefix — ideal for prefix caching.
- **Simple production setups** where cache persistence, cross-engine reuse, or RAG non-prefix reuse are not requirements.

### Operational costs of adding LMCache (caveats)
- Adds a separate daemon process and memory overhead.
- Can slow down restart times (tested: ~20–30 seconds slower with a 30-second minimum memory-release wait).
- Support for newer/non-standard model architectures was found to be inconsistent in some testing.
  - Source: https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents

---

## Summary Table

| Dimension | vLLM Prefix Caching | LMCache |
|---|---|---|
| **What is cached** | KV cache blocks, prefix-only | KV cache blocks, prefix + non-prefix (CacheBlend) |
| **Storage location** | GPU VRAM; optionally CPU RAM (still in-process) | CPU RAM → local disk → Redis/Valkey/S3/Mooncake/NIXL/GDS (tiered) |
| **Process boundary** | Inside vLLM process | Standalone daemon, no fate-sharing with engine |
| **Persists across restart?** | No | Yes (with remote/disk backends) |
| **Cross-replica sharing** | No (each pod isolated) | Yes (via Redis, S3, Mooncake, etc.) |
| **Cross-engine reuse** | No | Yes (vendor-neutral, engine-independent) |
| **P/D disaggregation** | Not natively | Yes (KV transfer over NVLink/RDMA/TCP) |
| **Operational overhead** | None (built-in) | Extra daemon, config, memory |
| **Best for** | Single-instance, prefix-heavy workloads (chat, agents) | RAG with varying chunk order, persistent caches, shared pools, P/D disaggregation |

---

## Open Questions
- The exact latest version numbers of both vLLM and LMCache could not be confirmed on the live PyPI pages (searches returned GitHub and documentation but not a clean version number grab). The latest LMCache release date and version should be verified from https://pypi.org/project/lmcache/ when needed for a decision.
- Performance benchmarks of LMCache on specific model sizes (e.g., 70B+) and hardware (AMD, Ascend) vary; the blog posts referenced cover specific models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-32B, DeepSeek) and may not generalize directly.

- LMCache also operates as a **standalone daemon process**, completely independent of the inference engine process.
  - Quote from the GitHub README: *"LMCache, as a standalone daemon process, manages KV cache independently from the inference engine process, so that KV cache will not be lost even if the inference engine crashes (i.e., no fate-sharing with engines)."*

---

## 3. When LMCache Is Worth Adding Over vLLM's Built-in Prefix Caching

### When LMCache adds clear value:

#### a) Cache persistence across engine restarts/crashes
- vLLM's prefix cache and CPU offload are both **wiped on restart** because they live inside the vLLM process.
- LMCache survives vLLM crashes and restarts because it runs as a separate process with persistent storage.
  - Quote from the MindStudio comparison: *"LMCache's real advantage shows up after a restart. Because it stores notes in a separate process, it survives a vLLM crash or reboot, while vLLM's own cache (GPU or CPU offload) is wiped clean and has to rebuild from scratch."* In testing, LMCache resumed near-instant responses (~141ms, 99.9% hit rate) after restart while vLLM fell back to full uncached latency (~1.35 seconds).
  - Source: https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents

#### b) RAG workloads with document chunks in varying positions
- vLLM's prefix cache only reuses at the prompt beginning. If RAG chunks appear at different positions or orders across queries, prefix caching misses them.
- LMCache's CacheBlend reuses KV blocks at **any position**, making it dramatically faster for RAG.
  - Source: https://blog.lmcache.ai/en/2024/10/09/beyond-prefix-caching-how-lmcache-speeds-up-rag-by-4-5x-by-one-line-of-change/
  - Source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.16444

#### c) Workloads exceeding GPU cache capacity
- When the KV cache demand exceeds what fits in GPU memory, vLLM's GPU-only prefix cache **hit rate collapses to 0%**.
- LMCache's tiered storage (CPU RAM → disk → remote backends) allows the cache to scale beyond GPU/DRAM limits.
  - Quote from the MindStudio testing: *"When the workload was scaled up to overflow available GPU cache (48 large documents against a GPU that could hold notes for far fewer), vLLM's GPU-only prefix cache saw its hit rate collapse to 0%, performing about as poorly as no caching at all. Switching on CPU offload fixed that, recovering hit rates above 99%."* Even then, LMCache with disk offload can exceed local RAM capacity entirely.
  - Source: https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents

#### d) Cross-engine or cross-replica KV cache sharing
- vLLM's prefix cache is **replica-scoped** — each vLLM pod manages its own cache in isolation.
- LMCache with Redis/S3/Mooncake backends enables a **shared cache pool** across multiple vLLM instances or even across different serving engines (vendor-neutral).
  - Source: https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache (engine-independent deployment, vendor-neutral)
  - Source: https://redis.io/blog/get-faster-llm-inference-and-cheaper-responses-with-lmcache-and-redis/

#### e) Prefill/Decode (P/D) disaggregation
- LMCache supports KV cache transfer from prefill workers to decode workers over NVLink, RDMA, or TCP.
  - Source: https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache

### When vLLM's built-in prefix caching is sufficient:

- **Single-instance deployments** where the KV cache fits within GPU memory. vLLM's prefix caching reduces TTFT dramatically (e.g., from 4.3 seconds to 0.6 seconds for repeat prompts) with zero added infrastructure cost.
- **Conversational AI / multi-turn agents** where the entire conversation history forms a natural growing prefix — ideal for prefix caching.
- **Simple production setups** where cache persistence, cross-engine reuse, or RAG non-prefix reuse are not requirements.

### Operational costs of adding LMCache (caveats)
- Adds a separate daemon process and memory overhead.
- Can slow down restart times (tested: ~20–30 seconds slower with a 30-second minimum memory-release wait).
- Support for newer/non-standard model architectures was found to be inconsistent in some testing.
  - Source: https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/lm-cache-vllm-coding-agents

---

## Summary Table

| Dimension | vLLM Prefix Caching | LMCache |
|---|---|---|
| **What is cached** | KV cache blocks, prefix-only | KV cache blocks, prefix + non-prefix (CacheBlend) |
| **Storage location** | GPU VRAM; optionally CPU RAM (still in-process) | CPU RAM → local disk → Redis/Valkey/S3/Mooncake/NIXL/GDS (tiered) |
| **Process boundary** | Inside vLLM process | Standalone daemon, no fate-sharing with engine |
| **Persists across restart?** | No | Yes (with remote/disk backends) |
| **Cross-replica sharing** | No (each pod isolated) | Yes (via Redis, S3, Mooncake, etc.) |
| **Cross-engine reuse** | No | Yes (vendor-neutral, engine-independent) |
| **P/D disaggregation** | Not natively | Yes (KV transfer over NVLink/RDMA/TCP) |
| **Operational overhead** | None (built-in) | Extra daemon, config, memory |
| **Best for** | Single-instance, prefix-heavy workloads (chat, agents) | RAG with varying chunk order, persistent caches, shared pools, P/D disaggregation |

### Default value: `0.92`

### What it controls

The `--gpu-memory-utilization` (also acceptably named `--device-memory-utilization`) argument controls **the fraction of GPU memory to be used for the model executor**, which is essentially the KV cache allocation. It accepts a value from 0 to 1, where, for example, `0.5` implies 50% of the GPU's total memory is reserved for the KV cache.

The memory that remains (the remaining ~8% by default) is used by the model weights and any overhead the CUDA runtime or other processes need.

### Important nuance: the effective default depends on `enable_extensible-kv-cache`

The actual default is context-sensitive. From the source code:

- **With extensible KV cache enabled** (the default on CUDA and ROCm): the effective default is **`1.0`** (100%) — the cache is sized from the actual free memory after CUDA graph capture rather than from a profiling estimate.
- **Without extensible KV cache** (or when `kv_cache_memory_bytes` is explicitly set): the effective default is **`0.92`**.

### Definitive source

**File:** [`vllm/config/cache.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/config/cache.py)

range from 0 to 1. For example, a value of 0.5 would imply 50% GPU memory
utilization. This is a per-instance limit, and only applies to the current

on the same GPU. For example, if you have two vLLM instances running on the

    if self.enable_extensible_kv_cache:

    return self.DEFAULT_GPU_MEMORY_UTILIZATION
```

# LMCache vs vLLM Built-in Prefix Caching — Detailed Comparison

## Important Assumption

This analysis assumes both systems are built on the PagedAttention mechanism as used in modern vLLM (v0.10+). All details are sourced from the live LMCache paper (arXiv:2510.09665), the LMCache GitHub repository, vLLM documentation, and the llm-d project blog.

---

## 1. What Does Each System Cache?

### vLLM's Built-in Prefix Caching

vLLM caches **KV cache blocks** (the Key and Value tensors from the self-attention mechanism) at the granularity of **fixed-size memory pages** (typically 16 tokens per layer per page, totaling ~62.5 KB for Llama-3.1-8B). The system uses **hash-based block matching** — each physical KV cache block is assigned a hash of the token sequence it represents, enabling exact prefix-match lookups. When a new request arrives whose token prefix matches a sequence of cached blocks, those physical GPU memory pages are directly reused.

From vLLM's docs: *"The core idea is simple — we cache the kv-cache blocks of processed requests, and reuse these blocks when a new request comes in with the same prefix as the processed request."* (vLLM docs, "Automatic Prefix Caching")

**Key detail:** vLLM's prefix caching is **prefix-only** — it only matches at the beginning of the input. It does not support caching KV states for tokens appearing at arbitrary positions within the prompt.

### LMCache

LMCache also caches **KV cache blocks** (Key/Value tensors), but at a **configurable chunk granularity** (default: 256 tokens per chunk). LMCache hashes each chunk independently, which enables:

- **Non-prefix KV reuse**: *"Non-prefix KV reuse: Extend KV reuse beyond prefix caching by reusing cached KV blocks at any position in the prompt."* (LMCache GitHub README)
- The **CacheBlend** technique allows selectively recomputing tokens for quality recovery when KV chunks are reused mid-prompt rather than at the prefix boundary. *(Yao et al., "CacheBlend: Fast large language model serving for RAG with cached knowledge fusion," EuroSys 2025)*

**This is a critical architectural difference:** vLLM only reuses KV blocks for exact prefix matches. LMCache can reuse chunks from anywhere in the prompt and selectively recomputes mismatched tokens.

---

## 2. Where is the Cache Stored?

### vLLM's Built-in Prefix Caching

| Tier | Supported? |
|------|-----------|
| **GPU memory** | **Yes** — this is the primary and effectively only storage location. KV blocks live in the PagedAttention buffer. |
| **CPU memory** | Partial — vLLM has native CPU offloading (available in recent versions) for **overflow** KV cache when GPU memory is exhausted, but this is a fallback, not the primary caching tier. |
| **Local disk (NVMe/SSD)** | **No** — vLLM has no built-in disk-based KV cache persistence. |
| **Remote/distributed storage (Redis, etc.)** | **No** — vLLM's caching is local to a single instance. |
| **Across multiple instances** | **No** — each vLLM pod manages its own cache in isolation. Standard load balancers scatter traffic, destroying cache locality in distributed deployments. |

### LMCache

| Tier | Supported? |
|------|-----------|
| **GPU memory** | Yes — active working set of KV caches. |
| **CPU RAM** | Yes — "hot cache" for recently used KV chunks, using pinned memory for efficient GPU↔CPU transfers. |
| **Local disk (NVMe/SSD)** | Yes — provides a large persistent tier for long documents and historical KV caches. |
| **Remote/distributed storage (Redis, Valkey, S3)** | Yes — persistent cross-instance storage with Redis/Valkey as the primary backend; also supports Mooncake, InfiniStore, S3-compatible object storage, NIXL, and GDS. |
| **Across multiple instances** | Yes — LMCache uses a centralized **KV cache controller** that maintains a global in-memory index of all cached KV blocks across all instances, enabling cross-instance cache lookups. |

From the LMCache paper: *"With LMCache, KV cache can be extracted from and loaded back to inference engines efficiently, stored in a hierarchy of storage devices (CPU memory, local disk, remote disk, and Redis)."*

---

## 3. How Does vLLM's Built-in Prefix Caching Work? What are its Limitations?

### How it works

1. **Block-level hashing:** Each request's KV cache is divided into fixed-size blocks (e.g., 128 tokens per block in newer vLLM). Each block is hashed based on its token sequence.
2. **Cache lookup:** When a new request arrives, vLLM hashes each block of the incoming prompt and checks if the hash exists in the cache.
3. **Block reuse:** If a block matches, the physical GPU memory pages are reused; no recomputation is needed for that block's tokens.
4. **Eviction:** When GPU memory fills up, blocks with the lowest access frequency are evicted (LRU-like eviction).

From the llm-d blog: *"vLLM's Automatic Prefix Caching: it intelligently identifies when requests share the same token sequence prefix. Instead of recomputing, it reuses the exact same memory pages from the cache through hash-based block matching."*

### Limitations

1. **GPU memory bound only:** The cache lives entirely in GPU memory. Since the KV cache for long contexts can far exceed GPU capacity (the LMCache paper's statistics show the portion exceeding GPU memory "has increased significantly over time"), most cached data is evicted before it can be reused by another query.

2. **Prefix-only reuse:** Only prefix matches are supported. If the repeated context appears mid-prompt (e.g., a retrieved document chunk in a RAG query), it cannot be reused.

3. **Single-instance scope:** Each vLLM pod has its own isolated cache. In multi-replica deployments, standard load balancers scatter related requests across different pods, causing widespread cache misses. The llm-d blog notes: *"Standard load balancers naively spread traffic evenly using cache-blind metrics, scattering related requests across different pods and destroying cache locality."*

4. **Fate-sharing with the engine:** If the vLLM process crashes, all KV cache is lost — there is no persistence layer.

5. **No cross-engine compatibility:** KV caches cached by one vLLM instance cannot be consumed by a different inference engine.

6. **Inefficient I/O at page granularity:** When offloading to CPU, vLLM transfers page-by-page (16-token pages), which the LMCache paper's evaluation shows achieves only **88 Gbps** effective bandwidth compared to LMCache's **400 Gbps** — because per-page transfers trigger individual CUDA memory copy kernel launches with metadata overhead.

---

## 4. How Does LMCache Work Architecturally? What storage backends does it support?

### Architecture

LMCache operates as a **layer** that sits between LLM inference engines and heterogeneous storage/network devices. Its key components:

1. **KV Connector** — An integration module plugged into the inference engine (vLLM/SGLang). It taps into the paged KV memory manager, intercepting KV cache writes and reads. During prompt processing, it checks if token sequences were seen before; on a cache hit, it fetches precomputed KV chunks from the backend, bypassing computation. On a miss, the engine computes KV as usual, and the Connector hands the newly generated KV data to LMCache for storage.

2. **Cache Index (Token Database)** — Maintains an internal index mapping token sequences to cached KV entries and their locations. Uses configurable chunking (default 256 tokens) and hashing.

3. **Memory Object & Allocator** — Manages KV cache entries using a custom allocator within the LocalCPUBackend, with pinned memory for fast GPU↔CPU transfers, NUMA-aware allocation, and LRU eviction.

4. **Asynchronous Offloading** — Offloading and loading happen asynchronously via background tasks (Disk Offload Task, Remote Offload Task), avoiding blocking inference threads.

5. **KV Cache Controller** — A centralized management daemon that provides APIs for lookup, pin/unpin, clear, compress/decompress, and move operations across all instances.

Two operational modes:
- **Storage Mode (KV cache offloading):** Persistent KV store — offloads infrequently used KV blocks from GPU to CPU/disk, persists popular caches across sessions.
- **Transport Mode (PD disaggregation):** Routes KV cache data between prefill and decode nodes in real-time via NIXL-based P2P channels.

From the LMCache paper (Section 6): *"The key design objectives are: Maximum flexibility, vLLM-native (aligns with scheduler-worker separation and piece-wise CUDA graph), Friendly to out-of-tree connectors, Minimum API-level overhead."*

### Supported Storage Backends

| Backend | Role |
|---------|------|
| **CPU DRAM (pinned memory)** | Hot cache tier |
| **Local disk (NVMe, SSD)** | Large persistent tier |
| **Redis / Valkey** | Distributed shared cache |
| **Mooncake** | KV cache-centric disaggregated storage |
| **InfiniStore (ByteDance)** | Distributed KV cache store |
| **S3-compatible object storage** | Cold/archive tier |
| **NIXL** | Cross-node P2P transfer transport |
| **GDS (GPUDirect Storage)** | Zero-copy GPU↔NVMe transfers |

---

## 5. When is LMCache Worth Adding Over vLLM's Built-in Prefix Caching?

LMCache is worth adding when any of these conditions apply:

### a) Cache demand exceeds GPU memory capacity
