## Repeatable Read vs. Serializable in PostgreSQL

### Core Difference

**Repeatable Read** uses *Snapshot Isolation*. It gives each transaction a stable snapshot of the database taken at the start of the first non-transaction-control statement in the transaction. No query within the transaction will see data committed by other transactions after the transaction began.

**Serializable** uses *Serializable Snapshot Isolation* — it works exactly the same as Repeatable Read but **adds monitoring for serialization anomalies** using predicate locks. If it detects that concurrent execution could produce a result inconsistent with *any* serial ordering of those transactions, it aborts one of them.

From the documentation:

> This isolation level [Serializable] works exactly the same as Repeatable Read except that it also monitors for conditions which could make execution of a concurrent set of serializable transactions behave in a manner inconsistent with all possible serial (one at a time) executions of those transactions.

Source: [13.2.3. Serializable Isolation Level](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html#XACT-SERIALIZABLE)

### Which Anomalies Each Prevents

| Isolation Level | Dirty Read | Nonrepeatable Read | Phantom Read | Serialization Anomaly |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Repeatable Read** | ✅ Prevented | ✅ Prevented | ✅ Prevented in PG (standard allows it, but PG's MVCC prevents it anyway) | ⚠️ **Possible** |
| **Serializable** | ✅ Prevented | ✅ Prevented | ✅ Prevented | ✅ Prevented |

From Table 13.1 in the documentation:

> The table also shows that PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read implementation does not allow phantom reads. This is acceptable under the SQL standard because the standard specifies which anomalies must *not* occur at certain isolation levels; higher guarantees are acceptable.

Source: [13.2. Transaction Isolation — Table 13.1](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html#MVCC-ISOLEVEL-TABLE)

### The Key Distinction: Serialization Anomalies

A **serialization anomaly** occurs when the result of committing a group of concurrent transactions is inconsistent with all possible orderings of those transactions one at a time.

**Repeatable Read does NOT guard against serialization anomalies.** The documentation gives this example — even a read-only transaction at this level may see an inconsistent state:

> even a read-only transaction at this level may see a control record updated to show that a batch has been completed but *not* see one of the detail records which is logically part of the batch because it read an earlier revision of the control record.

Source: [13.2.2. Repeatable Read Isolation Level](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html#XACT-REPEATABLE-READ)

**Serializable detects and prevents them** using predicate locking. The docs illustrate this with a classic example:

> Serializable transaction A computes `SELECT SUM(value) FROM mytab WHERE class = 1` (gets 30) and inserts 30 as a new row with `class = 2`. Concurrently, Serializable transaction B computes `SELECT SUM(value) FROM mytab WHERE class = 2` (gets 300) and inserts 300 as a new row with `class = 1`. If either transaction were running at the Repeatable Read isolation level, both would be allowed to commit; but since there is no serial order of execution consistent with the result, using Serializable transactions will allow one transaction to commit and will roll the other back.

Source: [13.2.3. Serializable Isolation Level](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html#XACT-SERIALIZABLE)

### SQLSTATE for Serialization Failure

A serialization failure always raises the SQLSTATE value **`'40001'`**.

From the documentation:

> It is important that an environment which uses this technique have a generalized way of handling serialization failures (which always return with an SQLSTATE value of '40001'), because it will be very hard to predict exactly which transactions might contribute to the read/write dependencies and need to be rolled back to prevent serialization anomalies.

Source: [13.2.3. Serializable Isolation Level](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html#XACT-SERIALIZABLE)

There are two distinct error *messages* associated with these failures, but both carry SQLSTATE `40001`:

- **Repeatable Read** triggers on concurrent updates:
  > `ERROR: could not serialize access due to concurrent update`

- **Serializable** triggers on read/write dependency cycles:
  > `ERROR: could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions`

In both cases, the application must abort the current transaction and retry from the beginning.

Source: [13.2.2. Repeatable Read Isolation Level](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html#XACT-REPEATABLE-READ) and [13.2.3. Serializable Isolation Level](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html#XACT-SERIALIZABLE)

---

### Summary

| Aspect | Repeatable Read | Serializable |
|---|---|---|
| Underlying technique | Snapshot Isolation | Serializable Snapshot Isolation |
| Prevents dirty read | Yes | Yes |
| Prevents nonrepeatable read | Yes | Yes |
| Prevents phantom reads | Yes (PostgreSQL-specific guarantee) | Yes |
| Prevents serialization anomalies | **No** | **Yes** (via predicate lock monitoring) |
| Serialization failure message | `could not serialize access due to concurrent update` | `could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions` |
| SQLSTATE | `40001` | `40001` |
| Blocking behavior | Never blocks for predicate locks | Only blocks when `SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE` is used |

**Authoritative source:** [PostgreSQL 18 Documentation — Section 13.2. Transaction Isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html)

A **serialization anomaly** occurs when the result of committing a group of concurrent transactions is inconsistent with all possible orderings of those transactions one at a time.

**Repeatable Read does NOT guard against serialization anomalies.** The documentation gives this example — even a read-only transaction at this level may see an inconsistent state:

> even a read-only transaction at this level may see a control record updated to show that a batch has been completed but *not* see one of the detail records which is logically part of the batch because it read an earlier revision of the control record.

Source: [13.2.2. Repeatable Read Isolation Level](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html#XACT-REPEATABLE-READ)

**Serializable detects and prevents them** using predicate locking. The docs illustrate this with a classic example:

> Serializable transaction A computes `SELECT SUM(value) FROM mytab WHERE class = 1` (gets 30) and inserts 30 as a new row with `class = 2`. Concurrently, Serializable transaction B computes `SELECT SUM(value) FROM mytab WHERE class = 2` (gets 300) and inserts 300 as a new row with `class = 1`. If either transaction were running at the Repeatable Read isolation level, both would be allowed to commit; but since there is no serial order of execution consistent with the result, using Serializable transactions will allow one transaction to commit and will roll the other back.

Source: [13.2.3. Serializable Isolation Level](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html#XACT-SERIALIZABLE)

### SQLSTATE for Serialization Failure

A serialization failure always raises the SQLSTATE value **`'40001'`**.

From the documentation:

> It is important that an environment which uses this technique have a generalized way of handling serialization failures (which always return with an SQLSTATE value of '40001'), because it will be very hard to predict exactly which transactions might contribute to the read/write dependencies and need to be rolled back to prevent serialization anomalies.

Source: [13.2.3. Serializable Isolation Level](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html#XACT-SERIALIZABLE)

There are two distinct error *messages* associated with these failures, but both carry SQLSTATE `40001`:

- **Repeatable Read** triggers on concurrent updates:
  > `ERROR: could not serialize access due to concurrent update`

- **Serializable** triggers on read/write dependency cycles:
  > `ERROR: could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions`

In both cases, the application must abort the current transaction and retry from the beginning.

Source: [13.2.2. Repeatable Read Isolation Level](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html#XACT-REPEATABLE-READ) and [13.2.3. Serializable Isolation Level](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html#XACT-SERIALIZABLE)

---

### Summary

| Aspect | Repeatable Read | Serializable |
|---|---|---|
| Underlying technique | Snapshot Isolation | Serializable Snapshot Isolation |
| Prevents dirty read | Yes | Yes |
| Prevents nonrepeatable read | Yes | Yes |
| Prevents phantom reads | Yes (PostgreSQL-specific guarantee) | Yes |
| Prevents serialization anomalies | **No** | **Yes** (via predicate lock monitoring) |
| Serialization failure message | `could not serialize access due to concurrent update` | `could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions` |
| SQLSTATE | `40001` | `40001` |
| Blocking behavior | Never blocks for predicate locks | Only blocks when `SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE` is used |

**Authoritative source:** [PostgreSQL 18 Documentation — Section 13.2. Transaction Isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html)

## Default value: **0.92**

## What `--gpu-memory-utilization` controls

From the authoritative source — vLLM's own `CacheConfig` class at [`vllm/config/cache.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/config/cache.py):

```python
DEFAULT_GPU_MEMORY_UTILIZATION: ClassVar[float] = 0.92
```

The field's docstring explains its purpose:

> **"The fraction of GPU memory to be used for the model executor, which can range from 0 to 1. For example, a value of 0.5 would imply 50% GPU memory utilization. This is a per-instance limit, and only applies to the current vLLM instance. It does not matter if you have another vLLM instance running on the same GPU."**

In practice, setting this value determines what fraction of the GPU's total VRAM is available for vLLM to use. The remaining fraction is reserved for the CUDA runtime, operating system, and other overhead. vLLM then uses the allocated portion for:

1. **Model weights** — the loaded LLM parameters.
2. **Activations** — intermediate tensors during forward pass.
3. **KV cache** — the cached key/value pairs for attention, which is typically the largest consumer and what this option most directly controls for throughput.

The remaining memory beyond `gpu_memory_utilization` (i.e. the `1.0 - gpu_memory_utilization` portion) is **not used by vLLM** and stays free for other processes on the GPU.

### Special note: extensible KV cache

vLLM has a newer "extensible KV cache" mode. The source code in `resolved_gpu_memory_utilization` reveals a nuanced default:

> *"If unspecified, **1.0** with the extensible KV cache (sized from measured memory) and **0.92** otherwise."*

So if you have `enable_extensible_kv_cache` enabled, the effective utilization defaults to `1.0`; otherwise it defaults to `0.92`.

I notice the brief mentions vLLM may have added cross-instance prefix caching in recent releases. Let me verify that quickly.



**Note:** I ran into a tool budget limit when trying to verify whether vLLM has added built-in cross-instance prefix caching in recent releases. I'll present the answer based on the verified material above.

---

## LMCache vs. vLLM Built-in Prefix Caching — Comparison

### 1. What Each One Caches

Both cache **KV key/value tensors** from the attention mechanism, computed during the prefill phase.

- **vLLM Automatic Prefix Caching (APC)**: Caches KV cache *blocks* (default 128-token blocks), indexed by a hash of their token sequences. Reuse is strictly **prefix-based** — it only matches when a new request shares the exact same initial token sequence as a previously cached block.
  > *"vLLM takes this further with Automatic Prefix Caching: it intelligently identifies when requests share the same token sequence prefix. Instead of recomputing, it reuses the exact same memory pages from the cache through hash-based block matching."* — [llm-d.ai/blog/kvcache-wins-you-can-see](https://llm-d.ai/blog/kvcache-wins-you-can-see) (Sept 24, 2025)

- **LMCache**: Also caches KV chunks (default 256 tokens per chunk), but adds:
  - **Non-prefix KV reuse** (CacheBlend): KV blocks can be reused at *any position* in the prompt, with partial recomputation for quality recovery — useful for RAG where retrieved documents appear at different prompt positions.
  - **Pluggable SERDE interface**: Token dropping, compression (e.g., CacheGen), and custom serialization.
  - **PD disaggregation**: KV transfer from prefill workers to decode workers over NVLink, RDMA, or TCP.
  > *"Extend KV reuse beyond prefix caching by reusing cached KV blocks at any position in the prompt."* — [LMCache GitHub README](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache)

### 2. Where the Cache Is Stored

| Aspect | vLLM APC | LMCache |
|---|---|---|
| **Primary tier** | GPU memory (VRAM) only | GPU → CPU DRAM (pinned, "hot cache") → Local disk (NVMe) → Remote backends |
| **Storage scope** | In-process, single vLLM instance | Standalone daemon, shared across multiple engine instances |
| **Persistence** | Lost on process crash/restart | Survives engine crashes; backed by disk/remote storage for cross-session reuse |
| **Remote backends** | None | Redis/Valkey, Mooncake, InfiniStore, S3-compatible object storage, NIXL, GDS |

vLLM's prefix cache is purely in-GPU memory:
> *"vLLM splits GPU memory into distinct pools… Prefix Cache (KV cache blocks from earlier requests, kept so later requests can reuse them)."* — [ScaleOps blog](https://scaleops.com/blog/vllm-kv-cache-prefix-cache-gpu-memory/) (Oct 26, 2024)

LMCache's hierarchical storage:
> *"LMCache implements a hierarchical storage system with three distinct tiers: GPU Memory, CPU DRAM, Local storage (e.g. NVMe GDS), Remote storage (e.g., Redis, Mooncake, InfiniStore)."* — [LMCache Architecture Overview](https://docs.lmcache.ai/developer_guide/architecture.html)

### 3. When LMCache Is Worth Adding

LMCache adds value in these scenarios where vLLM's built-in caching falls short:

**a) Multi-node / distributed inference** — vLLM's prefix cache is confined to a single process. A request routed to a different pod won't find prefixes cached on the original pod:
> *"vLLM's prefix caching breaks in distributed deployments: Standard load balancers scatter related requests across pods, destroying cache locality."* — [llm-d.ai](https://llm-d.ai/blog/kvcache-wins-you-can-see)

**b) Cross-engine KV reuse** — LMCache is vendor-neutral, integrating with vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM. KV caches stored via one engine can be retrieved by another.

**c) Fault tolerance** — LMCache runs as a standalone daemon; KV cache survives vLLM engine crashes. With vLLM APC, a process restart wipes everything.

**d) Persistent caching** — With remote backends (Redis, S3), LMCache persists KV caches beyond the lifetime of individual calls — useful for recurring large prompts (system prompts, retrieved documents) across restarts.

**e) Prefill-decode disaggregation** — LMCache natively supports transferring KV from prefill to decode workers. vLLM does not provide this natively.

**f) RAG with CacheBlend** — Non-prefix KV reuse at arbitrary prompt positions is specifically designed for RAG workloads.

**When it's NOT worth it:** On light workloads with good GPU memory headroom, LMCache can add overhead (worse TTFT and ITL) because the offload/retrieve path has its own cost:
> *"In a single-node setup, LMCache competes directly with fast local GPU reuse and often loses unless pressure is severe. In a distributed system, LMCache may enable reuse that local prefix caching alone cannot provide at all."* — [LMCache-and-vLLM-Prefix-Caching experiment](https://github.com/aneeshp10/LMCache-and-vLLM-Prefix-Caching)

### 4. Architecture Comparison

| Dimension | vLLM APC | LMCache |
|---|---|---|
| **Deployment** | Single-node, in-process | Standalone daemon (multi-process) |
| **Scope** | One vLLM process | Multiple engine instances; multi-node via remote backends |
| **Fault tolerance** | Cache lost if vLLM dies | Independent daemon; KV survives engine crash |
| **Storage tiers** | GPU only | GPU → CPU DRAM → Disk → Remote |
| **P/D disaggregation** | Not natively | Yes (NIXL, RDMA, TCP) |
| **Compression** | None | Pluggable SERDE (CacheGen, token dropping) |

### Caveat
I was unable to fully verify whether vLLM has added cross-instance prefix caching in recent 2024–2025 releases — its roadmap reportedly includes distributed prefix cache sharing and native P/D disaggregation. If you're evaluating for production, checking the latest vLLM release notes is recommended.

> *"vLLM's prefix caching breaks in distributed deployments: Standard load balancers scatter related requests across pods, destroying cache locality."* — [llm-d.ai](https://llm-d.ai/blog/kvcache-wins-you-can-see)

**b) Cross-engine KV reuse** — LMCache is vendor-neutral, integrating with vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM. KV caches stored via one engine can be retrieved by another.

**c) Fault tolerance** — LMCache runs as a standalone daemon; KV cache survives vLLM engine crashes. With vLLM APC, a process restart wipes everything.

**d) Persistent caching** — With remote backends (Redis, S3), LMCache persists KV caches beyond the lifetime of individual calls — useful for recurring large prompts (system prompts, retrieved documents) across restarts.

**e) Prefill-decode disaggregation** — LMCache natively supports transferring KV from prefill to decode workers. vLLM does not provide this natively.

**f) RAG with CacheBlend** — Non-prefix KV reuse at arbitrary prompt positions is specifically designed for RAG workloads.

**When it's NOT worth it:** On light workloads with good GPU memory headroom, LMCache can add overhead (worse TTFT and ITL) because the offload/retrieve path has its own cost:
> *"In a single-node setup, LMCache competes directly with fast local GPU reuse and often loses unless pressure is severe. In a distributed system, LMCache may enable reuse that local prefix caching alone cannot provide at all."* — [LMCache-and-vLLM-Prefix-Caching experiment](https://github.com/aneeshp10/LMCache-and-vLLM-Prefix-Caching)

### 4. Architecture Comparison

| Dimension | vLLM APC | LMCache |
|---|---|---|
| **Deployment** | Single-node, in-process | Standalone daemon (multi-process) |
| **Scope** | One vLLM process | Multiple engine instances; multi-node via remote backends |
| **Fault tolerance** | Cache lost if vLLM dies | Independent daemon; KV survives engine crash |
| **Storage tiers** | GPU only | GPU → CPU DRAM → Disk → Remote |
| **P/D disaggregation** | Not natively | Yes (NIXL, RDMA, TCP) |
| **Compression** | None | Pluggable SERDE (CacheGen, token dropping) |

### Caveat
I was unable to fully verify whether vLLM has added cross-instance prefix caching in recent 2024–2025 releases — its roadmap reportedly includes distributed prefix cache sharing and native P/D disaggregation. If you're evaluating for production, checking the latest vLLM release notes is recommended.

I will call web_agent with your full request.



Here is the full answer returned by the sub-agent:

---

## Repeatable Read vs. Serializable in PostgreSQL

### Core Difference

**Repeatable Read** uses *Snapshot Isolation*. It gives each transaction a stable snapshot of the database taken at the start of the first non-transaction-control statement in the transaction. No query within the transaction will see data committed by other transactions after the transaction began.

**Serializable** uses *Serializable Snapshot Isolation* — it works exactly the same as Repeatable Read but **adds monitoring for serialization anomalies** using predicate locks. If it detects that concurrent execution could produce a result inconsistent with *any* serial ordering of those transactions, it aborts one of them.

From the documentation:

> This isolation level [Serializable] works exactly the same as Repeatable Read except that it also monitors for conditions which could make execution of a concurrent set of serializable transactions behave in a manner inconsistent with all possible serial (one at a time) executions of those transactions.

Source: [13.2.3. Serializable Isolation Level](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html#XACT-SERIALIZABLE)

### Which Anomalies Each Prevents

| Isolation Level | Dirty Read | Nonrepeatable Read | Phantom Read | Serialization Anomaly |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Repeatable Read** | ✅ Prevented | ✅ Prevented | ✅ Prevented in PG (standard allows it, but PG's MVCC prevents it anyway) | ⚠️ **Possible** |
| **Serializable** | ✅ Prevented | ✅ Prevented | ✅ Prevented | ✅ Prevented |

From Table 13.1 in the documentation:

> The table also shows that PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read implementation does not allow phantom reads. This is acceptable under the SQL standard because the standard specifies which anomalies must *not* occur at certain isolation levels; higher guarantees are acceptable.

Source: [13.2. Transaction Isolation — Table 13.1](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html#MVCC-ISOLEVEL-TABLE)

### The Key Distinction: Serialization Anomalies

A **serialization anomaly** occurs when the result of committing a group of concurrent transactions is inconsistent with all possible orderings of those transactions one at a time.

**Repeatable Read does NOT guard against serialization anomalies.** The documentation gives this example — even a read-only transaction at this level may see an inconsistent state:

> even a read-only transaction at this level may see a control record updated to show that a batch has been completed but *not* see one of the detail records which is logically part of the batch because it read an earlier revision of the control record.

Source: [13.2.2. Repeatable Read Isolation Level](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html#XACT-REPEATABLE-READ)

**Serializable detects and prevents them** using predicate locking. The docs illustrate this with a classic example:

> Serializable transaction A computes `SELECT SUM(value) FROM mytab WHERE class = 1` (gets 30) and inserts 30 as a new row with `class = 2`. Concurrently, Serializable transaction B computes `SELECT SUM(value) FROM mytab WHERE class = 2` (gets 300) and inserts 300 as a new row with `class = 1`. If either transaction were running at the Repeatable Read isolation level, both would be allowed to commit; but since there is no serial order of execution consistent with the result, using Serializable transactions will allow one transaction to commit and will roll the other back.

Source: [13.2.3. Serializable Isolation Level](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html#XACT-SERIALIZABLE)

### SQLSTATE for Serialization Failure

A serialization failure always raises the SQLSTATE value **`'40001'`**.

From the documentation:

> It is important that an environment which uses this technique have a generalized way of handling serialization failures (which always return with an SQLSTATE value of '40001'), because it will be very hard to predict exactly which transactions might contribute to the read/write dependencies and need to be rolled back to prevent serialization anomalies.

Source: [13.2.3. Serializable Isolation Level](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html#XACT-SERIALIZABLE)

There are two distinct error *messages* associated with these failures, but both carry SQLSTATE `40001`:

- **Repeatable Read** triggers on concurrent updates:
  > `ERROR: could not serialize access due to concurrent update`

- **Serializable** triggers on read/write dependency cycles:
  > `ERROR: could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions`

In both cases, the application must abort the current transaction and retry from the beginning.

Source: [13.2.2. Repeatable Read Isolation Level](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html#XACT-REPEATABLE-READ) and [13.2.3. Serializable Isolation Level](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html#XACT-SERIALIZABLE)

---

### Summary

| Aspect | Repeatable Read | Serializable |
|---|---|---|
| Underlying technique | Snapshot Isolation | Serializable Snapshot Isolation |
| Prevents dirty read | Yes | Yes |
| Prevents nonrepeatable read | Yes | Yes |
| Prevents phantom reads | Yes (PostgreSQL-specific guarantee) | Yes |
| Prevents serialization anomalies | **No** | **Yes** (via predicate lock monitoring) |
| Serialization failure message | `could not serialize access due to concurrent update` | `could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions` |
| SQLSTATE | `40001` | `40001` |
| Blocking behavior | Never blocks for predicate locks | Only blocks when `SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE` is used |

**Authoritative source:** [PostgreSQL 18 Documentation — Section 13.2. Transaction Isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html)

Here is the verdict on the two-part claim, based on the official PostgreSQL documentation (PostgreSQL 18.6, section 13.2 — *Transaction Isolation*).

---

## Part 1: "PostgreSQL's default transaction isolation level is REPEATABLE READ"

**This is FALSE.** PostgreSQL's default transaction isolation level is **READ COMMITTED**, not REPEATABLE READ.

The official docs (Table 13.1 in section 13.2) list four isolation levels. READ COMMITTED is the level automatically chosen for each new transaction if the user does not explicitly set one. (Note: this lookup hit a tool budget limit on this turn, so I could not retrieve the exact "default = read committed" passage live — but this is a well-established fact confirmed in the same documentation.)

## Part 2: "At that level [REPEATABLE READ], phantom reads can occur"

**This is also FALSE for PostgreSQL.** The official documentation states explicitly:

> **Table 13.1. Transaction Isolation Levels**
>
> | Isolation Level | Dirty Read | Nonrepeatable Read | Phantom Read | Serialization Anomaly |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | Repeatable read | Not possible | Not possible | *"Allowed, but not in PG"* | Possible |

And then in Section 13.2.2:

> *The Repeatable Read isolation level … is a stronger guarantee than is required by the SQL standard for this isolation level, and **prevents all of the phenomena described in Table 13.1 except for serialization anomalies**.*

The table entry *"Allowed, but not in PG"* under Phantom Read for Repeatable Read means: the SQL standard *permits* phantom reads at this level, but **PostgreSQL's implementation prevents them entirely** (using multi-version concurrency control — MVCC). Phantom reads only become a possibility at the SQL standard's lower levels (Read Committed and Read Uncommitted).

---

### Summary

| Claim component | Verdict | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Default level is REPEATABLE READ | **False** — default is READ COMMITTED | PostgreSQL docs section 13.2 |
| Phantom reads occur at REPEATABLE READ | **False** — PostgreSQL prevents them at this level | Table 13.1 + §13.2.2 of the docs |

<acknowledgement>: Understood. The user wants to know the default value and precise meaning of vLLM's `--gpu-memory-utilization` option, cited from official documentation. I'll delegate a web search to find this.



The web_agent has provided the following answer:

---

**Default Value: `0.92`**

The default is defined as a class constant in `CacheConfig` in the file `vllm/config/cache.py`:

```python
@config
class CacheConfig:
    DEFAULT_GPU_MEMORY_UTILIZATION: ClassVar[float] = 0.92
```

### What It Controls

From the field-level docstring in `vllm/config/cache.py`:

> **"The fraction of GPU memory to be used for the model executor, which can range from 0 to 1. For example, a value of 0.5 would imply 50% GPU memory utilization. This is a per-instance limit, and only applies to the current vLLM instance. It does not matter if you have another vLLM instance running on the same GPU. For example, if you have two vLLM instances running on the same GPU, you can set the GPU memory utilization to 0.5 for each instance. On non-GPU installs, this value controls the corresponding device memory utilization."**

> *"If unspecified, 1.0 with the extensible KV cache (sized from measured memory) and 0.92 otherwise; see `resolved_gpu_memory_utilization`."*

### How GPU Memory Is Actually Allocated

1. **vLLM first loads the model weights** onto the GPU. These weights consume a fixed amount of VRAM.
2. **The remaining GPU memory** (i.e., `total_VRAM × resolved_gpu_memory_utilization − weight_memory`) is used to **pre-allocate the KV cache** (the blocks of cached attention keys and values). The KV cache is what lets vLLM avoid recomputing KV states for previously seen tokens.
3. **What you set controls the upper bound** of total memory reserved for the model executor (weights + KV cache). The KV cache block count (`num_gpu_blocks`) is computed from the memory that remains after the weights are placed, up to the fraction specified.

With the default of `0.92`, vLLM will try to use 92% of each GPU's total VRAM for the combined model executor. Since model weights are fixed, that effectively means the KV cache gets whatever space is left after loading the weights.

**Important nuance with the extensible KV cache** (`--enable-extensible-kv-cache`, now enabled by default on CUDA/ROCm): When this mode is active, the `resolved_gpu_memory_utilization` becomes `1.0` — the KV cache is sized dynamically from the memory actually free after CUDA graph capture, rather than from a profiling estimate. So with extensible KV cache, `gpu_memory_utilization` is effectively a ceiling, not a strict allocation target.

### CLI Argument Definition

The `--gpu-memory-utilization` flag is auto-generated from the `CacheConfig.gpu_memory_utilization` field in `vllm/engine/arg_utils.py`. The `EngineArgs` dataclass holds:

```python
gpu_memory_utilization: float | None = CacheConfig.gpu_memory_utilization
```

This maps to `float | None` with validation bounds `gt=0, le=1` (from the `Field` in `CacheConfig`), and the default is inherited from `CacheConfig.gpu_memory_utilization` which is `None` — meaning the default resolution logic in `resolved_gpu_memory_utilization` kicks in.

For example, if you have two vLLM instances running on the same GPU, you can set the GPU memory utilization to 0.5 for each instance. 1. **vLLM first loads the model weights** onto the GPU. These weights consume a fixed amount of VRAM.
2. **The remaining GPU memory** (i.e., `total_VRAM × resolved_gpu_memory_utilization − weight_memory`) is used to **pre-allocate the KV cache** (the blocks of cached attention keys and values). The KV cache is what lets vLLM avoid recomputing KV states for previously seen tokens.
3. **What you set controls the upper bound** of total memory reserved for the model executor (weights + KV cache). The KV cache block count (`num_gpu_blocks`) is computed from the memory that remains after the weights are placed, up to the fraction specified.

With the default of `0.92`, vLLM will try to use 92% of each GPU's total VRAM for the combined model executor. Since model weights are fixed, that effectively means the KV cache gets whatever space is left after loading the weights.

The `--gpu-memory-utilization` flag is auto-generated from the `CacheConfig.gpu_memory_utilization` field in `vllm/engine/arg_utils.py`. The `EngineArgs` dataclass holds:

```python
gpu_memory_utilization: float | None = CacheConfig.gpu_memory_utilization
```

This maps to `float | None` with validation bounds `gt=0, le=1` (from the `Field` in `CacheConfig`), and the default is inherited from `CacheConfig.gpu_memory_utilization` which is `None` — meaning the default resolution logic in `resolved_gpu_memory_utilization` kicks in.

## Summary Assumption

This brief assumes vLLM's V1 engine with automatic prefix caching enabled (the default in recent releases) as the baseline, and LMCache as a standalone daemon process integrated alongside it. All facts are sourced from live pages fetched during this task.

---

## 1. What Each One Caches

### vLLM Built-in Prefix Caching

**What is cached:** Key-value (KV) tensors — specifically, the per-layer key and value attention tensors computed during the prefill phase for each block of tokens. vLLM divides the prompt into fixed-size blocks (default 16 tokens per block), computes the KV cache for each block, and stores it in GPU memory.

**How it works:** vLLM indexes each KV block by a **hash of its token IDs**. When a new request starts, vLLM computes the hash of the leading token sequences and checks whether precomputed KV blocks exist for those hashes. If they do, the prefill is skipped for the matching blocks — only the divergent suffix is computed. This is **Automatic Prefix Caching** (not the older explicit-prefix approach).

> From the vLLM docs (Automatic Prefix Caching): *"Prefix caching kv-cache blocks is a popular optimization in LLM inference to avoid redundant prompt computations. The core idea is simple – we cache the kv-cache blocks from earlier requests and reuse them by later ones."*

**What is NOT cached:**
- Attention output tensors (only KV tensors are cached)
- Embedding outputs
- Intermediate activation values
- Anything computed during the decode (generation) phase — only the **prefill** KV blocks are cached

### LMCache

**What is cached:** LMCache also caches **KV cache chunks** (tensors), but with a critical architectural difference. It operates as a **standalone daemon** (not embedded in the inference engine) and manages KV cache data that it extracts from vLLM's paged KV memory manager via an integration connector.

From the LMCache architecture docs: *"Integrated into the LLM engine (vLLM), the Connector taps into the paged KV memory manager. During prompt processing, it checks if token sequences were seen before: Cache hit: Fetches precomputed KV cache chunks from LMCache, bypassing computation; Cache miss: Model computes KV as usual, then Connector hands newly-generated KV data to LMCache for storage."*

**Additional capabilities beyond prefix caching:**
- **Non-prefix KV reuse**: LMCache's CacheBlend feature can reuse cached KV blocks at **any position** in the prompt, not just as prefixes, selectively recomputing tokens for quality recovery.

> *"Non-prefix KV reuse: Extend KV reuse beyond prefix caching by reusing cached KV blocks at any position in the prompt. This leverages CacheBlend to selectively recompute tokens for quality recovery."* (LMCache README)

- **PD disaggregation**: LMCache supports KV cache transfer from prefill workers to decode workers over NVLink, RDMA, or TCP, enabling split-engine deployment.

---

## 2. Where the Cache Is Stored

### vLLM Built-in Prefix Caching

| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Storage location** | **In-process, GPU memory only** |
| **Granularity** | KV blocks (16-token chunks by default) stored in GPU memory pools managed by vLLM's PagedAttention allocator |
| **Persistence** | **Ephemeral** — cached data is lost when the vLLM process terminates. It survives only for the lifetime of the process. |
| **Cross-request scope** | Within a single vLLM process on a single node |
| **Eviction** | LRU, triggered when GPU memory pressure forces it (controlled by `--gpu-memory-utilization`) |

From the ScaleOps blog: *"The prefix cache is the set of KV cache blocks that vLLM keeps from earlier requests for reuse by later ones... The prefix cache only grows. Every unique prefix, including one-off RAG queries and completed chat turns, is stored until memory is full. LRU eviction starts only then."*

### LMCache

| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Storage location** | **Multi-tier, distributed** — GPU memory, CPU DRAM (pinned), local disk (NVMe/SSD), and remote backends |
| **Tier 1: GPU memory** | Active working set of KV caches currently in use by the model |
| **Tier 2: CPU DRAM** | "Hot cache" for recently used KV chunks, using pinned memory for efficient GPU↔CPU transfers. Acts as a staging layer. |
| **Tier 3: Local storage** | Disk-backed backend (SSD/NVMe) for larger, less-frequently-accessed KV data |
| **Tier 4: Remote storage** | Redis/Valkey, Mooncake, InfiniStore, S3-compatible object storage, NIXL, GDS |
| **Persistence** | **Persistent across requests, sessions, and even process restarts** when backed by disk or remote storage |
| **Eviction** | LRU on CPU tier, with configurable policies per backend |

From the LMCache architecture docs, the data flow:

> *"When the model generates new key-value (KV) cache chunks on the GPU, LMCache can: (1) Offload overflow KV caches from GPU to CPU DRAM, freeing precious GPU memory; (2) Asynchronously write KV caches from CPU to disk or remote storage using LRU eviction policies; (3) Prefetch hot KV caches from disk/remote storage back to CPU when needed; (4) On-demand reuse of cached segments by moving them from CPU back to GPU."*

**Key architectural difference:** LMCache runs as a **separate daemon process**, decoupled from the inference engine. This means KV cache is **not fate-shared** with the engine — it survives engine crashes.

> *"LMCache, as a standalone daemon process, manages KV cache independently from the inference engine process, so that KV cache will not be lost even if the inference engine crashes (i.e., no fate-sharing with engines)."* (LMCache README)

---

## 3. When LMCache Is Worth Adding on Top of vLLM's Built-in Caching

LMCache adds value in scenarios where vLLM's built-in prefix cache is insufficient:

### (a) Distributed / Multi-Node Cache Sharing

vLLM prefix caching is scoped to a single process on a single node. In a horizontally-scaled deployment with multiple vLLM workers (e.g., behind a load balancer or across a Ray cluster), **different workers cannot share cached KV blocks**.

> *"vLLM prefix caching reuses KV state within a single node. LMCache adds a distributed cache layer so multiple vLLM workers on different machines can share the same cached KV state."* (Deployment blog)

If your workload has repeated prompts across different instances (e.g., a common system prompt, shared RAG documents, multi-turn conversation threads distributed across workers), LMCache enables **cross-node KV cache sharing** via remote backends like Redis or Mooncake.

### (b) Persistent Cache Across Process Restarts

Since vLLM's prefix cache is in-process and lost on restart, any cache warm-up cost must be paid after every deployment, rolling restart, or crash. LMCache persists KV cache to disk or remote storage, enabling **cache hot-reload** after process restart.

> *"LMCache, as a standalone daemon process... KV cache will not be lost even if the inference engine crashes."*

### (c) GPU Memory Pressure Relief via Offloading

In long-context or high-concurrency scenarios, vLLM's prefix cache can consume significant GPU memory. LMCache can **offload cold KV blocks to CPU or disk**, freeing GPU memory for active workloads, while still enabling reuse of hot blocks.

> *"Offload overflow KV caches from GPU to CPU DRAM, freeing precious GPU memory."* (LMCache docs)

### (d) Prefill-Decode Disaggregation

LMCache supports moving KV cache from prefill workers to decode workers over RDMA/NVLink/TCP, enabling a **disaggregated inference architecture** where different nodes specialize in prefill vs. generation.

> *"Support KV cache transfer from prefill workers to decode workers over NVLink, RDMA, or TCP through transport layers such as NIXL."* (LMCache README)

vLLM does not natively support this form of KV cache transfer across worker roles.

### (e) Agentic / Multi-Turn Workloads with Cross-Request Reuse

For multi-turn conversations or agentic workflows where conversation history is long and partially repeated across turns, LMCache's non-prefix KV reuse (CacheBlend) can reuse cached segments at arbitrary positions in the prompt, not just at the prefix boundary.

### (f) Compression and SERDE

LMCache provides a pluggable SERDE interface for **KV cache compression** (e.g., CacheGen), enabling bandwidth-efficient transfers to remote backends and higher storage density. This is an extra dimension beyond what vLLM's built-in cache provides.

---

## 4. Direct Comparison Table

| Feature | vLLM Prefix Caching | LMCache |
|---|---|---|
| **Caches** | KV tensors (prefill blocks) | KV tensors (prefill + non-prefix via CacheBlend) |
| **Scope** | Single vLLM process, single node | Distributed across nodes via remote backends |
| **Storage** | In-process GPU memory | Multi-tier: GPU → CPU pinned RAM → local disk → remote (Redis, Mooncake, S3, etc.) |
| **Persistence** | Ephemeral (lost on process exit) | Persistent across restarts when backed by disk/remote |
| **Cache sharing** | None across processes | Yes, via P2P or remote storage |
| **Compression** | FP8 KV cache quantization (native) | Pluggable SERDE (CacheGen, etc.) |
| **Process model** | Embedded in vLLM | Standalone daemon, integrates as a sidecar |
| **Fate sharing** | Yes — engine crash = cache loss | No — cache survives engine crash |
| **PD disaggregation** | No native support | Supported via KV transfer backends |
| **Non-prefix reuse** | No | Yes (CacheBlend) |
| **Complexity** | Zero (enabled by default) | Requires daemon deployment, backend config, networking |
| **Overhead** | Near-zero (hash-based lookup) | Additional inter-process communication, async I/O |

---

Here are the findings from the official PostgreSQL 18 documentation.

---

## REPEATABLE READ vs SERIALIZABLE Isolation Levels

### Anomalies Prevented (Table 13.1)

| Phenomenon | Repeatable Read | Serializable |
|---|---|---|
| **Dirty read** | Not possible | Not possible |
| **Nonrepeatable read** | Not possible | Not possible |
| **Phantom read** | Allowed by SQL standard, *but not in PostgreSQL* | Not possible |
| **Serialization anomaly** | **Possible** | Not possible |

### Repeatable Read (Snapshot Isolation)

PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ is implemented using **Snapshot Isolation**. Key characteristics:

- A query within a REPEATABLE READ transaction sees a snapshot of the database as of the **start of the first non-transaction-control statement** in the transaction (not per-query). Successive `SELECT` commands within the same transaction see the same data.
- It **prevents dirty reads, nonrepeatable reads, and phantom reads** (the last more strongly than the SQL standard requires).
- It does **not** prevent **serialization anomalies**: the committed result of concurrent transactions may be inconsistent with every possible serial ordering. The documentation explains: *"This view will not necessarily always be consistent with some serial (one at a time) execution of concurrent transactions of the same level."*
- A concurrent update can cause an error at commit time:

  > *"if the first updater commits … then the repeatable read transaction will be rolled back with the message `ERROR:  could not serialize access due to concurrent update`"*

### Serializable (Serializable Snapshot Isolation)

The SERIALIZABLE level is **strictly stronger** than REPEATABLE READ. From the docs:

> *"This level emulates serial transaction execution for all committed transactions; as if transactions had been executed one after another, serially, rather than concurrently."*

The critical difference:

> *"like the Repeatable Read level, applications using this level must be prepared to retry transactions due to serialization failures. In fact, this isolation level works exactly the same as Repeatable Read except that it also monitors for conditions which could make execution of a concurrent set of serializable transactions behave in a manner inconsistent with all possible serial executions of those transactions."*

PostgreSQL implements this via **predicate locking** (locks that show up in `pg_locks` with `mode = SIReadLock`). These predicate locks detect read/write dependencies between concurrent transactions that could produce a serialization anomaly. The example in the docs shows two concurrent transactions computing sums over overlapping partitions and inserting results into each other's partition — under SERIALIZABLE, the second to commit is rolled back:

> *"if A had executed before B, B would have computed the sum 330, not 300, and similarly the other order would have resulted in a different sum computed by A."*

Error message for serialization anomalies:

> `ERROR:  could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions`

### The SQLSTATE for Serialization Failure

Both isolation levels can raise serialization failures, and the SQLSTATE is the same:

> **"Such an error's message text will vary according to the precise circumstances, but it will always have the SQLSTATE code `40001` (`serialization_failure`)."**
> — Section 13.5, *Serialization Failure Handling*

Additionally, the SERIALIZABLE docs confirm:

> *"...handling serialization failures (which always return with an SQLSTATE value of '40001'), because it will be very hard to predict exactly which transactions might contribute to the read/write dependencies and need to be rolled back to prevent serialization anomalies."*

### Key Practical Takeaway

- **Repeatable Read** gives you a stable snapshot but can silently commit results that no serial ordering could produce. It only errors on *conflicting concurrent updates* to the same row.
- **Serializable** adds runtime detection of read/write dependency patterns that could cause serialization anomalies. It may roll back a transaction even when no concurrent update touched the same rows — because the *logical* ordering of operations across multiple rows could not be serialized.
- Applications using either level **must implement retry logic** for SQLSTATE `40001` errors. The official guidance: *"It is important to retry the complete transaction, including all logic that decides which SQL to issue and/or which values to use."*

## REPEATABLE READ vs SERIALIZABLE Isolation Levels

### Anomalies Prevented (Table 13.1)

| Phenomenon | Repeatable Read | Serializable |
|---|---|---|
| **Dirty read** | Not possible | Not possible |
| **Nonrepeatable read** | Not possible | Not possible |
| **Phantom read** | Allowed by SQL standard, *but not in PostgreSQL* | Not possible |
| **Serialization anomaly** | **Possible** | Not possible |

### Repeatable Read (Snapshot Isolation)

PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ is implemented using **Snapshot Isolation**. Key characteristics:

- A query within a REPEATABLE READ transaction sees a snapshot of the database as of the **start of the first non-transaction-control statement** in the transaction (not per-query). Successive `SELECT` commands within the same transaction see the same data.
- It **prevents dirty reads, nonrepeatable reads, and phantom reads** (the last more strongly than the SQL standard requires).
- It does **not** prevent **serialization anomalies**: the committed result of concurrent transactions may be inconsistent with every possible serial ordering. The documentation explains: *"This view will not necessarily always be consistent with some serial (one at a time) execution of concurrent transactions of the same level."*
- A concurrent update can cause an error at commit time:

  > *"if the first updater commits … then the repeatable read transaction will be rolled back with the message `ERROR:  could not serialize access due to concurrent update`"*

### Serializable (Serializable Snapshot Isolation)

The SERIALIZABLE level is **strictly stronger** than REPEATABLE READ. From the docs:

> *"This level emulates serial transaction execution for all committed transactions; as if transactions had been executed one after another, serially, rather than concurrently."*

The critical difference:

> *"like the Repeatable Read level, applications using this level must be prepared to retry transactions due to serialization failures. In fact, this isolation level works exactly the same as Repeatable Read except that it also monitors for conditions which could make execution of a concurrent set of serializable transactions behave in a manner inconsistent with all possible serial executions of those transactions."*

PostgreSQL implements this via **predicate locking** (locks that show up in `pg_locks` with `mode = SIReadLock`). These predicate locks detect read/write dependencies between concurrent transactions that could produce a serialization anomaly. The example in the docs shows two concurrent transactions computing sums over overlapping partitions and inserting results into each other's partition — under SERIALIZABLE, the second to commit is rolled back:

> *"if A had executed before B, B would have computed the sum 330, not 300, and similarly the other order would have resulted in a different sum computed by A."*

Error message for serialization anomalies:

> `ERROR:  could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions`

### The SQLSTATE for Serialization Failure

Both isolation levels can raise serialization failures, and the SQLSTATE is the same:

> **"Such an error's message text will vary according to the precise circumstances, but it will always have the SQLSTATE code `40001` (`serialization_failure`)."**
> — Section 13.5, *Serialization Failure Handling*

Additionally, the SERIALIZABLE docs confirm:

> *"...handling serialization failures (which always return with an SQLSTATE value of '40001'), because it will be very hard to predict exactly which transactions might contribute to the read/write dependencies and need to be rolled back to prevent serialization anomalies."*

### Key Practical Takeaway

- **Repeatable Read** gives you a stable snapshot but can silently commit results that no serial ordering could produce. It only errors on *conflicting concurrent updates* to the same row.
- **Serializable** adds runtime detection of read/write dependency patterns that could cause serialization anomalies. It may roll back a transaction even when no concurrent update touched the same rows — because the *logical* ordering of operations across multiple rows could not be serialized.
- Applications using either level **must implement retry logic** for SQLSTATE `40001` errors. The official guidance: *"It is important to retry the complete transaction, including all logic that decides which SQL to issue and/or which values to use."*

---

### Sources

1. PostgreSQL 18, §13.2 *Transaction Isolation* — `https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html`
2. PostgreSQL 18, §13.5 *Serialization Failure Handling* — `https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/mvcc-serialization-failure-handling.html`

## vLLM `--gpu-memory-utilization` — Default Value & Purpose

### Default Value

The default value has **changed between vLLM versions**:

| vLLM Version | Default Value |
|---|---|
| Up to v0.10.x | **0.9** (90%) |
| Current "stable" / latest docs | **0.92** (92%) |

Source snippets from the official docs show:
- **Older docs** (e.g. `docs.vllm.ai/en/v0.8.2/`, `docs.vllm.ai/en/v0.10.0/`): *"If unspecified, will use the default value of **0.9**."*
- **Latest docs** (`docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/configuration/engine_args/`): *"If unspecified, will use the default value of **0.92**."*

### What It Controls

From the official documentation:

> **"The fraction of GPU memory to be used for the model executor."**

More specifically, it controls:

- **The percentage of each GPU's total memory** that vLLM is allowed to use — encompassing model weights, activations, **and** KV cache.
- vLLM uses this fraction to **pre-allocate the GPU KV cache**. A higher value gives more KV cache space, which allows more concurrent requests.
- It is **a per-instance limit**, meaning you can run multiple vLLM instances on the same physical GPU by setting it lower (e.g., `"if you have two vLLM instances running on the same GPU, you can set the GPU memory utilization to 0.5 for each instance"`).
- The valid range is **0 to 1** (0% to 100%).

From the vLLM forums:

> *"The `gpu_memory_utilization` parameter sets the fraction of each GPU's memory that vLLM will use for model weights, activations, and KV cache."*

From the optimization docs:

> *"Increase `gpu_memory_utilization`. vLLM pre-allocates GPU cache using this percentage of memory. By increasing utilization, you can provide more KV cache space."*

### Key Practical Implications
- **Too high (e.g., 1.0):** Can cause OOM errors because vLLM may pre-allocate too large a cache, leaving no headroom.
- **Too low:** Limits the KV cache, reducing the number of concurrent sequences the model can serve.
- The fraction is consumed **first** by model weights, with the remaining budget going to the KV cache.

---

### Sources
- **Engine Arguments docs:** `https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/configuration/engine_args/` (stable) — shows default 0.92
- **Engine Arguments docs (v0.8.2):** `https://docs.vllm.ai/en/v0.8.2/models/engine_args.html` — shows default 0.9
- **vLLM Forums:** `https://discuss.vllm.ai/t/what-does-gpu-memory-utilisation-include/1651`
- **Optimization docs:** `https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/configuration/optimization/`

---

**In summary:** The current default on the latest stable docs is **0.92**, though older versions used **0.9**. It controls the **fraction of GPU memory reserved for the model executor** — specifically, how much of the GPU's memory is available for model weights + KV cache, with the remainder left as headroom to prevent OOM.

# LMCache vs. vLLM Built-in Prefix Caching: A Comparison

## 1. What Does Each One Cache?

| Aspect | vLLM Automatic Prefix Caching (APC) | LMCache |
|---|---|---|
| **Cached object** | KV cache blocks (key and value tensors from the attention mechanism) computed during the prefill phase | KV cache **chunks** — aligned segments of KV tensors (default 256 tokens per chunk), serializable byte arrays |
| **Indexing mechanism** | Token-level **radix tree** (tries) built from token IDs; each leaf is a KV block | Chunk-level **hash-based index** mapping token sequences to cached KV entries and their storage locations |
| **Granularity** | Block-level reuse; block size is determined internally by vLLM's paged attention manager | Chunk-level reuse with configurable chunk size (`--chunk-size`, default 256 tokens); can also reuse non-prefix KV at arbitrary prompt positions via **CacheBlend** |
| **Scope of reuse** | Same vLLM instance only | Cross-request, cross-session, cross-engine, and **cross-node** (with P2P and coordinator) |

**Sources:**
- vLLM APC: [docs.vllm.ai — Prefix Caching](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/design/prefix_caching/) — *"Prefix caching kv-cache blocks is a popular optimization... we cache the kv-cache blocks of processed requests, and reuse these blocks when a new request comes in with the same prefix"*
- LMCache: [docs.lmcache.ai](https://docs.lmcache.ai/) — *"LMCache is a KV cache management layer for LLM inference. It turns KV cache from a temporary state into reusable AI-native knowledge"*
- [LMCache architecture guide](https://docs.lmcache.ai/developer_guide/architecture.html) — *"Maintains an internal index mapping token sequences to cached KV entries and their locations"*
- [Non-prefix KV reuse (CacheBlend)](https://docs.lmcache.ai/) — *"Extend KV reuse beyond prefix caching by reusing cached KV blocks at any position in the prompt"*

## 2. Where Is the Cache Stored?

| Tier | vLLM APC | LMCache |
|---|---|---|
| **L0 (fastest)** | GPU VRAM — active KV blocks are always in GPU memory | GPU VRAM for the active working set; LMCache can **offload overflow** to CPU |
| **L1 (hot cache)** | **Not available.** The prefix cache lives entirely within GPU memory reservation (`--gpu-memory-utilization`). No CPU RAM tier. | **CPU DRAM** by default (configurable via `--l1-size-gb`). Uses pinned memory for efficient GPU↔CPU transfers. Optionally NVMe via GPUDirect Storage. |
| **L2 (persistent)** | **Not available.** When GPU memory fills up, old blocks are **LRU-evicted** and lost forever. | **Rich L2 ecosystem:** local disk/SSD/NVMe, S3-compatible object storage, Redis/Valkey, Mooncake, InfiniStore, NIXL, GDS. Asynchronously backed. |
| **Cross-node** | **Not supported.** Confined to a single vLLM process. | **Supported** via P2P sharing, prefill-decode disaggregation, and multi-server coordination with transports like NIXL over NVLink/RDMA/TCP. |
| **Survival across restarts/crashes** | **Lost.** Cache is in-process GPU memory with fate-sharing — if vLLM crashes, the prefix cache is gone. | **Persistent.** LMCache runs as a **standalone daemon** process, independent from the inference engine. KV cache survives engine crashes and restarts when L2 storage is configured. |

**Sources:**
- vLLM GPU-only storage: [scaleops.com — vLLM KV Cache & Prefix Cache](https://scaleops.com/blog/vllm-kv-cache-prefix-cache-gpu-memory/) — *"The prefix cache only grows. Every unique prefix... is stored until memory is full. LRU eviction starts only then, and there is no shrink-on-idle."*
- LMCache multi-tier: [docs.lmcache.ai](https://docs.lmcache.ai/) — *"Persistent, tiered KV cache offloading and reuse: Move KV caches out of GPU memory into a tiered storage hierarchy spanning CPU memory, local storage, and remote backends"*
- LMCache L2 backends: [supported storages](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/l2_storage/supported_storages.html) — *"Redis/Valkey, Mooncake, InfiniStore, S3-compatible object storage, NIXL, and GDS."*
- LMCache standalone daemon: [docs.lmcache.ai](https://docs.lmcache.ai/) — *"Engine-independent deployment: LMCache, as a standalone daemon process, manages KV cache independently from the inference engine process, so that KV cache will not be lost even if the inference engine crashes (i.e., no fate-sharing with engines)."*
- [LMCache cross-engine quickstart](https://docs.lmcache.ai/getting_started/quickstart.html) — vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM all connecting to the same LMCache server.

## 3. When Is LMCache Worth Adding?

### Advantages of LMCache

| Scenario | Why LMCache Helps |
|---|---|
| **Multi-turn conversations & long-context RAG** | System prompts and document chunks repeat across turns. LMCache's CPU RAM + disk tiers keep these hot without competing for GPU memory, which vLLM's cache is evicted under pressure. [docs.lmcache.ai](https://docs.lmcache.ai/) — *"reduces TTFT and improves throughput, especially for long-context agentic, multi-turn conversation, and knowledge-augmented workloads"* |
| **Cache persistence across engine restarts** | vLLM APC is lost on crash. LMCache's standalone daemon + L2 means the cache survives. |
| **Cross-engine / vendor-neutral caching** | Running vLLM + SGLang + TensorRT-LLM and wanting a shared cache — LMCache is the only option. |
| **Prefill-decode disaggregation across GPU nodes** | LMCache supports KV transfer over NVLink/RDMA/TCP via NIXL. vLLM APC has no cross-node capability. |
| **KV compression / quantization / encryption** | LMCache has built-in serde (fp8 halves storage, TurboQuant, AES-GCM encryption, CacheGen). vLLM APC stores raw KV blocks. [serde docs](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/serde.html) |
| **Production observability** | Per-request and token-level cache hit metrics, Grafana-ready Kubernetes metrics. vLLM exposes only a basic prefix cache hit rate. |
| **Cross-node fleet-wide cache sharing** | Redis, S3, Mooncake for shared L2 across GPU nodes. [Redis blog](https://redis.io/blog/throughput-optimizing-redis-for-l2-kv-cache-reuse/) — *"34.6% TTFT improvement with LMCache + Redis over vLLM baseline on long-document QA."* |

### Limitations of LMCache (When vLLM APC Suffices)

| Limitation | Implication |
|---|---|
| **Added infrastructure complexity** | Requires a separate `lmcache server` process, connector config, and potentially L2 setup. vLLM APC is one flag (`--enable-prefix-caching`, on by default in V1). [scaleops.com](https://scaleops.com/blog/vllm-kv-cache-prefix-cache-gpu-memory/) |
| **CPU RAM overhead** | L1 consumes host RAM. A 7B model with 10,000 tokens generates ~1.2 GB of KV cache. |
| **L2 latency penalty** | Prefetch from disk/Redis over network is slower than in-GPU hits. [Redis blog](https://redis.io/blog/throughput-optimizing-redis-for-l2-kv-cache-reuse/) — notes SLO of 2 GB/s for L2 to outrun prefill. |
| **Single-instance with high prefix reuse + sufficient GPU memory** | vLLM APC provides essentially all the benefit with zero additional infrastructure. |

### Decision Guide

| Use case | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| Single vLLM instance, shared prefixes, sufficient GPU memory | **vLLM APC alone** |
| Multi-turn chat / RAG / long-context, GPU memory constrained | **LMCache** |
| Multiple serving engines sharing cache | **LMCache** |
| Prefill-decode disaggregation across nodes | **LMCache** |
| Cache persistence across crashes | **LMCache** |
| KV compression / encryption | **LMCache** |
| Low-prefix-reuse, bursty traffic | **vLLM APC alone** — LMCache's L2 prefetch overhead may hurt |

## Summary

**vLLM's built-in prefix caching** is an excellent, zero-config optimization for single-instance deployments with shared prompt prefixes. It caches KV blocks in GPU VRAM using a radix tree, reducing TTFT for repeated prompts. Its limitation is that the cache is **GPU-bound, single-instance, and ephemeral** — evicted under memory pressure and lost on engine restart.

**LMCache** is a **multi-tier, engine-independent KV cache management layer** that extends beyond prefix caching. It stores KV chunks in a hierarchy (GPU → CPU RAM → disk/Redis/S3/remote), survives engine crashes, works across serving engines and nodes, and supports compression, encryption, and prefill-decode disaggregation. Its cost is added infrastructure complexity, CPU RAM usage, and configuring a standalone daemon.

**LMCache is worth adding when:** you need cross-engine/cross-node cache sharing, cache persistence beyond engine lifecycles, long-context or multi-turn workloads that overflow GPU memory, or KV compression/encryption. For simple single-instance vLLM deployments with high prefix reuse and adequate GPU memory, vLLM APC alone is the pragmatic choice.

# LMCache vs. vLLM Built-in Prefix Caching: A Comparison

## 1. What Does Each One Cache?

| Aspect | vLLM Automatic Prefix Caching (APC) | LMCache |
|---|---|---|
| **Cached object** | KV cache blocks (key and value tensors from the attention mechanism) computed during the prefill phase | KV cache **chunks** — aligned segments of KV tensors (default 256 tokens per chunk), serializable byte arrays |
| **Indexing mechanism** | Token-level **radix tree** (tries) built from token IDs; each leaf is a KV block | Chunk-level **hash-based index** mapping token sequences to cached KV entries and their storage locations |
| **Granularity** | Block-level reuse; block size is determined internally by vLLM's paged attention manager | Chunk-level reuse with configurable chunk size (`--chunk-size`, default 256 tokens); can also reuse non-prefix KV at arbitrary prompt positions via **CacheBlend** |
| **Scope of reuse** | Same vLLM instance only | Cross-request, cross-session, cross-engine, and **cross-node** (with P2P and coordinator) |

**Sources:**
- vLLM APC: [docs.vllm.ai — Prefix Caching](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/design/prefix_caching/) — *"Prefix caching kv-cache blocks is a popular optimization... we cache the kv-cache blocks of processed requests, and reuse these blocks when a new request comes in with the same prefix"*
- LMCache: [docs.lmcache.ai](https://docs.lmcache.ai/) — *"LMCache is a KV cache management layer for LLM inference. It turns KV cache from a temporary state into reusable AI-native knowledge"*
- [LMCache architecture guide](https://docs.lmcache.ai/developer_guide/architecture.html) — *"Maintains an internal index mapping token sequences to cached KV entries and their locations"*
- [Non-prefix KV reuse (CacheBlend)](https://docs.lmcache.ai/) — *"Extend KV reuse beyond prefix caching by reusing cached KV blocks at any position in the prompt"*

## 2. Where Is the Cache Stored?

| Tier | vLLM APC | LMCache |
|---|---|---|
| **L0 (fastest)** | GPU VRAM — active KV blocks are always in GPU memory | GPU VRAM for the active working set; LMCache can **offload overflow** to CPU |
| **L1 (hot cache)** | **Not available.** The prefix cache lives entirely within GPU memory reservation (`--gpu-memory-utilization`). No CPU RAM tier. | **CPU DRAM** by default (configurable via `--l1-size-gb`). Uses pinned memory for efficient GPU↔CPU transfers. Optionally NVMe via GPUDirect Storage. |
| **L2 (persistent)** | **Not available.** When GPU memory fills up, old blocks are **LRU-evicted** and lost forever. | **Rich L2 ecosystem:** local disk/SSD/NVMe, S3-compatible object storage, Redis/Valkey, Mooncake, InfiniStore, NIXL, GDS. Asynchronously backed. |
| **Cross-node** | **Not supported.** Confined to a single vLLM process. | **Supported** via P2P sharing, prefill-decode disaggregation, and multi-server coordination with transports like NIXL over NVLink/RDMA/TCP. |
| **Survival across restarts/crashes** | **Lost.** Cache is in-process GPU memory with fate-sharing — if vLLM crashes, the prefix cache is gone. | **Persistent.** LMCache runs as a **standalone daemon** process, independent from the inference engine. KV cache survives engine crashes and restarts when L2 storage is configured. |

**Sources:**
- vLLM GPU-only storage: [scaleops.com — vLLM KV Cache & Prefix Cache](https://scaleops.com/blog/vllm-kv-cache-prefix-cache-gpu-memory/) — *"The prefix cache only grows. Every unique prefix... is stored until memory is full. LRU eviction starts only then, and there is no shrink-on-idle."*
- LMCache multi-tier: [docs.lmcache.ai](https://docs.lmcache.ai/) — *"Persistent, tiered KV cache offloading and reuse: Move KV caches out of GPU memory into a tiered storage hierarchy spanning CPU memory, local storage, and remote backends"*
- LMCache L2 backends: [supported storages](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/l2_storage/supported_storages.html) — *"Redis/Valkey, Mooncake, InfiniStore, S3-compatible object storage, NIXL, and GDS."*
- LMCache standalone daemon: [docs.lmcache.ai](https://docs.lmcache.ai/) — *"Engine-independent deployment: LMCache, as a standalone daemon process, manages KV cache independently from the inference engine process, so that KV cache will not be lost even if the inference engine crashes (i.e., no fate-sharing with engines)."*
- [LMCache cross-engine quickstart](https://docs.lmcache.ai/getting_started/quickstart.html) — vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM all connecting to the same LMCache server.

## 3. When Is LMCache Worth Adding?

### Advantages of LMCache

| Scenario | Why LMCache Helps |
|---|---|
| **Multi-turn conversations & long-context RAG** | System prompts and document chunks repeat across turns. LMCache's CPU RAM + disk tiers keep these hot without competing for GPU memory, which vLLM's cache is evicted under pressure. [docs.lmcache.ai](https://docs.lmcache.ai/) — *"reduces TTFT and improves throughput, especially for long-context agentic, multi-turn conversation, and knowledge-augmented workloads"* |
| **Cache persistence across engine restarts** | vLLM APC is lost on crash. LMCache's standalone daemon + L2 means the cache survives. |
| **Cross-engine / vendor-neutral caching** | Running vLLM + SGLang + TensorRT-LLM and wanting a shared cache — LMCache is the only option. |
| **Prefill-decode disaggregation across GPU nodes** | LMCache supports KV transfer over NVLink/RDMA/TCP via NIXL. vLLM APC has no cross-node capability. |
| **KV compression / quantization / encryption** | LMCache has built-in serde (fp8 halves storage, TurboQuant, AES-GCM encryption, CacheGen). vLLM APC stores raw KV blocks. [serde docs](https://docs.lmcache.ai/mp/serde.html) |
| **Production observability** | Per-request and token-level cache hit metrics, Grafana-ready Kubernetes metrics. vLLM exposes only a basic prefix cache hit rate. |
| **Cross-node fleet-wide cache sharing** | Redis, S3, Mooncake for shared L2 across GPU nodes. [Redis blog](https://redis.io/blog/throughput-optimizing-redis-for-l2-kv-cache-reuse/) — *"34.6% TTFT improvement with LMCache + Redis over vLLM baseline on long-document QA."* |

### Limitations of LMCache (When vLLM APC Suffices)

| Limitation | Implication |
|---|---|
| **Added infrastructure complexity** | Requires a separate `lmcache server` process, connector config, and potentially L2 setup. vLLM APC is one flag (`--enable-prefix-caching`, on by default in V1). [scaleops.com](https://scaleops.com/blog/vllm-kv-cache-prefix-cache-gpu-memory/) |
| **CPU RAM overhead** | L1 consumes host RAM. A 7B model with 10,000 tokens generates ~1.2 GB of KV cache. |
| **L2 latency penalty** | Prefetch from disk/Redis over network is slower than in-GPU hits. [Redis blog](https://redis.io/blog/throughput-optimizing-redis-for-l2-kv-cache-reuse/) — notes SLO of 2 GB/s for L2 to outrun prefill. |
| **Single-instance with high prefix reuse + sufficient GPU memory** | vLLM APC provides essentially all the benefit with zero additional infrastructure. |

### Decision Guide

| Use case | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| Single vLLM instance, shared prefixes, sufficient GPU memory | **vLLM APC alone** |
| Multi-turn chat / RAG / long-context, GPU memory constrained | **LMCache** |
| Multiple serving engines sharing cache | **LMCache** |
| Prefill-decode disaggregation across nodes | **LMCache** |
| Cache persistence across crashes | **LMCache** |
| KV compression / encryption | **LMCache** |
| Low-prefix-reuse, bursty traffic | **vLLM APC alone** — LMCache's L2 prefetch overhead may hurt |

## Summary

**vLLM's built-in prefix caching** is an excellent, zero-config optimization for single-instance deployments with shared prompt prefixes. It caches KV blocks in GPU VRAM using a radix tree, reducing TTFT for repeated prompts. Its limitation is that the cache is **GPU-bound, single-instance, and ephemeral** — evicted under memory pressure and lost on engine restart.

**LMCache** is a **multi-tier, engine-independent KV cache management layer** that extends beyond prefix caching. It stores KV chunks in a hierarchy (GPU → CPU RAM → disk/Redis/S3/remote), survives engine crashes, works across serving engines and nodes, and supports compression, encryption, and prefill-decode disaggregation. Its cost is added infrastructure complexity, CPU RAM usage, and configuring a standalone daemon.

**LMCache is worth adding when:** you need cross-engine/cross-node cache sharing, cache persistence beyond engine lifecycles, long-context or multi-turn workloads that overflow GPU memory, or KV compression/encryption. For simple single-instance vLLM deployments with high prefix reuse and adequate GPU memory, vLLM APC alone is the pragmatic choice.

## Repeatable Read vs Serializable in PostgreSQL

### Anomalies Prevented by Each Level

Per **Table 13.1** in the [PostgreSQL 18 documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html#XACT-ISOLEVEL-TABLE), here is the full picture:

| Phenomenon | Repeatable Read | Serializable |
|---|---|---|
| Dirty Read | Not possible | Not possible |
| Nonrepeatable Read | Not possible | Not possible |
| Phantom Read | **Not possible** (PostgreSQL provides a stronger guarantee than the SQL standard requires) | Not possible |
| **Serialization Anomaly** | **Possible** | **Not possible** |

Both levels prevent dirty reads, nonrepeatable reads, and phantom reads. The **only difference** is that **SERIALIZABLE additionally prevents serialization anomalies**, while REPEATABLE READ does not.

### What Is a Serialization Anomaly?

As the docs describe:

> *The result of successfully committing a group of transactions is inconsistent with all possible orderings of running those transactions one at a time.*

**Concrete example** from the documentation ([Section 13.2.3](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html#XACT-SERIALIZABLE)):

With a table `mytab` containing `(class=1, value=10), (class=1, value=20), (class=2, value=100), (class=2, value=200)`:

- Transaction A reads `SUM(value)` for `class=1` → gets **30**, then inserts a row `(class=2, value=30)`.
- Transaction B reads `SUM(value)` for `class=2` → gets **300**, then inserts a row `(class=1, value=300)`.
- Both commit at REPEATABLE READ → both succeed, but the final state could not arise from any serial execution order. At SERIALIZABLE, one of them is rolled back.

### How the Difference Is Implemented

- **REPEATABLE READ** uses **Snapshot Isolation**. It gives each transaction a stable snapshot from the start of the transaction. It will prevent phantom reads and nonrepeatable reads, but it does not check whether the *combination* of concurrent transactions produces an inconsistent result.

  > *"The Repeatable Read isolation level is implemented using a technique known in academic database literature … as *Snapshot Isolation*."*

- **SERIALIZABLE** builds on Snapshot Isolation and adds **predicate locking** ( Serializable Snapshot Isolation per [Ports 2012](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/biblio.html#PORTS12)). It monitors read/write dependencies among concurrent transactions and, when those dependencies could lead to a serialization anomaly, it aborts one of the conflicting transactions:

  > *"Serializable … works exactly the same as Repeatable Read except that it also monitors for conditions which could make execution of a concurrent set of serializable transactions behave in a manner inconsistent with all possible serial executions of those transactions."*

  Predicate locks appear as `SIReadLock` in `pg_locks`.

### Serialization Failure SQLSTATE

Both REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE can raise serialization failures, and they always carry the same SQLSTATE code:

> **"…serialization failures (which always return with an SQLSTATE value of '40001')"**

([Section 13.2.3](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html#XACT-SERIALIZABLE), quoted under [Section 13.5](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/mvcc-serialization-failure-handling.html)):

> *"Such an error's message text will vary according to the precise circumstances, but it will always have the SQLSTATE code **40001** (`serialization_failure`)."*

Common error messages include:
- `ERROR: could not serialize access due to concurrent update` (REPEATABLE READ, when the transaction tries to modify a row changed by another committed transaction)
- `ERROR: could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions` (SERIALIZABLE, when predicate-lock analysis detects a potential serialization anomaly)

### Key Takeaway

In PostgreSQL, the practical difference between REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE is:

1. **REPEATABLE READ** = Snapshot Isolation — safe against dirty reads, nonrepeatable reads, and phantom reads, but **not** against serialization anomalies.
2. **SERIALIZABLE** = Serializable Snapshot Isolation (predicate locking) — adds detection of serialization anomalies at the cost of some overhead and a higher chance of hitting a `40001` failure requiring a full transaction retry.

Both levels require applications to handle `SQLSTATE 40001` and retry the entire transaction.

---

**Sources:**
- [PostgreSQL 18: 13.2. Transaction Isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html) (Sections 13.2.2 and 13.2.3)
- [PostgreSQL 18: 13.5. Serialization Failure Handling](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/mvcc-serialization-failure-handling.html)

<acknowledgement>: Understood: Find official PostgreSQL documentation passages that support or contradict the two-part claim: (1) PostgreSQL's default transaction isolation level is REPEATABLE READ, and (2) at that level, phantom reads can occur.




I was able to get evidence on the second part of the claim (phantom reads at REPEATABLE READ) before hitting the tool budget. The first query (default isolation level) did not return results. Here is what I found:

---

**Claim Part 1: "PostgreSQL's default transaction isolation level is REPEATABLE READ"**

❌ **Contradicted** — The web fetch budget was reached before this question could be answered. However, this is widely known from the PostgreSQL docs: the default is `READ COMMITTED`, not `REPEATABLE READ`. The user's claim of `REPEATABLE READ` as the default is **false**.

---

**Claim Part 2: "at that level [REPEATABLE READ] phantom reads can occur"**

❌ **Contradicted by official documentation.**

From *PostgreSQL 18.6 Documentation*, section 13.2 (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html):

1. **Table 13.1 — Transaction Isolation Levels**, for the `Repeatable Read` row:
   > "Phantom Read — **Allowed, but not in PG**"

2. Section 13.2.2 ("Repeatable Read Isolation Level"):
   > "The Repeatable Read isolation level only sees data committed before the transaction began; it never sees either uncommitted data or changes committed by concurrent transactions during the transaction's execution. **…This is a stronger guarantee than is required by the SQL standard for this isolation level, and prevents all of the phenomena described in Table 13.1 except for serialization anomalies.**"

3. Section 13.2:
   > "The table also shows that **PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read implementation does not allow phantom reads.** This is acceptable under the SQL standard because the standard specifies which anomalies must not occur at certain isolation levels; higher guarantees are acceptable."

4. The same section notes:
   > "The Repeatable Read isolation level is implemented using a technique known in academic database literature and in some other database products as **Snapshot Isolation**."

---

**Summary:**

| Claim | Verdict | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Default level is REPEATABLE READ | **False** — PostgreSQL defaults to `READ COMMITTED` | (budget hit before fetch; well-known from docs) |
| Phantom reads can occur at REPEATABLE READ | **False** — PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read (implemented as Snapshot Isolation) explicitly **prevents** phantom reads | PostgreSQL 18.6 docs, §13.2 & §13.2.2 |

**Both parts of the claim are false.** The official documentation shows that PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ level is stricter than the SQL standard minimum — it prevents phantom reads, unlike the SQL standard's Repeatable Read definition.
